# HydroModPy documentation

<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/index.html -->
# HydroModPy

A Python toolbox for automated, reproducible, catchment-scale modelling of shallow groundwater. One TOML file takes a catchment from its digital elevation model to a calibrated model: where the water table sits, where it reaches the ground, which streams it keeps flowing, and how all of it changes with the seasons.

Important

This documentation follows the 2.0 pre-release line, version 2.0.0a5. Install it with `pip install --pre hydromodpy`. Projects written for version 1 should stay pinned to an exact tag such as `v1.0.0`.

## What HydroModPy does

Physically based groundwater models are expensive to deploy at the scale of a catchment: data, mesh, parameters, calibration and post-processing rarely follow the same path from one site to the next. HydroModPy turns the construction, the run, the calibration and the analysis of a shallow groundwater model into one workflow that can be replayed on many catchments, with the same inputs and the same outputs.

It automates the steps that take the most time:

1. Catchment extraction from a digital elevation model.
1. Forcing and observations: recharge, climate series, groundwater heads, gauged discharge, mapped stream networks and intermittency.
1. Mesh and vertical discretisation suited to shallow basement aquifers, with parameters given per zone or per cell, in steady state or in transient.
1. Calibration that combines heads, discharge and the extent of the stream network to constrain the hydraulic properties.
1. Outputs that can be reopened, stored with their provenance and the licence of the data they come from, then drawn as figures or exported to standard formats.

First a FloPy-driven MODFLOW-NWT toolbox, HydroModPy now runs several solvers behind one configuration validated by Pydantic, and stores its runs in a columnar layout (DuckDB catalog, Zarr fields, Parquet tables) that makes them reproducible and easy to inspect.

## What’s new

# Understand HydroModPy

HydroModPy simulates the groundwater of a catchment from its relief, its geology and its rainfall. It computes where the water table is, where it reaches the surface, which streams it feeds and how all this changes through the seasons. Every result depends on assumptions. This part of the site says which ones, and how to read the maps without over-interpreting them. It needs no prerequisite, and every technical term links to the Glossary.

## What you find here

## When not to use this

HydroModPy is built for shallow groundwater at the scale of a catchment. Do not rely on it for these cases, or only with an expert.

- Deep or confined aquifers, and large sedimentary basins. The model describes a shallow aquifer whose top rises and falls with the recharge. See the limits in the theory.
- Aquifers where water moves mostly through conduits, such as karst. The model treats the ground as a continuous porous medium.
- Floods and river hydraulics. In the default setup there is no water level, no flood and no travel time in the channel (How the model makes streams).
- Decisions at the scale of a field or a plot. A cell is 75 m wide in example 04, and a map is read at the scale of the hillside.
- Water quality, unless a transport computation has been set up for it. The maps of this part of the site are about water, not about what it carries.
- Climate projections taken as forecasts. The model replays the forcing it is given. A projection is only as good as the climate data and the evaluation behind it.
- A single result taken as certain. Without a validation on data that the calibration has not seen, read a result as an indication (What “validated” means here, How sure is the model?).

## One catchment as a common thread

The pages rely on example 04 of HydroModPy: the Nançon catchment (Ille-et-Vilaine, 64.6 km²), simulated from 2000 to 2002 with a monthly step. The example shows how the seepage network grows in winter and shrinks in summer, and how the hydraulic conductivity and the specific yield of the aquifer are calibrated against the mapped network and against the flow measured at the outlet.

This is a demonstration example. Its results illustrate how to read the outputs. They are not a study of the catchment.

## Who this is for, and where to go next

- You decide, you fund or you read a report based on HydroModPy: start with In five minutes, then What the model computes and Reading the results.
- You judge the quality of a result: How sure is the model?, What “validated” means here, Where the data come from and Can I check what was run?.
- You are building a model: the staircase builds one step by step, and the reference describes each parameter.
- You are installing the tool for the first time: Get started.

# Can I check what was run?

Yes. A result of HydroModPy is not only a map. It comes with the record of what produced it, and that record can be read without the person who made the run. This page lists what is kept, and what you can ask for when you receive a result. The word for this record is provenance.

## What a run keeps

Every finished run has its own folder. In it you find:

- The configuration that ran. A frozen copy of the TOML file, not the file as it is today. The run is stored with a fingerprint of that configuration, so two runs can be told apart or matched.
- A provenance record, `provenance.json`. It names the version of HydroModPy, the commit of the code it came from, the version of Python, the machine, the packages installed, and the solver with its version and the SHA-256 checksum of its binary.
- A manifest, `manifest.json`, written last. It lists the input files the configuration declared, each with its checksum, the output files, the period, the geometry and the scores. A run folder without a manifest is an incomplete run by construction.

A checksum is a short code computed from the content of a file. If one byte changes, the code changes. A checksum that matches is a strong sign that the file is the one that was used.

## What the project keeps

At the root of a project, the lockfile `hydromodpy.lock` pins what fed the runs: the version of the code, the solver binaries with their checksums, the versions of the file formats, and every cached input with its checksum and size. It is written after a successful run when the project has a data cache. If the write fails, a warning says so and the run is not lost.

The lockfile answers a wider question than the manifest of one run: in what state was the whole data cache before the run?

## What you can ask for

| You want to know | You ask for | Command |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What exactly was run? | The summary of the run: solver, status, duration, size of the grid, parameters, scores and the start of the configuration fingerprint. The frozen configuration and the provenance record are files of the run folder, which you can open. | `hmp catalog show <run>` |
| What differs between two runs? | The comparison of the two. | `hmp catalog diff <run A> <run B>` |
| Whether the data cache is still the one that was used | A check of the cache against the lockfile. | `hmp dev lock verify` |
| To replay a run with exactly the same data | A run that refuses any fresh download and stops on a checksum that does not match. | `hmp run --frozen <file>` |
| To rerun a stored run, changing one setting | A rerun from the stored configuration. | `hmp catalog rerun <run> --set path=value` |
| Whether the log of operations was altered | A check of its chain of hashes. | `hmp audit verify` |

The options of each command are in the command reference.

## What this does not prove

A record shows what was run. It does not show that the run was a good idea. Two identical records mean two identical computations, and a correct computation can still rest on a poor assumption or a poor dataset. For that, read What “validated” means here and Where the data come from.

A note on recorded data: the record contains the name of the machine and the user. Remove them before you share a run folder outside your organisation if that matters to you.

## Where to go next

- Where the data come from: the origin of each input.
- hmp run: `--frozen` runs from the cache, with no download.
- Glossary: the terms of this page.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/understand/glossary.html -->
# Glossary

The terms used in this part of the site, with a short definition. Where a term has a setting in the configuration file, the second line of its entry says where. A term can be cited from another page with `{term}`unconfined aquifer``.

On the pages of this part, a term underlined with dots shows its definition when you point at it or move the keyboard focus to it. On a touch screen, tap it once for the definition and a second time to open this page.

**actual evapotranspiration**: The part of the potential evapotranspiration that is really taken, limited by the water available in the soil. Abbreviated AET. The soil reservoir computes it.
**aquifer**: Rock or sediment saturated with water, which lets the water move and stores it.
**aquifer thickness**: Depth of the modeled layer below the ground surface: 30 m in example 04. This is an assumption. The depth to water table cannot exceed it. In the file: `domain.depth_model.thickness`.
**available water capacity**: Water that roots can take from the soil, in mm. Abbreviated AWC. It sets how much water the soil keeps before it lets water pass to the water table. In the file: `flow.sinks_sources.recharge.soil.ru`.
**baseflow**: The part of the river flow that comes from the aquifer. In the model: the water that leaves the aquifer through the drains, summed over the catchment.
**BD Topage**: The reference hydrographic network of France, published by Sandre. HydroModPy can download it as a mapped network. It is not the same product as the BD TOPO. In the file: `data.hydrography`.
**BD TOPO**: The topographic database of the French national mapping agency (IGN). Example 04 takes its mapped network from the permanent reaches of this database. In the file: `data.hydrography`.
**calibration**: Tuning of the model parameters (here K, then Sy) so that its results look like observations. A calibrated result is not, for that reason, validated (see validation). In the file: `calibration.protocol.name`.
**catchment**: Surface that gathers water toward a single exit point, the outlet. In HydroModPy, it is drawn from the relief and the position of the outlet. In the file: `geographic.catchment.catch_def`.
**cell**: One square of the computation grid: 75 m wide in example 04. The model computes one value per cell, and the maps count cells. The set of cells that cuts the model area is the mesh.
**conductance**: How freely a drain passes water for a given rise of the water table. Unless you declare one, the model derives it from the hydraulic conductivity and from the thickness of the clogging layer of the drain bed. In the file: `solver.drain_bed_thickness_m`.
**criterion**: A number that a calibration drives toward a target, over many trials. It must behave well along that search. The same number, only read, is a diagnostic.
**depth to water table**: Distance between the ground and the top of the water table, in meters, never negative. Figure: `watertable_depth_map`, in `display.figures`.
**diagnostic**: A number that you read to describe a result, put in a report or use to compare two runs. It is not driven to a target. See criterion.
**digital elevation model**: Map of the ground elevation, on a regular grid. Abbreviated DEM. In the file: `data.dem`.
**downslope distance**: Distance a cell travels along the slope before it reaches a network. Written \(D_{so}\) from the simulated network to the mapped one, and \(D_{os}\) in the opposite direction. It measures how far apart two networks are.
**drain**: Condition that lets water leave the aquifer when the water table reaches its elevation, never the reverse. In example 04, the drains are placed at the ground surface and their capacity (the conductance) is deduced from K. In the file: `flow.active_bc`.
**ensemble**: A set of runs of the same model with different parameters or inputs. The spread between the runs shows how much a result depends on those choices. See How sure is the model?.
**equifinality**: Several different sets of parameters reproduce the observations about equally well. The calibration then cannot say which set is right. See How sure is the model?.
**excess**: A cell where the model puts a stream and the map has none. See valid.
**forcing**: What drives the model through time: the recharge, or the rainfall and the potential evapotranspiration from which a soil reservoir computes it.
**GR4J**: A rainfall-runoff model that treats a catchment as a single unit. HydroModPy can calibrate it in place of the distributed model.
**groundwater**: Water that fills the pores of the ground below the water table.
**Hub’Eau**: The public interface to French water data. HydroModPy can download the discharge measured at a gauging station from its hydrometry service. In the file: `data.hydrometry`.
**hydraulic conductivity**: How easily the subsurface lets water pass, written K, in m/s. It cannot be measured at the scale of a catchment: it is calibrated. In the file: `flow.param.K.field.value`.
**hydraulic head**: Elevation of the water table at a point. It is the unknown that the model computes in each cell; the depth to water table is deduced from it. In the file (initial state): `flow.ic.h.type`.
**hydrograph**: Curve of the flow as a function of time.
**indicative**: A reliability label. No field measurement was compared with this result. See reliability label.
**initial condition**: State of the water table at the start of the computation. In example 04, a first month in steady state provides it. In the file: `flow.ic.h.type`, `flow.first_period_steady`.
**interfluve**: The higher ground between two valleys. The water table is deep under it.
**intermittent flow**: A stream that flows for only part of the year. On the intermittence map: a cell that flows at some time steps of the year, not at all of them.
**lockfile**: The file `hydromodpy.lock` at the root of a project. It pins the input data by checksum and records the version of the code and of the solver binary. See Can I check what was run?.
**mapped network**: Streams drawn on a map (here, the permanent reaches of the BD TOPO). It is a reference to compare and calibrate against, not an input to the flow computation. In the file: `data.hydrography`.
**mesh**: The set of cells that cuts the model area. The word grid means the same thing when the cells are squares.
**missing**: A cell where the map has a stream and the model puts none. See valid.
**MODFLOW 6**: The groundwater flow code of the United States Geological Survey (USGS). It is the solver of example 04. HydroModPy also runs MODFLOW-NWT, an older code of the same family, and a Boussinesq solver written for HydroModPy.
**NANCON station**: The gauge at the outlet of the Nançon catchment. Example 04 compares the discharge measured there with the simulated one. In the file: `data.hydrometry`.
**NSE**: Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency: compares simulated and measured flow. 1 is a perfect match, 0 is the same as predicting the mean of the measurements, and a negative value is worse. The “log” variant computes it on the logarithms to give weight to low flows. In the file: `calibration.protocol.transient_metric`.
**numerical check**: A reliability label. An internal check of the computation, independent of the calibration. See reliability label.
**objective**: What a calibration tries to reach: one or several criteria, each computed on an observation such as the stream network or the discharge. In the file: `calibration.objective_blocks.metric`.
**outlet**: Exit point of the catchment, where the flow is measured. In the file: `geographic.catchment.x_outlet`.
**percent bias**: Volume gap between the simulated flow and the measured flow, as a percentage of the measured volume. Abbreviated PBIAS. It is positive when the model underestimates, that is when it is too dry, and negative when it overestimates.
**perennial flow**: A stream that flows all year. On the intermittence map: a cell that flows at every time step of the year.
**persistence**: Share of the time steps during which a cell flows, over the whole simulation.
**potential evapotranspiration**: Amount of water that the atmosphere could take back from a soil that is well supplied with water. Abbreviated PET. In the file: `data.etp`.
**provenance**: The record of what produced a result: the version of the code, the solver, the input files and their checksums. See Can I check what was run?.
**reach**: A stretch of stream between two points.
**reanalysis**: A gridded estimate of past weather or hydrology, made by running a model over all the observations available. SIM2 is one.
**recharge**: Water that reaches the water table from the soil. It is supplied, or computed by a soil reservoir. In the file: `flow.sinks_sources.recharge`, `data.recharge`.
**reliability label**: One of three words that tell how far a result can be trusted: numerical check, calibrated and indicative. They are used under every figure of Reading the results.
**resolution**: The size of one cell, 75 m in example 04. A feature smaller than the resolution is not drawn.
**runoff**: Water that reaches the stream without passing through the water table. In example 04, it is given to the model as data and is added to the drainage to form the simulated flow. In the file: `data.runoff`.
**scoring window**: Period over which the calibration compares simulated and measured flow. In example 04, 2001 and 2002; the year 2000 is used as spin-up. In the file: `calibration.protocol.scoring_window`.
**seepage**: Cell where the water table reaches the ground surface and where water leaves the aquifer. Rebuilt on read from the head and the ground surface (or from the surface excess of a Boussinesq run); nothing to set.
**seepage threshold**: Fraction of its own recharge that a cell must give back to count as seepage: 0.01 % by default. Another threshold changes the network maps. In the file: `calibration.outputs.<name>.tau_specific_ratio`.
**SIM2**: Météo-France reanalysis on an 8 km grid, which supplies rainfall and potential evapotranspiration to the soil reservoir. In the file: `data.etp`.
**simulated network**: Extension downstream, following the slope of the terrain, of the cells where the aquifer gives water back to the surface. It does not result from a hydraulic river computation.
**soil reservoir**: Simple daily balance: the soil fills with rain, empties by evapotranspiration and lets the surplus pass to the water table. In the file: `flow.sinks_sources.recharge.soil`.
**specific yield**: Share of the rock volume that drains when the water table falls, written Sy, without dimension. It sets the speed at which the water table empties and refills. In the file: `flow.param.Sy.field.value`.
**spin-up**: Start of the simulation that is not scored, while the initial state of the model fades out. In example 04, the year 2000. In the file: `calibration.protocol.scoring_window`.
**spring**: A place where groundwater comes out of the ground. A seepage cell is a spring of the model.
**steady state**: Computation where nothing changes with time: the recharge is a constant mean. In the file: `flow.flow_regime`.
**stream head**: The upstream end of a stream, where it starts to flow. The heads dry up first in summer.
**stress period**: Interval over which the forcing is held constant. It is one month in example 04. The solver may cut it into smaller time steps. In the file: `simulation.time.step_value`, `simulation.time.substeps_per_period`.
**time step**: On the maps and curves of this part of the site, the unit of time of the results: one month in example 04. Strictly, the month is a stress period and the solver may cut it into smaller steps.
**TOML**: The plain-text format of the configuration file. One TOML file describes a whole run. The files of example 04 are walked through in Get started.
**transient**: Computation where the recharge and the water table vary from one time step to the next. In the file: `flow.flow_regime`.
**trial**: One run of the model with one set of parameter values, tried by a calibration. A calibration runs many trials and keeps the best.
**uncertainty**: How far a result could be from the truth. See How sure is the model?.
**unconfined aquifer**: Aquifer whose top is not trapped under an impermeable layer: it rises and falls freely with the recharge. HydroModPy targets this type of aquifer.
**valid**: A cell where the simulated network and the mapped network both pass. With excess and missing, it gives the three classes of the confusion map.
**validation**: A comparison of a model with measurements that the calibration has not seen. See What “validated” means here.
**visible flow**: Minimum flow that a cell must carry to count as “flowing” on the persistence maps: 1 L/s by default. It is a convention. In the file: `calibration.outputs.<name>.extent.visible_flow`.
**water budget**: What enters the aquifer (recharge), what leaves it (drainage) and the change in storage. Its closure is a numerical check of the solver.
**water table**: The top of the groundwater: the level below which the ground is saturated. The model computes its elevation in every cell, as the hydraulic head.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/understand/how-sure.html -->
# How sure is the model?

Not completely, and no groundwater model is. This page says where the doubt comes from, what HydroModPy reports about it, and how to read a result with it in mind. The word for this doubt is uncertainty.

## Where the doubt comes from

- The inputs. The rain that reaches the water table, the relief, the position of the mapped streams and the flow measured at the gauge all carry errors. A model cannot be more precise than its inputs.
- The parameters. The hydraulic conductivity K and the specific yield Sy cannot be measured at the scale of a catchment. They are found by calibration, and calibration does not give a single answer.
- The structure. The model is a simplification: in example 04, one layer of constant thickness, one value of K for the whole aquifer, a monthly step and cells of 75 m (What the model computes). Two models with different simplifications can both look right.
- The observations. The mapped network holds only the reaches someone chose to draw, and a gauge has its own error.

## Several answers can look equally good

Example 04 shows it. When K varies, the simulated discharge at the outlet does not tell the values apart, but the extent of the seepage does (Reading the results). This is equifinality: different sets of parameters reproduce the observations about equally well. A good fit to the discharge alone does not tell which set is right.

This is why HydroModPy can calibrate on several observations at once, such as the discharge and the stream network, and why it reports a range beside each calibrated value instead of a single number.

## What HydroModPy reports

A range beside the calibrated value. After the search, HydroModPy reports the range of values that the search tried and that scored almost as well as the best one. It reads this range off the trials already run. It is not a probability distribution: a probability needs an error model on each observation, and the scores used here do not provide one. Three methods exist: a free one that reads the trials already run, one that restarts the search from other starting points and can find a second optimum, and one that disturbs each parameter a little to see which ones trade off against each other. [calibration.uncertainty] lists them.

A narrow range has two possible causes. The parameter may be well constrained, or the search may never have tried far from the best value. The range alone does not tell which.

An ensemble band. When you run the same model many times with different parameters or inputs, the `ensemble_band` figure draws the median of the runs and a band between two percentiles of them. The wider the band, the less the runs agree. It shows the spread of the runs that you chose to make, so it is a lower bound of the doubt, not a full measure of it. The ensemble is only as varied as you made it.

Honest labels. Under every figure of Reading the results, a reliability label says whether the result was checked, calibrated or only indicative.

## What example 04 does not show

Each figure of example 04 comes from one run. None carries a range or a band. The example is a demonstration of how to read the outputs, and it does not claim the precision of a study.

## Reading a result with the doubt in mind

1. Ask what was calibrated. A result that the calibration sought is expected to look right.
1. Ask whether another set of parameters would give the same fit. If the report shows a range, look at its width.
1. Ask what the model leaves out (What the model computes) and whether it matters for your question.
1. Prefer a comparison to an absolute value. The difference between two scenarios, run with the same inputs and assumptions, is more robust than either run alone.
1. Read the verification and the validation of the model (What “validated” means here).

## Where to go next

- What “validated” means here: what has been checked, and how.
- [calibration.uncertainty]: the ranges, method by method.
- Glossary: the terms of this page.

# In five minutes

One map, five sentences. If you read nothing else, read this page.

Fig. 1 Look at: the blue trunk that flows all year and the orange ends that dry up first. Does not show: which reaches dry up in the field, or any other year.

`flow_intermittence_map`, year 2002, demonstration model of example 04.

1. HydroModPy computes, for a whole catchment and for each month, the level of the groundwater under the ground, from the relief, the properties of the rock and the rain that reaches the water table.
1. Where that level reaches the ground, water comes out: these points are the springs of the model.
1. The streams are what these springs feed downhill. On the map, a stream is blue when it flows all year, orange when it flows part of the year, and grey when it never flows.
1. This map is a demonstration, not a study of the catchment: it was not compared with observations of dry reaches, so it is labelled indicative. Other results carry the labels calibrated or numerical check, and the label says how far to trust them (reliability label).
1. Every result depends on assumptions and on data, so read its caption, its label and the limits before you decide anything with it.

<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/understand/network-metrics.html -->
# Scoring a simulated stream network

A model makes a network of streams. A map draws another one. To say how well they agree, you need a number, and there are several ways to get one. This page tells what each way answers, and separates two uses that look alike: a diagnostic, which you read, and a criterion, which a calibration drives to a target.

It has no equation and no name of a metric. The equations of the downslope method are in Downslope distance between two networks. The names of the metrics, and how to write them to a file, are in [analysis.comparison] and [calibration.outputs].

## The two networks

- The simulated network is not computed by a river model. The model finds the cells where the water table reaches the ground, and the network extends these seepage cells downstream, following the slope of the ground (What the model computes).
- The mapped network is the network drawn on a map. In example 04, it is the permanent reaches of the BD TOPO.

A score never gives the truth about the model. It gives the distance between two drawings, and each drawing has its own errors. The mapped network holds the reaches someone chose to draw. The simulated one depends on the cell size, on the threshold that decides what counts as seepage and, in a run that changes with time, on the month you look at.

## Four ways to compare two networks

| Way | What it compares | What it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overlap of lines | The two networks as lines | What share of the length of each network lies near the other? |
| Overlap of cells | The cells of the simulated network and the cells the map crosses | How many cells do the two share, miss or add? |
| Straight-line distance | The same two sets of cells | How far apart do the two patterns sit, as the crow flies? |
| Downslope distance | The two networks, along the paths the water takes | How far must the water walk to get from one network to the other, in each direction? |

### Overlap of lines

Both networks are treated as lines, with a small tolerance around each. A stretch of one network is matched when it lies inside the tolerance of the other, and missing or extra when it does not. The result is a set of lengths and shares, and the largest gap between the two drawings.

Use it to compare two maps, such as the observed network and the one derived from the relief. It does not read the model cells and it does not know where the water goes: a stretch near the map counts as matched even if the water leaves it in another valley.

### Overlap of cells

This way works on the cells of the model. A cell is simulated when the model puts water there, and mapped when the map crosses it. Then the cells are counted:

- the cells in both sets (the overlap);
- the mapped cells the model did not reach (missing);
- the simulated cells away from the map (extra).

From these counts come two shares: the coverage, the share of mapped cells that the model found, and the precision, the share of simulated cells that are on the map. A low coverage says the simulated network is under-developed. A low precision says it spreads where the map has nothing. Two combined scores fold the two shares into one number.

One detail changes the numbers. This way marks every cell the map touches, so a line becomes a ribbon of cells. The downslope method draws the map one cell wide, like the simulated network. The cell counts of the two ways are therefore not comparable.

### Straight-line distance

Same cells, but now the question is how far. For each simulated cell, the code measures the straight distance to the nearest mapped line. For each mapped cell, it measures the distance to the nearest simulated cell. That gives two numbers, one per direction, each summarised by its mean, its median, its high values and its maximum.

A distance gives more than a count. Two simulated cells that miss the map, one by a cell and one by a kilometre, count the same in the overlap and weigh very differently here. But the distance is straight, so it ignores the relief. It crosses a ridge as if it were not there.

### Downslope distance

This is the method of [Abhervé et al., 2023]. The distance is the length of the path the water follows downslope, not the straight line.

- From each simulated cell, how far does the water go before it meets the mapped network? The mean is the excess side: if the model makes too much stream, simulated water travels far to reach a map that has no stream near it.
- From each mapped cell, how far does the water go before it meets the simulated network? The mean is the deficit side: if the model makes too little stream, mapped streams have no simulated stream to flow into.

The two directions are kept apart on purpose, because they tell opposite stories. The calibration uses the gap between them, in absolute value, as its cost. It also keeps their average as a diagnostic, and the three classes of cells that the confusion map draws: valid, excess and missing. The maps are explained on Comparison with the mapped network.

The average walk has a validity length. When it is longer than that length, the two networks are further apart than the map can be trusted to place them, and the score says little about the hydrogeology. By default the length is two cells, widened by the positional accuracy you declare for the map. A violation is a warning unless you ask for an error with `on_roptim_violation`.

## Diagnostic or criterion

The same number can be read, or it can be minimised. The two uses have different needs.

A diagnostic describes. You read it, put it in a report, compare two runs with it. It has no need to be symmetric or monotonic. The four ways above all work as diagnostics, and the overlap and straight-line ways are only diagnostics.

A criterion is a cost that a search drives to a target, over many trials. It must behave well along that search. For the downslope method, the cost is the gap between the excess side and the deficit side, and its target is zero. Zero does not mean that the two networks coincide. It means that the simulated network has as much excess as deficit. A model can reach it with a large excess and a large deficit that cancel, which is why the confusion map and the average walk stay on the table next to it.

Why not use a straight-line distance as the criterion?

- A straight-line distance crosses divides. A seepage cell on the far side of a ridge counts as close to the map, when its water leaves into the other valley. The downslope distance follows the water, so it cannot cheat that way.
- A mean straight-line distance has no sign. It cannot say whether the model has too much stream or too little, and a search needs that sign to know which way to move the parameter.
- A count of cells moves in steps, and its best value depends on how the map is drawn on the grid.

Why not minimise the average walk, then? It is large at both ends of a parameter sweep, so it does have a minimum in the middle. But nothing puts that minimum at the point where excess and deficit balance. They are two different estimators. Use the average walk to compare two structures that are both balanced, and the gap to find the parameter inside one structure.

## What moves a score

Before you compare two scores, check that they were computed the same way.

- The seepage threshold. A cell counts as seepage only above a share of its own recharge (seepage threshold). Another threshold changes the simulated network, and so every score.
- The way the map is drawn on the grid. The rule for the mapped network (`calibration.outputs.<name>.observed_rasterization`) moves the number of mapped cells and where they sit. A one-cell gap can come from this rule and not from the model.
- The cell size. Distances are in metres, but they are measured from cell to cell. A coarse grid cannot place a stream closer than about a cell.
- The state that is read. A steady run gives one network. A run that changes with time gives one network per time step. A calibration can score one state, or two bounds: the complete network and the permanent one. A cell is counted as flowing above a visible flow.
- The map. The permanent network of a map does not hold the temporary streams. An “excess” can be a real stream the map ignores.

## Where to go next

- Reading the results: the maps that show these scores for example 04.
- How the model makes streams: how the model makes a network.
- Downslope distance between two networks: the equations, the assumptions and the limits of the downslope method.
- [calibration.outputs]: the network criterion of a calibration.
- [analysis.comparison]: the overlap and distance scores of several runs.

# Reading the results

This page is a reading guide to the main outputs of example 04 (the Nançon catchment, see Understand HydroModPy). For each map or curve: what it shows, how to read it, the pitfalls, and what makes it reliable or only indicative. For a first look, In five minutes is shorter. Every figure and every number on this page comes from one run, described in Where these figures come from.

## Three rules before reading

1. One map, one month. Snapshot maps show a single month. In example 04, it is October 2002, the driest month of the series according to the comments in the configuration file: so the map shows the case where the network is at its smallest. A map of a wet month would show much more.
1. A cell is 75 m wide. A stream fills one cell in width, and we count cells, not metres of stream. The maps are read at the hillslope scale (see resolution).
1. Calibrating is not validating. In a calibrated run, the simulated network and the discharge are what the calibration tried to reproduce (Calibration in two stages). Their agreement is expected. A validation compares with measurements that the calibration has not seen (What “validated” means here).

## In one table

Three reliability labels are used, and each figure below carries one:

- An internal check of the computation, independent of the calibration.
- The agreement was sought by the calibration, so it is not independent evidence.
- No field measurement was compared with this result in the example.

| Figure | Question | Label |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water table depth | How deep is the water table? | |
| Seepage cells | Where does water come out of the ground? | |
| Comparison with the mapped network | Does the model find the mapped streams? | |
| Flow persistence | Which reaches dry up, and when? | |
| Simulated against observed discharge | Are the volume and the season of the discharge right? | |
| The water budget | How much water comes in and goes out? | for the closure, for the values |

## Water table depth

Fig. 2 Look at: where the water table is close to the ground (dark) and where it is deep (pale). Does not show: a measured level, or any depth beyond the 30 m of the model.

`watertable_depth_map`, October 2002. Color bar: “Depth of the water table below land surface (m)”.

What the map shows. The distance between the ground and the top of the water table, in metres, for each cell. It is derived from the hydraulic head: ground elevation minus water table elevation, set to zero when the water table reaches the ground. This is the depth to water table.

How to read it. Dark blue: the water table is close to the ground, which is where water can come out. Pale yellow: the water table is deep. The water table is close to the ground in the valley bottoms and deep under the interfluves (the higher ground between two valleys), which the map shows clearly.

Pitfalls.

- The scale stops at the model thickness. The modelled aquifer is 30 m thick (an assumption, see What the model computes). A pale yellow colour means “at the bottom of the model”, not “at exactly 30 m”. In this run, about 5.2% of the cells of the catchment (598 of 11,488) have, in October 2002, the water table within 0.5 m of the bottom (computed from the stored data of the run).
- The pattern follows the relief by construction. K is uniform and the drains are at the surface: a water table close to the ground in the valleys is the expected result of the setup, not a discovery.
- This is a monthly mean state, not the level of a given day.

Reliability. Indicative. Example 04 does not compare this map with piezometer levels. The overall shape is consistent with the physics of the setup; the absolute depths are not validated.

## Seepage cells

Fig. 3 Look at: the blue cells, where the water table reaches the ground and water comes out. Does not show: streams, or how much water comes out of a cell.

`seepage_map`, October 2002. Legend: “seepage (112 cells)”, “no seepage (11,376 cells)”.

What the map shows. The cells where the water table reaches or exceeds the ground surface, one by one, with no extension downstream. This is the raw state of the model: in this run, 112 cells of the 11,488 cells of the catchment in October 2002.

How to read it. Each blue cell is a point where water appears, a spring. These are not streams: isolated cells or short lines of cells are normal. The pale cells outside the catchment outline are in the model margin and are not counted.

Pitfalls.

- This is not the network. The simulated network extends the seepage cells downstream (Comparison with the mapped network). The two maps do not use the same definition of a cell that “seeps”, so their cell counts cannot be compared.
- The extent depends on K. Example 04 observes this: when K varies, the simulated discharge does not tell the values apart, but the seepage area does. This is why the calibration of K relies on the network.
- A cell is a yes or no state. It says nothing about the flow that comes out.

Reliability. Indicative. The map is consistent with the computation, but no observation of a spring or a seep is compared with it in the example.

## Comparison with the mapped network

Fig. 4 Look at: how much yellow and red remain around the dark blue. Does not show: which of the two networks is right, or the months other than October.

`seepage_network_confusion_map`, October 2002. Dark blue “valid” (297 cells), yellow “excess” (62), red “missing” (174).

What the map shows. Each cell belongs to a single class:

- valid (dark blue): the simulated network and the mapped network both pass through this cell;
- excess (yellow): only the model puts a stream there;
- missing (red): only the map puts a stream there;
- grey: no stream.

The mapped network is made of the permanent reaches of the BD TOPO, placed on the model grid. The simulated network is the downstream extension of the seepage cells, following the slope of the terrain (What the model computes).

How to read it. A perfect agreement would be all dark blue: we look for little yellow and little red at the same time. In this run, the model misses 174 of the 471 mapped cells (37%), mostly at the upstream ends and on the side branches (red), and adds 62 cells (yellow) in a few short stretches beside the main axis. A plain count of cells does not say whether a small gap comes from a good fit or from two errors that cancel each other: the map shows it.

Fig. 5 Look at: the cells far from the mapped network, in the darker classes. Does not show: whether the mapped network itself is complete.

`downslope_distance_map`, October 2002. Distance traveled downslope by each simulated cell before it reaches the mapped network: 0 to 75 m (299 cells), 75 to 500 m (54), 500 to 1000 m (10), more than 1000 m (0).

The second map no longer counts the cells that coincide: it measures how far each one is off. A simulated cell that coincides with the mapped network is at 0 m. The four classes are those of the reference paper (Abhervé et al., 2023). Its counts cannot be compared one to one with those of the previous map: the two maps do not count exactly the same cells. How the scores are built is on Scoring a simulated stream network.

Pitfalls.

- The mapped network holds only the permanent reaches. An “excess” can be a real temporary stream that the map ignores, or an error of the model: the map does not settle it.
- One month only, October 2002.
- The threshold matters. A cell is counted as seepage if it returns more than 0.01% of its own recharge (the seepage threshold, setting `calibration.outputs.<name>.tau_specific_ratio`). Another threshold moves the three classes.
- The mapped network is placed on the 75 m grid with a transfer rule: a one-cell gap can come from the transfer and not from the model. This run uses the default rule (`calibration.outputs.<name>.observed_rasterization`): it places each stream head of the map on a nearby cell, within 100 m, and draws the rest of the reach down the slope of the model, so that field ditches below a head do not count as model errors (How the model makes streams).

Reliability. Calibrated. K was adjusted so that this network looks like the map: a good agreement is the goal reached, not an independent validation. The method itself is published and peer reviewed (Abhervé et al., 2023).

## Flow persistence

Fig. 6 Look at: the dark cells that flow almost all the time and the light ones that flow only in the wettest months. Does not show: the discharge of a reach, or any year-to-year change.

`flow_persistence_map`, January 2000 to December 2002. Color bar: “Timesteps flowing (%)”. Title: 772 cells ever flowing in the 36 months.

What the map shows. For each cell, the share of the 36 months during which it flows (the persistence). Dark blue: almost always. Light blue: only in the wettest months. Grey: never.

Fig. 7 Look at: the orange stream heads, which dry up first, and the blue trunk that keeps flowing. Does not show: which reaches really dry up in the field.

`flow_intermittence_map`, year 2002. Blue “perennial” (336 cells), orange “intermittent” (128), gray “dry” (11,024).

The second map classes each cell over a single calendar year (2002): perennial if it flows all 12 months, intermittent if it flows some months, dry if it never flows. The stream heads are orange: they dry up first.

How to read it. A cell “flows” if it is downstream of a seepage cell and carries at least 1 L/s of water coming from the aquifer (the visible flow, setting `calibration.outputs.<name>.extent.visible_flow`). This is not the same meaning as on the seepage map, which counts only the exit points.

Pitfalls.

- The time step is monthly. A reach that dries up for two weeks does not appear. “Intermittent” means: dry at least one month in the year.
- The 1 L/s threshold is a convention. The parameter documentation notes that no value is agreed on: thresholds from 1 to 3 L/s are used in the field, and Zanetti et al. (2024) use 10 L/s for a simulated discharge. Another threshold changes the layout.
- The three years include the first year, 2000, which serves as the spin-up of the model. And three years say nothing about the year-to-year variability.
- The year 2002 is the driest year of the series according to the comment in the example. So the orange reaches are orange for a dry year.
- The two maps do not cover the same duration (36 months against 12): a cell can be dark on one and orange or grey on the other without any contradiction.

Reliability. Indicative. The only network compared with a map is the permanent network of October. The example uses no field observation of dry reaches: the distinction between perennial and intermittent is a model output, not verified.

## Simulated against observed discharge

Fig. 8 Look at: whether the blue line follows the black dashes in season and in volume, in the gray window. Does not show: daily discharge, or a period the calibration has not used.

`hydrograph_log_nse`. Blue line: total simulated discharge. Black dashes: discharge observed at the NANCON station. Gray area: scoring window, 24 of the 36 months. Logarithmic vertical axis, in m³/s.

What the curve shows. The monthly discharge at the outlet, simulated and measured at the NANCON station (the daily measurement is averaged over each month). The simulated discharge is the total: what leaves the aquifer through the drains, plus the runoff given as input data, since this model has no stream network. The figure itself states: “total discharge only: this run stores no groundwater / surface split”. This curve is a hydrograph.

How to read it. The axis is logarithmic: low flows weigh as much as floods, and a gap of 0.1 to 0.2 m³/s is as visible as a gap of 1 to 2. This is intended: the calibration of Sy uses a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency computed on the logarithms, which gives weight to the recessions (Calibration in two stages). The grey area is the scoring window (2001 and 2002); 2000, the spin-up year, is not scored.

The scores of this run. The run metrics table covers the 36 months, spin-up included: Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) 0.68, and volume bias (PBIAS) +20.5%. A positive PBIAS means that the model underestimates: here the simulated discharge is lower than the measured one, so the model is too dry. Recomputed on the 2001 and 2002 window only, from the stored series, the same measures give an NSE of about 0.94 and a bias of about +8%. The first year therefore weighs a lot: the model clearly underestimates the discharge of 2000.

To put these numbers in context, Moriasi et al. (2007) propose, for catchment models at the monthly time step, to judge an agreement “satisfactory” from an NSE of 0.50 and a volume bias of ±25%, and “good” from 0.65 and ±15%. This scale comes from other catchment models: it gives a reference, not a threshold specific to HydroModPy.

Pitfalls.

- Runoff is an input. It is given to the model as data: only the groundwater part is computed. A good agreement of the total does not prove that the groundwater part is right.
- Sy was calibrated on this window. A high NSE on 2001 and 2002 shows that the calibration worked, not that the model would predict another period.
- A good discharge agreement does not tell K values apart. Several K values give a similar discharge (see Seepage cells). This is equifinality, and How sure is the model? comes back to it.
- The monthly time step smooths the flood peaks and says nothing about the discharge of a given day.

Reliability. Calibrated. The season and the volume are well reproduced over the calibrated period. The test that would count, a period or a catchment not used for calibration, is not in the example.

## The water budget

Fig. 9 for the closure, for the values. Look at: the winter months, when recharge exceeds drainage, and the summer months, when drainage continues alone. Does not show: the change in storage, or the water outside the delineated catchment.

`flux_timeseries`. Blue: recharge, which enters the aquifer. Red: drainage, which leaves it. In m³/s, over the delineated catchment. Title: “positive = into the aquifer”.

What the curve shows. The two fluxes that cross the aquifer, month by month: recharge (positive, it enters) and drainage through the drains (negative, it leaves). The change in storage is not plotted: it is the difference between the two curves. Together they form the water budget.

How to read it.

- In winter, the aquifer fills up. In January 2001, recharge reaches 3.1 m³/s for a drainage of 1.7 m³/s: the difference goes into storage.
- In summer, it slowly empties and feeds the streams. From July to September 2002, recharge is almost zero (0.01 to 0.02 m³/s) and drainage continues at 0.24 to 0.29 m³/s. This is the baseflow: the water stored in winter that sustains the streams in dry periods.
- The first month is in steady state, so recharge and drainage are roughly equal there.

Pitfalls.

- m³/s, not mm. The figure can also be plotted as a water depth, which is easier to compare with rainfall: see the options of `flux_timeseries` in the catalog of figures.
- The catchment and not the domain. The model extends beyond the catchment (a margin of 10% more area); the figure says “frame: the delineated catchment”.
- The `water_budget` bar chart has another use: it adds up the flows stored at each time step: it is a sum of flows, not a volume.

Reliability. Two things to tell apart. The closure of the budget is a numerical check: the run reports a budget error of 0.00%, meaning that the solver conserves water. It does not say that the model is right. The values are what was put in as input (the recharge) and what K and Sy allow to store and release: they stay indicative as long as the recharge has not been compared with another estimate.

## Other figures you will meet

A report made with HydroModPy can contain figures that example 04 does not use. The reading rules below hold for any run. Each figure has an entry in the catalog of figures.

| Figure | How to read it | Take care |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water-table elevation (`piezometric_map`) | Elevation of the water table at one time step, in the same datum as the ground. Water flows from high to low, across the lines of equal height. | It is the head of the model, not a measurement, unless the report overlays measured levels. |
| Piezometric head, simulated against observed (`piezo_timeseries_sim_obs`) | The simulated level at one well, against the level measured there, time step after time step. | A model can follow the season and miss the level by metres: look at both. Check that the well was not used to calibrate. |
| Flow-duration curve (`duration_curve`) | The flow on the vertical axis, and on the horizontal axis the share of time during which that flow is exceeded. The left end is the floods, the right end the low flows. | It forgets the order of events: two very different years can give the same curve. |
| Simulated against observed scatter (`scatter_one_to_one`) and residuals (`residuals`) | Each dot is one time step. On the 1:1 line the model is exact. The residuals are the simulated value minus the observed one. | A residual that has a pattern, such as always positive in winter, shows a missing process. A random residual is the best case. |
| Mass-balance closure error (`mass_balance_error`) | The gap between what the solver put in and took out, in percent, time step by step. It should stay small and steady. | It checks the arithmetic of the solver only. A small error means the solver converged, not that the model is right (label Numerical check). |
| Ensemble envelope (`ensemble_band`) | The median of a set of runs and a band between two percentiles. The wider the band, the less the runs agree. | The band shows the spread of the runs you made. It is not a full measure of the uncertainty (How sure is the model?). |

## Where these figures come from

The eight figures are real outputs of the run `nancon_intermittence_mf6_calibrated_transient_storage`. It was produced on 2026-10-09 by `hmp run run_calibration.toml` with HydroModPy 2.0.0a4, from the files of example 04. It is the run promoted from trial 8 of the second calibration stage: K = 7.96e-5 m/s, then Sy = 0.045. The mapped network is placed on the grid by the default `heads` rule, as described under Comparison with the mapped network.

The images are redrawn from the stored run, the way `hmp viz show` draws them, for instance `hmp viz show nancon_intermittence_mf6_calibrated_transient_storage seepage_map`. The titles carry no run name, and the legends are in English. The repository keeps, for every image, the run, the command and the option that made it, in `tools/docs/figures/figures.toml`.

Each figure exists in a light and a dark version, and the page shows the one that matches the theme. The dark version recolours the background, the texts and the light greys, such as the dry cells of the intermittence map and the ground of the seepage map.

To draw a figure of an existing run again, at another date, see the catalog of figures and hmp viz.
