<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/understand/stream-network.html -->
# How the model makes streams

HydroModPy does not draw rivers. It computes a water table. Where the water table reaches the ground, water leaves the aquifer. Those exits are the sources of the streams, and the stream network is what they generate downhill.

This page follows that chain: the exits, the network they generate, why the network breathes with the seasons, and how it is compared with a map. It uses no equation. The equations are in Downslope distance between two networks.

## Where the water table reaches the ground

With the drainage condition, the model places a drain in every cell that has no fixed head, at the elevation of the ground. A drain lets water out when the water table rises to the ground surface, and in that direction only. Water that has left does not come back, and a river does not feed the aquifer in this setup.

Fig. 10 Look at: the cells where the head of the water table is above the ground line: only they release water. Does not show: how much water a drain releases, or a real catchment.

How much water a drain passes for a given rise of the water table depends on the hydraulic conductivity K of the cell: the more permeable the ground, the more freely it drains. The drain is not a free exit. Unless you declare a conductance, the model derives it from K and from the thickness of the clogging layer of the drain bed (the thin, less permeable film that lines a stream bed). The drain follows K, and this is why the extent of the network carries information on K.

In example 04, drains are the only way water leaves the aquifer: the list of boundary conditions of the model names the drain and nothing else.

## A seepage cell is a point, not a stream

A cell where the aquifer gives water back to the ground is a seepage cell. It is a point where water appears, a spring, and not a stretch of river. Isolated cells and short lines of cells are normal.

Fig. 11 Look at: the isolated blue cells, each a point where water leaves the aquifer. Does not show: any stream, which is drawn in the next step.

The `seepage_map` of example 04, October 2002, the driest month of the series according to the comments of the example file (Reading the results).

The map above shows the raw state of the water table. For the network, the model asks a slightly different question: how much water leaves the cell. A cell counts as a source when it gives back more than a small share of the mean recharge over its area (the seepage threshold). The test is made on the flux because the water budget fixes the flux, while “the head touches the ground” is a geometric condition that changes a lot when the drain conductance moves. The setting is `tau_specific_ratio`.

## Seepage cells draw the network

The water that leaves the aquifer in a seepage cell flows downhill over the ground. The simulated network is every cell this water goes through, from each source as far as the slope leads it. The slope is the one of the digital elevation model, read on the model cells. Pits (cells lower than all their neighbours, where water would be trapped) are filled first, so that every cell has a way down.

Fig. 12 Look at: the order of the steps: sources, routing downstream, then a threshold that gives the active network. Does not show: a river volume. The network is a view drawn after the computation, and the water budget fields stay untouched.

Fig. 13 Look at: the blue trunk and the orange upstream ends. Does not show: which reaches dry up in the field.

The `flow_intermittence_map` of example 04, year 2002, from the calibrated run. Blue cells flow every month of the year, orange cells some months, gray cells never.

Three things follow from this construction.

- The network has no width, depth or velocity. In the drain setup, the model does not compute the river. A cell “flows” means that the aquifer feeds it, directly or from upstream. There is no water level, no flood and no travel time in the channel. The routed streams described below are the exception.
- Its shape depends on the relief. A coarser cell size or a different digital elevation model moves the paths. A stream occupies one cell, so a map is read at the scale of the hillside, not of the field (see resolution).
- A flow threshold keeps only cells that carry water. On the flow maps, a downstream cell flows only if the water routed to it reaches a minimum discharge (the visible flow). It is a convention. See visible flow.

## Why the network grows in winter and shrinks in summer

The recharge feeds the water table. In winter the recharge is large and the water table rises. More cells reach the ground and give back water above the threshold, and the water of each of them reaches farther downhill. In summer the recharge is small, the water table drops, and the sources retreat toward the valley bottoms. The upstream ends of the streams dry up first, and only the reaches fed by the lowest water table keep flowing.

The model repeats this at every stress period, a month in example 04. For each period it finds the seepage cells, draws the network, and counts the cells that flow. Over a year, a cell is then:

- perennial, if it flows at every time step of the year;
- intermittent, if it flows at some time steps and not all;
- dry, if it never flows.

Example 04 shows it. The comment of its configuration file says that the seepage cells and the active network expand and contract with the wet winters and the dry summers. The maps of the example draw October 2002 because it is the driest month of the record.

Two limits come with a monthly step. A reach that dries up for two weeks does not appear, and “intermittent” means dry for at least one time step.

## What sets the size of the network

Two quantities compete: how fast the ground carries water away (K) and how much water arrives (the recharge). If the ground is permeable compared with the recharge, the water table stays deep, and the network retracts into the valley bottoms. If it is not, the water table reaches the ground on the hillsides, and the network reaches the upper slopes. The extent of the network is a function of the ratio of K to the recharge. This is what the calibration on the stream network exploits (Downslope distance between two networks). In example 04, the discharge at the outlet does not tell values of K apart, but the extent of the seepage does.

## What else can take water out

The drain is the way the model lets the aquifer produce streams. Other conditions exist, and they answer other questions. They should not be confused with it.

| You want | The model uses | What you give | What the model computes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The model to decide where water emerges | A drain at the ground (the default) | Nothing, or a drain conductance (`flow.bc.<name>.value`) | Where the water table reaches the ground, and how much water leaves |
| To impose the water level of a river on known cells | A fixed-head stream boundary (`stream` in `flow.active_bc`) | The head, on the cells tagged as river | The exchange with the aquifer, in either direction |
| The water that leaves to travel down a river | A routed stream network ([flow.sinks_sources.sfr]) | The reaches and their properties | The routing of the water along the reaches |
| A lake whose level moves | A lake package ([flow.sinks_sources.lakes]) | A footprint and a stage-volume-area table | The stage and the exchange with the aquifer |

The stream boundary is not available with MODFLOW-NWT. It prescribes a level: it supposes you know where the river is and how high its water stands. A drain supposes neither. Choose the drain when the network is the question.

Fig. 14 Look at: the direction of the arrows. With a stream boundary, you impose the water level of the river and the model computes the exchange. Does not show: the drain, which decides by itself where water comes out.

Whatever the condition, the network is read from the same quantity: the water the aquifer releases to the surface in each cell, summed over every condition that releases water.

## Comparing with a mapped network

A mapped network is the set of streams drawn on a map, such as the permanent reaches of the BD TOPO. It is a reference. The model never receives it.

- It is not burned into the relief.
- It does not place drains.
- It does not set K.

The model is built from the relief, the geology, the recharge and the thickness. The map is read afterwards, to score and to draw (Reading the results). You declare it as a data source ([data.hydrography]), and the code treats it as a diagnostic, not as a model input.

To compare the two networks, the lines of the map are first placed on the model cells. By default HydroModPy keeps only the places where the map says a stream starts, and lets the slope of the model draw the path below them (`observed_rasterization`). Field ditches and rectified reaches follow paths that a model on a digital elevation model cannot reproduce, and drawn cell by cell they would count as errors of the model.

Then the comparison goes both ways, along the slope.

- From each cell of the simulated network, follow the slope down until you meet the mapped network. A long walk means the model makes a stream where the map has none: an excess.
- From each cell of the mapped network, follow the slope down until you meet the simulated network. A long walk means the model misses a stream of the map: a deficit.

When K increases, the simulated network retracts and the deficit grows. When K decreases, the network spreads and the excess grows. The calibration looks for the value of K where the two mean walks are equal. Scoring a simulated stream network says how to read these scores, and Downslope distance between two networks defines the distances.

Calibrating on the map is not validating against it. The agreement of a calibrated run with the map is what the calibration looked for.

## What the network is not

- It is not a river model. In the drain setup there is no hydraulics in the channel.
- It is not a budget term. The water that leaves the aquifer is the release of the drains. The network is a way to read where it leaves and where it goes.
- It is not a measurement. It becomes evidence only through a comparison with a map that the calibration has not seen.
- It is not a line. It is a set of cells, one set for each time step.

## Where to go next

- Reading the results: the maps of example 04, one by one.
- Scoring a simulated stream network: how a simulated network is scored.
- [calibration.outputs]: the network criterion of a calibration.
- Downslope distance between two networks: the distances and the criterion, with equations.
- How water leaves the aquifer: how water leaves the aquifer.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/understand/what-it-computes.html -->
# What the model computes

HydroModPy solves the flow of water in the saturated part of the ground of a catchment, the part that lies below the water table. For each cell of the map and each time step, it computes the height of the water table (the hydraulic head), given how much water arrives from the soil, how fast the ground carries and stores it, and where it can leave. Everything else (water table depth, seepage, flow, stream network) is derived from this.

Terms that link to the Glossary are defined there.

## In one diagram

In example 04, the stream network is not an input. The model produces springs, and the network is derived from these springs. The mapped streams and the flow measured at the outlet are used to compare and to calibrate (see Calibration in two stages).

## What it computes

| Result | What it means in the model | Where to read it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The water table | The hydraulic head of each cell, hence the elevation of the water table and its depth below the ground (never negative). | Water table depth |
| Seepage | The cells where the water table reaches the ground surface. Water leaves the aquifer there through a drain placed at the surface. | Seepage cells |
| Baseflow | The water that leaves the aquifer through the drains, summed over the whole catchment: the groundwater part of the flow at the outlet. | Simulated against observed discharge, The water budget |
| Intermittence | For each month, the cells that flow. Over a year: always (perennial), sometimes (intermittent), never (dry). | Flow persistence |
| The budget | What enters the aquifer (the recharge), what leaves it (the drainage) and the change in the stock of water. | The water budget |

A note on the “simulated network”. A cell where the aquifer gives water back to the surface is a point where a stream appears, not a stretch of river. The model extends these cells downstream, following the slope of the ground, down to the outlet. This extension is the simulated network, the one that is compared with the map of streams. In this setup, which is the default, there is no hydraulic computation of the river. The How the model makes streams page shows the options that route the water along declared reaches.

## What it is computed from

| Data | Role | In example 04 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relief | It gives the ground surface, hence the elevation at which water leaves. It delimits the catchment from the outlet and tells where the water flows downstream. | A digital elevation model, 75 m cells; 64.6 km² catchment traced from the outlet. |
| Geology | It sets how easily water moves (the hydraulic conductivity K) and the volume of water released when the water table drops (the specific yield Sy). One value for the whole aquifer, or one per zone of a geological map ([flow.param]). | A single value of K and a single value of Sy for the whole catchment: the geological map is not used. Both are calibrated (Calibration in two stages). |
| Recharge | The water that reaches the water table. It is provided (a series from a file, or SIM2 data from Météo-France), or computed by a soil reservoir from rainfall and potential evapotranspiration (theory). | A single monthly recharge series for the whole catchment, and a runoff series (data sources). |
| Thickness | The depth of the aquifer below the ground surface. It is an assumption, not a measurement. | 30 m everywhere. |
| Observations | The mapped network and the flow measured at the outlet are not part of the physical computation. They are used to compare the results and to calibrate K and Sy. | The permanent stretches of the BD TOPO and the NANCON station. |

Where each dataset comes from is on Where the data come from.

In the drain setup of example 04, the solver is MODFLOW 6, the reference code of the United States Geological Survey (USGS). HydroModPy prepares the data, runs MODFLOW 6 and reads its results back. Other solvers exist, see Other solvers below.

## The assumptions to keep in mind

Each row says what the model assumes and what that changes when reading the maps. The rows marked “example 04” describe that configuration file, not the software: another model can lift them. The rows marked “drain setup” hold for the drain condition used in example 04 and not for the other conditions of How the model makes streams.

| Assumption | Consequence for reading |
| --- | --- |
| Unconfined aquifer, a single layer of constant thickness below the ground (example 04: 30 m). | No deep aquifer and no layers of different kinds. The depth of the water table cannot exceed the thickness of the model. |
| Uniform K and Sy (example 04). | The pattern of the water table mostly follows the relief. Geological contrasts are not represented. |
| Water leaves through drains placed at the ground surface, in one direction only (drain setup). | Water that leaves does not return to the aquifer. A river does not feed the aquifer in this setup. |
| The efficiency of a drain depends on K and on the thickness of the clogging layer of the drain bed (How the model makes streams). | The larger K is, the more the aquifer is drained. This is why the seepage network carries information on K. |
| Identical recharge over the whole catchment, monthly average (example 04). | No variation of rainfall from one hillside to another, or from one day to another within the month. |
| One stress period per month, and the first month in steady state. | The first month sets the starting state. The documentation of the setting that cuts a month into several steps, `simulation.time.substeps_per_period`, states that a single step per month changes the monthly flow by 4 to 28 % compared with a refined computation, depending on the case. |
| No hydraulic model of the rivers (drain setup). | No water level, flood or propagation. A stream that “flows” means: the aquifer feeds it. |
| The simulated network follows the slope of the ground downstream of the seepage cells. | Its shape depends on the digital elevation model and on the cell size. |
| If the recharge comes from the soil reservoir (theory): the soil ignores the height of the water table, and snow counts as rain. | A high water table does not reduce the soil reserve. The documentation of the soil reservoir judges it unsuitable for a snow-covered catchment. Available with MODFLOW 6 only. |

The intended range of validity of the project, as the scientific documentation states it: shallow aquifers at catchment scale, unconfined or weakly confined, where the relief, the stream network and the geology organise the flow. Large deep sedimentary basins and coupled surface and atmosphere models fall outside this range. The limits are listed in the theory of the flow problem, and the page What “validated” means here says how far the model has been tested.

## Other solvers

Example 04 uses MODFLOW 6. HydroModPy runs two other flow solvers behind the same configuration file: MODFLOW-NWT, an older code of the same family, and a Boussinesq solver that is part of HydroModPy. They do not support the same boundaries or the same meshes. Lakes, reservoirs and routed streams, for example, need MODFLOW 6. A lumped rainfall-runoff model, GR4J, can be calibrated in place of the distributed model. The list of solvers says what each one supports. Every statement about the solver on this page is about example 04.

## Calibration in two stages

K cannot be measured at catchment scale. The model of example 04 infers it, a step called calibration, in two stages, with the method published by Abhervé et al. (2023, Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 27, 3221-3239). The example file also cites their 2025 article for the second stage:

1. K is adjusted, in steady state, until the simulated seepage network matches the mapped network.
1. Sy is adjusted, in monthly transient state, against the flow measured at the outlet, with the first year used as spin-up.

Direct consequence: in a calibrated run, the map of the network and the flow curve show what was adjusted. Their agreement is expected. It does not prove on its own that the model is right. The page Reading the results comes back to this point map by map. The settings of this method are those of [calibration.protocol].

## What it does not compute

- River hydraulics in the drain setup: water level, floods, propagation, storage in the riverbed. The routed stream option of MODFLOW 6 adds a routing of the water along declared reaches (How the model makes streams).
- Surface runoff, unless it is provided as data (example 04) or, with the soil reservoir, for the sealed part of the surface. The groundwater model does not produce floods.
- The unsaturated zone in detail. The soil reservoir is a simple budget (usable reserve, evapotranspiration, delay before reaching the water table), not an infiltration model.
- Abstractions, unless they are declared as wells in the configuration.
- Water quality. Solute transport and particle tracking exist separately and are not covered here. Neither are lakes and reservoirs, which exist as an option of MODFLOW 6.
- The future by default. The model replays the forcings it is given. For a climate projection, projection data must be provided. Comparison with measurements then no longer makes sense.

## The limits of this example

- A single catchment and three years: the result says nothing about the variability from one year to the next.
- The figures and the numbers of Reading the results come from one calibrated run, described at the end of that page. A new run gives different values.
- No comparison with piezometer levels or with field flow observations: example 04 does not use them.
- A 75 m cell: a map is read at the scale of the hillside, not of the field.

Next: Reading the results. To know when not to use the model, see the end of the door index.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/understand/what-validated-means.html -->
# What “validated” means here

The word validated is used loosely. In this documentation it has a narrow meaning. This page separates four kinds of evidence, because they do not answer the same question.

## Four kinds of evidence

| Evidence | The question it answers | What it does not answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Numerical verification | Does the code solve the equations it claims to solve? | Whether the equations describe your catchment. |
| Calibration | Can the parameters be tuned so that the model reproduces the observations? | Whether the model would predict anything it was not tuned on. |
| Validation | Does the calibrated model reproduce measurements it has not seen, on another period or on another catchment? | Whether it holds under conditions unlike all those tested. |
| Peer review | Have independent experts read the method and found it sound? | Whether a given run is right. |

### Numerical verification

HydroModPy checks its solvers against references that do not come from HydroModPy: a closed-form solution, a published MODFLOW 6 example, a manufactured solution, or a parameter that a calibration must find again. Each check is a test, run in continuous integration, and Validation lists every one with the reference it uses and the threshold it must stay under. On the maps of Reading the results, the label refers to this kind of evidence, for instance the closure of the water budget.

### Calibration

A calibration adjusts parameters until the results look like observations. When a calibrated result agrees with those observations, the agreement is what the calibration looked for. It is not independent evidence. The label says so.

### Validation

A validation compares the model with measurements that the calibration did not use, such as a period held out, or a neighbouring catchment. This is the test that counts for a prediction. Example 04 contains none: the same years are used to calibrate and to look at the results, and the figures say so. A study that relies on HydroModPy for a decision should include one.

The papers and the catchments where HydroModPy has been used are listed in Applications and papers.

### Peer review

The two-stage method of calibration used in example 04 is published and peer reviewed (Abhervé et al., 2023, Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 27, 3221-3239). The technical note that describes the toolbox is published and peer reviewed too (Gauvain et al., 2026, Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 30, 5571-5592), but it describes version 1.0. The review did not cover the code of version 2 that this site documents. A published method does not make a particular run right, and a run is no more reliable for being made with a reviewed method.

## What this means for a decision

- A result labelled Numerical check is safe to read as a statement about the solver.
- A result labelled Calibrated shows that the calibration worked.
- A result labelled Indicative is a model output that no measurement has confirmed.
- None of the three labels is a validation. If a decision depends on a result, ask for a validation on data that the calibration did not see, and read How sure is the model?.

## Where to go next

- Validation: every test of the code against a reference.
- How sure is the model?: how far a result can be wrong.
- Can I check what was run?: how to check what produced a result.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/understand/where-the-data-come-from.html -->
# Where the data come from

A result is only as good as its inputs. This page names the data that HydroModPy can read, who produces them, how fine they are, and what to do about their licences. It is written for a reader who must judge a result, not for one who must download data: the keys that declare the data are in [data].

## What the model reads

The model reads its data from files that you give it, or from public providers that it can download from. Example 04 uses files of the project. The last column says what it used.

| Data | Producer | Form and fineness | Example 04 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Relief (digital elevation model) | The national mapping agency (IGN): BD ALTI at 25 m, or RGE ALTI at 1 m or 5 m | Regular grid | A raster file with 75 m cells |
| Geological map | The geological survey (BRGM): a map at 1:1,000,000, or the harmonised map at 1:50,000 | Polygons, with the scale of the map as limit | Not used: one value of K for the catchment |
| Mapped streams | Sandre and the French Biodiversity Office (BD Topage); the Copernicus land service (EU-Hydro); OpenStreetMap. A file of your own works too, such as the BD TOPO of IGN | Lines | The permanent reaches of the BD TOPO, from a file of the project |
| Discharge at a gauge | The public interface Hub’Eau (French Biodiversity Office and BRGM), for the national hydrometry | Daily series at a station | The NANCON station, averaged by month |
| Observed flow state of small streams | Hub’Eau, from the national low-flow observatory | Visits at stations | Not used |
| Groundwater levels | Hub’Eau, from the national portal for groundwater data (ADES) | Series at wells | Not used |
| Rain and evapotranspiration | Météo-France, the SIM2 reanalysis | 8 km grid | The recharge and the runoff are series given as files of the project |
| Climate projections | Météo-France, distributed through the DRIAS portal (Explore2) | 8 km grid | Not used |
| Sea level | The naval hydrographic service (SHOM), tide gauges | Series at a gauge | Not used |

This list is read from the data sources that the code knows. The generated page Data sources gives the complete list of the sources, the producer of each and the section of the file that takes it.

## Fineness matters

Each input has its own scale, and the model cannot be finer than the inputs that control a result.

- The rain comes on an 8 km grid. The catchment of example 04 is 64.6 km², so a few grid points cover it. In example 04, one monthly recharge series serves the whole catchment: no difference between two hillsides.
- The relief sets where water leaves the ground, and the cell of the model is 75 m. A map is read at the scale of the hillside (resolution).
- A geological map at 1:50,000 draws zones that are hundreds of metres wide. It does not tell the conductivity of a particular field.
- A mapped stream network draws what someone chose to draw, with a positional error. The score of a network takes it into account only if that error is declared (Scoring a simulated stream network).

## Licences

Public data do not all carry the same licence. The licence of each source, when the code knows it, is listed on the generated page Data sources. Where the code does not know it, the page says so. It does not guess.

Three rules follow from the way the code records licences.

- A file you provide has the licence you declare. The model cannot know the licence of your file. You state it in a small companion file next to the data.
- A result inherits from its inputs. A run states the combined licence of what it read, and writes it into the attributes of its field files and the footers of its tables. If one input has no known licence, the run states undetermined. A run cannot promise more than its least known input allows.
- Undetermined is not forbidden. It means that nobody recorded the terms. Read the terms of the producer before you reuse or redistribute a result.

This page is not legal advice. Cite the producer of the data that a result relies on.

## Can I check which data were used?

Yes. Each run lists its input files with their checksums, and the project can pin the whole data cache. See Can I check what was run?.

## Where to go next

- Data sources: every source, its producer and its licence.
- [data]: declare or download the data of a project.
- What “validated” means here: why a good input is not a validated result.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/index.html -->
# Get started

Install HydroModPy, run a first model in under a minute, then climb example 04 in six files. The first file of the staircase is the shortest configuration that solves. The last one computes the recharge from a soil reservoir.

## Quick start

Five commands. Run them in a terminal where Python 3.11 to 3.13 is available, and in a virtual environment if you keep one (Install has the variants for Windows and conda).

```
pip install --pre hydromodpy
hmp workspace init
hmp run ~/hydromodpy/projects/example/run_demo.toml
hmp example add 04
hmp run ~/hydromodpy/projects/04_streamflow_intermittence_in_transient/step1_minimal.toml
```

What each command does, and how long it took on a clean machine (a 2-core laptop, fast connection):

| Command | What it does | Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pip install --pre hydromodpy` | Installs the package and its geospatial wheels, 1.3 GB in a clean environment. | about 2 min |
| `hmp workspace init` | Makes `~/hydromodpy`, with 27 data folders and the project `example`. | 8 s |
| `hmp run .../run_demo.toml` | Solves a synthetic 1 km square with MODFLOW-NWT. No download, except the solver itself the very first time. | 9 to 15 s |
| `hmp example add 04` | Fetches the Nançon catchment, 92 MiB, most of it a regional DEM. Cached by content: a second workspace costs nothing. | 20 s |
| `hmp run .../step1_minimal.toml` | Solves the real catchment in steady state with MODFLOW 6, draws five figures and writes four files. | 25 to 45 s |

The clock on the last line of a run, `Run completed`, is shorter than what you wait: Python starts, imports the geospatial stack and reads the configuration first. Count 15 to 30 s more than the figure. The numbers above are measured, on a machine that was sometimes busy with other work.

A run ends with this, the name and the first eight characters of the run id being yours:

```
Run completed: nancon_step1_minimal [3fd2f8e3] 19s
next: hmp catalog show nancon_step1_minimal | hmp catalog diff nancon_step1_minimal <other> | hmp export nancon_step1_minimal --list
```

The figure of that run is `watertable_depth_map`, in `runs/nancon_step1_minimal/figures/`: the depth of the water table below the land surface, from 0 m (dark) to 30 m, which is the thickness of the model.

You see `WARNING` lines on the way. They are expected, and step 1 says what each one means.

## Then

When the staircase is done, After the staircase leads to your own catchment, to the calibration files of example 04 and to the Python API.

Looking for one parameter? Go to the reference.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/staircase/index.html -->
# The staircase

Example 04 models the Nançon catchment (Ille-et-Vilaine) with MODFLOW 6. It ships as a staircase of six TOML files. Each file inherits another one and writes only what it changes, so the page of a step shows you only what that step adds.

| Step | File | What it adds | Inherits | Needs | Time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `step1_minimal.toml` | The shortest file that runs: steady state, local DEM, one K, one recharge rate | nothing | the example files | 15 to 25 s |
| 2 | `step2_local_data.toml` | The mapped stream network and the gauge, from local files, compared with the simulated seepage | step 1 | the example files | 15 to 25 s |
| 3 | `step3_api_data.toml` | The same data, fetched from the BD Topage and Hub’Eau APIs | step 2 | network, first run | about 40 s |
| 4 | `step4_transient.toml` | Monthly transient run, 2000-2002, forced by observed recharge and runoff | step 2 | the example files | 1 to 2 min |
| 5 | `step5_export.toml` | The results written out in every format | step 4 | the example files | 1 to 2 min |
| 6 | `step6_soil_reservoir.toml` | Daily run, 2015-2020, recharge computed by a soil reservoir | `project.toml` | network, first run | about 18 min |

Steps 1, 2, 4 and 5 run offline once the example is added. Steps 3 and 6 read APIs on their first run and use the cache after that. The times are the `Run completed` figure of the last line, measured on 2 cores; the command takes 15 to 30 s longer, because Python starts and imports first.

Step 3 is a variant of step 2, not a rung above it. Step 6 starts again from `project.toml`, the frozen reference model of the example.

```
step 1 ── step 2 ─┬─ step 3   same data, from APIs
                  └─ step 4 ── step 5
project.toml ── step 6
```

## What each step shows

One figure of each step, the one that carries its idea. Each page shows the others.

The images come from real runs of these files. The command that made each one is in `tools/docs/figures/figures.toml`.

## Get the example once

```
hmp workspace init ~/hydromodpy
hmp example add 04 -w ~/hydromodpy
cd ~/hydromodpy/projects/04_streamflow_intermittence_in_transient
```

`hmp example add` downloads the files of the example, 92 MiB, most of it a regional DEM of 90 MiB. Files are cached by content, so a second workspace costs nothing. `hmp example list` shows the examples your version ships and `hmp example show 04` lists the files one by one.

## Run a step

Run any step from that folder. Each run writes its figures to `runs/<name>/figures/` and its exports to `share/<name>/`, where `<name>` is the `simulation.name` of the file.

Command line

```
hmp run step1_minimal.toml
```

Python

```
import hydromodpy as hmp

run = hmp.run("step1_minimal.toml")
print(run.name)
```

A relative path is read from the folder you are in. `hmp.run` returns the Run, whose reference page lists what it reads.

## Run a step twice

Run an unchanged file a second time and nothing is computed. The command prints two lines on the error stream and exits with code 0:

```
Config identical to completed run 'nancon_step1_minimal' [3fd2f8e3]; nothing to do.
Re-run with --force to run it again.
```

`hmp run --force` computes it again. In Python, `hmp.run(path)` returns the existing `Run` and logs a warning, and `hmp.run(path, force=True)` computes it again.

Edit the file, even one value, and the second run is a new one. It lands next to the first, as `runs/nancon_step1_minimal.v2/`, then `.v3`, because `simulation.if_exists` is `"version"` by default. Set it to `"replace"` and the older run goes to the trash instead. hmp catalog lists, compares and deletes them.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/concepts.html -->
# Concepts

Four words name the things on disk. This page is the whole mental model you need before the staircase.

```
~/hydromodpy/                          workspace
├── workspace.toml
├── data/                              inputs shared by every project
│   ├── dem/
│   ├── hydrometry/
│   └── ...                            27 folders, one per variable
└── projects/
    ├── example/                       a project: the synthetic demo
    │   ├── project.toml               marks the root of the project
    │   ├── run_demo.toml              a file you run
    │   ├── runs/demo/                 a run
    │   ├── share/demo/                its exports
    │   └── .hmp/index.duckdb          the catalog
    └── 04_streamflow_intermittence_in_transient/
        ├── project.toml
        ├── step1_minimal.toml ...
        └── sessions/                  calibration sessions
```

Workspace. A folder made by `hmp workspace init`, `~/hydromodpy` by default. It holds the input data in `data/`, one flat folder per variable, and your projects in `projects/`. Several projects share the same `data/`. A workspace is optional: a project folder alone also works, with its input data in a `data/` folder next to `project.toml`. HydroModPy takes the first of: `workspace.root` or `workspace.data_dir` in the file, the `HMP_WORKSPACE` environment variable, the workspace that holds the project under `projects/`, and the project folder itself.

Project. A folder that has a `project.toml`: that file marks the root. In a workspace it is a subfolder of `projects/`. The project holds the TOML files you run and everything those runs write. Create one with `hmp project new <name>`; list them with `hmp project list`.

Run. One execution of one TOML file. It writes a folder `runs/<name>/`, where `<name>` is the `simulation.name` of the file. The folder holds the frozen resolved config (`config.toml`), the fields (`fields.zarr`), the tables (`tables.parquet`), the figures and, written last, `manifest.json`. These are open formats: `xarray`, `zarr` and `pandas` read a run without HydroModPy. Running an unchanged file again does nothing; an edited file makes `<name>.v2` (see The staircase).

Catalog. The index of the runs of one project, a DuckDB file at `.hmp/index.duckdb`. `hmp catalog ls` lists the runs. The disk is the truth and the catalog is derived from it: `hmp catalog reindex` rebuilds it from `runs/` and `sessions/`, and its reference says what a rebuild cannot restore.

## Reading a TOML file

- `workflow.mode` is required. It picks the operation that `hmp run` starts: `simulation`, `calibration`, `overview`, `comparison`, `testbed` or `site_selection`.
- Each section is a request: what to model or produce, when, where. The parameter reference groups the sections by the question they answer, and marks each key for the user, the developer or the expert (the profiles).
- A file names a parent with `base_config` and writes only what changes. The staircase is built this way. The merge rules are in the grammar.

Next: the quick start, or the staircase if you have already run the demo.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/install.html -->
# Install

HydroModPy needs Python 3.11, 3.12 or 3.13. The current pre-release is `2.0.0a5`; the versions page lists the others. On a fast connection pip needs about two minutes, and a clean environment weighs 1.3 GB: most of it is the geospatial and scientific wheels.

## Install the package

Linux and macOS

```
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install --pre hydromodpy
```

Windows

In PowerShell:

```
py -3.12 -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install --pre hydromodpy
```

conda or micromamba

You do not need a clone of the repository. Save this file as `environment.yml`:

```
name: hmp
channels:
  - conda-forge
dependencies:
  - python=3.12
  - pip
  - pip:
      - --pre
      - hydromodpy
```

Then create and activate the environment:

```
micromamba create -f environment.yml
micromamba activate hmp
```

With conda, write `conda env create -f environment.yml` and `conda activate hmp`. If pip cannot find a wheel for one geospatial library on your platform, add that library under `dependencies:` before the `pip:` entry: conda installs it first and pip keeps it.

The `--pre` flag is needed while version 2 is published as `2.0.0aN`. Without it, pip installs the latest stable release, which is version 1, and `hmp --version` prints `1.0.0`.

The package installs two commands, `hmp` and `hydromodpy`. They are the same program. Check the version:

```
hmp --version
```

To upgrade later, run `pip install --pre --upgrade hydromodpy`.

## Get the solver binaries

MODFLOW 6, MODFLOW-NWT, MODPATH and MT3D-USGS are not part of the package. They are downloaded into the HydroModPy cache folder (`~/.cache/hydromodpy/bin/` on Linux) the first time a solver runs. To fetch them now, for example before going offline:

```
hmp install-binaries
```

`--subset mf6,mfnwt` takes only some of the programs and `--upgrade` downloads them again. The other options are in the command reference. The environment variable `HMP_BIN` points HydroModPy at a folder of your own binaries, flat, with the file names `mf6`, `mfnwt` and so on. When it is set, HydroModPy reads that folder and downloads nothing. The data still need the network once: a first run fills the cache of the workspace, and hmp run –frozen then refuses any new download.

## Check the install

```
hmp doctor
```

`hmp doctor` prints one line per check: Python, the core dependencies, the optional ones, each solver binary, and the workspace (`~/hydromodpy`, or the one you give with `--workspace`). It exits with an error code when a check is `KO`. A `WARN` does not change the exit code. On a fresh machine, the binaries and the workspace are `WARN`, because nothing exists yet:

```
WARN   solver:mf6                   not cached, not on PATH
       -> Run 'hmp install-binaries --subset mf6' (or let the first simulation trigger a lazy download).
WARN   workspace                    /home/you/hydromodpy does not exist
       -> Run 'hmp workspace init <workspace>' to scaffold one
```

Both are fixed by the next steps. The other options of the command are in the command reference. From Python:

```
import hydromodpy
print(hydromodpy.__version__)
```

## Tested platforms

The continuous integration of the repository runs these jobs. A platform that is not listed may work; nothing checks it.

| Platform | Python | What runs there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux (Ubuntu) | 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 | Every push to `main` and `dev`: lint, architecture gate, fast tests. Python 3.13: unit and integration tests. Weekly: end-to-end tests and the full regression suite (3.12) |
| macOS | 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 | Weekly: unit tests, fast regression and analytical validation, on an install from a clone |
| Windows | 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 | The same weekly job as macOS |

The jobs install from a clone with `pip install -e ".[test,calibration]"`, not from PyPI, and they do not run the staircase. The PETSc backend of the Boussinesq solver is Linux only, and its smoke test is the only job that installs from conda-forge. The other solvers do not need it. The workflows are in `.github/workflows/` and described in Reading a failing check.

## Install troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hmp: command not found` | The environment that holds the command is not active, or the folder of pip scripts is not on `PATH` (a `pip install --user`). | Activate the environment. Or call the module, which is the same program: `python -m hydromodpy --version`. On Windows the command is `.venv\Scripts\hmp.exe`. |
| `hmp --version` prints `1.0.0` | `--pre` was left out, so pip took the stable release. | `pip install --pre --upgrade hydromodpy`. |
| `ImportError: ... cannot open shared object file` when `gmsh`, `pyvista` or `rasterio` loads, on Linux | A system library is missing. The Dockerfile of the repository installs `libglu1-mesa` for gmsh and pyvista, and `libexpat1` for rasterio. | On Debian or Ubuntu: `sudo apt-get install libglu1-mesa libexpat1`. |
| `Could not download the MODFLOW binaries of release <tag> from <address>: [Errno 111] Connection refused. ...` from `hmp install-binaries`, or `step 'run_solver' failed: NetworkError: Could not download ...` from the first run. Exit code 16 | The binaries are downloaded from GitHub and the machine has no direct route to it. | Behind a proxy, set `HTTPS_PROXY` (`urllib` reads it). Offline, download the executables elsewhere, copy them in one flat folder and set `HMP_BIN` to it. |
| `use GITHUB_TOKEN env to bypass rate limit` | GitHub limits the unauthenticated requests that look up the release. | Set `GITHUB_TOKEN` to a token of your own and run the command again. |
| `WARN solver:mf6 not cached, not on PATH` from `hmp doctor` | Nothing was downloaded yet. | Run `hmp install-binaries`, or run any simulation: the first one downloads. |
| Pip builds a library for a long time, or fails on `rasterio` or `pyproj` | No wheel for your Python or platform. | Use the conda tab above and let conda-forge provide that library. |

Every exit code and its category are listed in Exit codes.

## Optional extras

Add an extra between brackets: `pip install --pre "hydromodpy[ide,viewer3d]"`.

- `ide`: JupyterLab, Spyder and PySide6.
- `viewer3d`: PyVista, for 3D views of the mesh.
- `calibration`: `cma` and `cmaes`, for the CMA-ES variants. The default `optuna` sampler is in the base install.
- `mesh`: `gmsh`.
- `mf6api`: `modflowapi` and `xmipy`.
- `viz`: `datashader` and `lttb`.
- `fair`: `pystac`, `stac-validator` and `rocrate`.
- `metrics`: `psutil` and `pynvml`.
- `duckdb`: DuckDB, which the base install already holds.
- `all`: `duckdb` and `metrics`. It is not every extra.

The extras `test`, `performance`, `profiling`, `docs` and `dev` are for people who work on HydroModPy itself; see Contribute. The generated list, with the packages and the version bounds, is on Optional dependencies.

## Shell completion

Optional. `hmp dev completion bash` prints a completion script for the shell, and `zsh` and `fish` print one for theirs. To load it in the current bash:

```
eval "$(hmp dev completion bash)"
```

The command reference gives where to install the script for bash, zsh and fish, as `hmp dev completion --help` does.

<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/staircase/next.html -->
# After the staircase

You ran the six steps, or enough of them. This page says where to go from there: your own catchment, the calibration files of example 04, the six Python scripts, the daily model and the Python API. Every file named here is already in your copy of example 04.

## Your own catchment

Keep the example open beside your project, and change one thing at a time.

1. Create the project: `hmp project new my_catchment`. It writes a `project.toml` and a `run_demo.toml` on a synthetic catchment, like the project `example` of the quick start. Run the demo first, to know the install is sound.
1. Put the outlet and a DEM under `[geographic.catchment]`, as `step1_minimal.toml` does. The overview draws the identity card of a catchment before any model exists, and costs seconds.
1. Bring the data: each section of [data] reads a public service (rain, evapotranspiration, the stream network, gauges) or a file of your own. The smallest valid file of each section is on Minimal files.
1. Grow the model one step at a time, as the staircase does: a steady run first, then time, then the forcing. Each file inherits the one before (The grammar of a HydroModPy file).

Public data come from French services (BD Topage, Hub’Eau, SIM2). For a catchment elsewhere, the list of data sources says what each one covers.

## The calibration files

Example 04 ships five files that calibrate the model of `project.toml`. Check one before you run it: `--check` loads the file, prints what each phase will do and runs nothing.

```
hmp calibrate run_calibration.toml --check
hmp calibrate run_calibration.toml --list-phases
hmp run run_calibration.toml
```

| File | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `run_calibration.toml` | K, then Sy, by the published protocol: K is moved until the simulated seepage network matches the mapped one, then Sy is read from the gauged hydrograph |
| `run_calibration_by_hand.toml` | The same calibration, written out as two phases |
| `run_calibration_composite.toml` | K and Sy together, the network and the hydrograph weighted. About an hour |
| `run_calibration_bdtopage.toml` | Two phases on BD Topage: K on the permanent and the full network, then Sy on the discharge. About an hour. Needs network |
| `run_calibration_api_daily.toml` | Every input from an API except the DEM, daily over 2015-2020. K takes five fixed values and each run is kept with its figures. Needs network |

The observed network and the gauge are targets: they score the model and are never an input to it. Calibration methods and metrics lists the methods and their options, Scoring a simulated stream network explains the network criterion, and How sure is the model? says what the result can and cannot say.

## The Python scripts

Six scripts sit next to the TOML files. Each finds the project from its own location, so you can run it from any folder, or step through it cell by cell (`# %%`) in Spyder or VS Code. They need the runs they read; the second column says which.

| Script | What it does | Needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `py1_run_and_plot.py` | Runs `step4_transient.toml` with `hmp.run`, then draws a figure of your own: the seepage area of the catchment against the discharge | the example files |
| `py2_edit_parameters.py` | Loads `project.toml` as a Python object, changes K and Sy, runs the variant and compares it with the reference | the example files. Two runs of about a minute each |
| `py3_read_exports.py` | Redraws a figure from the exported files alone (GeoPackage, GeoTIFF, CSV, NetCDF), without importing HydroModPy | the exports of step 5 |
| `py4_sweep_k.py` | Five values of K on one `Project`, which builds the mesh once. The discharge does not tell the K apart, the seepage area does | the example files. Five runs of about a minute each |
| `py5_catalog.py` | Opens the catalog of the project, compares the scores of the runs, redraws a figure at other dates and exports a state the TOML did not ask for | a run of `project.toml` |
| `py6_monthly_maps.py` | The twelve months of 2002 on one sheet, and the 36 months as a GIF | a run of `project.toml` |

`hmp run project.toml` makes the run that scripts 5 and 6 read, and `py2_edit_parameters.py` makes it too. The scripts are the starting point of your own: copy one and change it.

## The daily model

`run_daily.toml` is `project.toml` at a daily step, 1096 stress periods instead of 36. It reads the daily series of the same catchment instead of the monthly ones. Count about thirty times the solver time and the stored fields of the monthly run. It is the file to read when you move from monthly to daily forcing. Step 6 is the other daily file, with a computed recharge.

## The Python API

Everything the command line does is a function of `import hydromodpy as hmp`. The scripts above run a file, edit a configuration in memory, run one model many times and read the results back as pandas and xarray objects. The reference of the Python API lists every function, and the exceptions say what a script can catch.

## Find your way

| You want to | Go to |
| --- | --- |
| Know what a key does | TOML parameters |
| Write the results as files | [[export]] |
| Find, compare or delete runs, rebuild the index | hmp catalog |
| Read what an exit code means | Exit codes |
| Read how the equations work | Theory |

# Step 1: the shortest file that runs

**Task**: Solve the Nançon catchment in steady state from one short file.
**Time**: 15 to 25 s for the run (the `Run completed` figure), 25 to 45 s for the command.
**Needs**: The example files (The staircase) and the MODFLOW 6 binary, downloaded on first use. No other network access.
**Gives**: Five figures and four files: the catchment outline, two GeoTIFFs and a water budget.

Step 1 cuts the catchment out of a regional DEM upslope of an outlet point, gives the aquifer one K and one recharge rate, and lets any cell drain at the ground surface: the excess water leaves as seepage. It inherits nothing, so this page shows the whole file. The aquifer is 30 m thick instead of the 50 m default.

## The file

`step1_minimal.toml` · the base of the staircase · keys link to their card

```
1# Step 1: the shortest file that runs. Nancon, steady state on the local DEM,
2# one K, one recharge rate, seepage at the ground surface. 21406 cells of 75 m.
3#
4#   hmp run step1_minimal.toml
5
6[workflow]
7mode = "simulation"
8# verbosity = "quiet" | "normal" (default) | "verbose" | "debug".
9# `hmp run -q | -v | --debug` wins over the key.
10
11[workspace]
12project_root = "."
13
14[simulation]
15name = "nancon_step1_minimal"
16
17[[simulation.process]]
18id = "flow_main"
19type = "flow"
20solvers = ["modflow6"]
21
22[geographic]
23# Places the delineated watershed on the mesh.
24crs_project = "EPSG:2154"
25
26# The catchment is cut out of a regional DEM, upslope of the outlet point.
27# buff_area widens the model domain by 10 % of the catchment area.
28[geographic.catchment]
29catch_def = "from_outlet_coord"
30dem_init_path = "DEM_armorican_massif.tif"
31x_outlet = 389285.910
32y_outlet = 6816518.749
33snap_dist = "150 m"
34buff_area = "10%"
35
36# 30 m of regolith and fissured bedrock, against the 50 m default.
37[domain.depth_model]
38kind = "constant_thickness"
39thickness = "30.0 m"
40
41[flow]
42# The default is transient; step 4 brings the time window and the forcing.
43flow_regime = "steady"
44param_list = ["K", "Sy"]
45active_sinks_sources = ["recharge"]
46# Any cell drains at the ground surface: the excess leaves as seepage.
47active_bc = ["drainage"]
48
49[flow.param.K.field]
50kind = "homogeneous"
51unit = "m/s"
52value = 5e-5
53
54# A steady solve never reads Sy; it is declared once here for step 4.
55[flow.param.Sy.field]
56kind = "homogeneous"
57unit = "-"
58value = 0.05
59
60# mm/d, the 2000-2002 mean of the observed recharge.
61[flow.sinks_sources.recharge]
62values = 0.78
63
64# The catchment, the depth to the water table and where it reaches the
65# surface, a section through the outlet, and what enters and leaves.
66[display]
67on_error = "raise"
68figures = [
69    "watershed_id_card",
70    "watertable_depth_map",
71    "seepage_map",
72    "cross_section",
73    "water_budget",
74]
75
76# South to north through the outlet, so the section cuts the tributaries
77# across. The west-east default crosses the valley once, at the southern edge.
78[display.overrides.cross_section]
79orientation = "sn"
80
81# What the run writes to share/nancon_step1_minimal/. A block says what
82# (variables) and when (time); the format follows the data. The next steps
83# inherit these three blocks.
84
85# The catchment outline: GeoPackage.
86[[export]]
87variables = "watershed"
88
89# The water table and the seepage cells: one GeoTIFF each. "last" is the one
90# state of a steady run, and the last month of a transient one.
91[[export]]
92variables = ["watertable_depth", "seepage_mask"]
93time = "last"
94
95# The water budget: CSV.
96[[export]]
97variables = "budget"
```

## Run it

Command line

```
cd ~/hydromodpy/projects/04_streamflow_intermittence_in_transient
hmp run step1_minimal.toml
```

`hmp run -v` prints every INFO line and `hmp run -q` only warnings and errors.

Python

```
import hydromodpy as hmp

run = hmp.run("step1_minimal.toml")
print(run.name)
```

If you have not fetched the example yet, start with The staircase. Running the file again does nothing, unless you edited it: see the rerun note.

## What you get

Five figures, in `runs/nancon_step1_minimal/figures/`, listed by `display.figures`:

| Figure | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| `watershed_id_card` | The topography, the outlet, and a table of facts: what was modelled, where, over which period, on which grid |
| `watertable_depth_map` | The depth of the water table below the land surface, in metres |
| `seepage_map` | The cells where the water table reaches the surface, a yes or no for each cell |
| `cross_section` | The land surface, the water table and the seepage segments along a line. Here the line runs south to north through the outlet, so it cuts the tributaries across |
| `water_budget` | One bar per component of the budget, inflow and outflow |

Three `[[export]] blocks` write four files, in `share/nancon_step1_minimal/`:

| Block | Files |
| --- | --- |
| `variables = "watershed"` | `watershed.gpkg`, the catchment outline |
| `variables = ["watertable_depth", "seepage_mask"]`, `time = "last"` | `watertable_depth_last.tif` and `seepage_mask_last.tif`, one GeoTIFF per variable. A steady run has one state, which `"last"` picks |
| `variables = "budget"` | `budget.csv`, the water budget |

The run also leaves a `RUN.txt` there, which is a note and not an export. Steps 2 to 4 inherit these three blocks.

## The warnings of the first run

The run prints `WARNING` lines. None is an error, and each has a reason.

| Warning | Why | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Outlet moved 130 m (limit 150 m) onto the flow network, from (389286, 6816519) to (389175, 6816450).` | The coordinate of the file does not fall on a stream cell of the DEM. The delineation starts from the nearest cell of the flow network, within `geographic.catchment.snap_dist`, here 150 m. The run warns when the move is more than half of that limit. | Nothing, here. A move close to the limit means the coordinate is far from the stream: check it. |
| `Simulated discharge is baseflow only: the run has no runoff forcing, so it underestimates a gauged total streamflow.` | The discharge of steps 1 and 2 is what the drains collect from the aquifer. A gauge measures that plus the surface runoff, and no runoff series is loaded. | Nothing, until step 4: it loads a runoff series, adds it to the discharge, and the warning goes. |
| `Runs of this workspace are sealed without creator_name, creator_institution and a known licence. Add creator_name = "..." and creator_institution = "..." under [workspace] in <workspace.toml>; a licence comes from the 'license' key of each input sidecar (<file>.json).` | A run is sealed with a record of who made it and under which licence, and the workspace says neither. It prints once per workspace, on its first run: if you ran the demo of the quick start, you saw it there. | Cosmetic. Write the two keys under `[workspace]` in `workspace.toml`, or start with `hmp workspace init --creator-name "Your name"`. |

## Key fields

[flow]

`# flow_regime = "transient"` : Whether the flow is solved as one equilibrium state or through time over the stress periods of [simulation.time].
**Path**: `flow.flow_regime`
**See**: simulation.time
**Values**:
- `"steady"` : Solves one equilibrium state, with no storage term: one stress period over the whole [simulation.time] window, whatever its step_value says, with the forcings averaged over the window.
- `"transient"` : Solves the heads through time; it starts from the state [flow.ic] gives.
**Accepted**: "steady" | "transient"
**Example**: `"steady"`, `"transient"`

`# active_bc = []` : Boundaries this run builds, by their canonical names: 'ocean', 'stream', 'north_side', 'south_side', 'east_side', 'west_side', 'drainage', 'lake', 'reservoir'.
**Path**: `flow.active_bc`
**More**: 'lake' and 'reservoir' build a MODFLOW 6 LAK package, so only the modflow6 solver takes them. An empty list builds no boundary.
**Accepted**: list of string
**Example**: `["ocean"]`, `["west_side", "east_side", "drainage"]`

[flow.param.K.field]

`# value = "1e-5 m/s"` : Hydraulic conductivity of the `K` table, in m/s. m/s [1e-14, 100] only if kind = "homogeneous" calibrable · log example value
**Path**: `flow.param.K.field.value`
**More**: A value outside 1e-14 .. 100 m/s is refused.
**Accepted**: number or "<n> m/s"
**Valid range**: [1e-14, 100] (refused outside)
**Unit**: m/s
**Example**: `"1e-5 m/s"`
**Calibration**: yes, search space log, prior log_uniform, bounds belong to the site: write them in `calibration.parameters.<name>.bounds`; the valid range [1e-14, 100] caps them
**Only if**: kind = "homogeneous"
**Same as**: `flow.param.<id>.field.value`, with the unit and range of `K`

[domain.depth_model]

`# thickness = 50.0` : Constant aquifer thickness applied below topography (canonical metres). m > 0 only if kind = "constant_thickness" calibrable · log
**Path**: `domain.depth_model.thickness`
**More**: Accepts inline units, e.g. '0.2 km'.
**Accepted**: number or "<n> m" (a bare number is read in the canonical unit)
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: m
**Calibration**: yes, search space log, prior log_uniform, bounds belong to the site: write them in `calibration.parameters.<name>.bounds`
**Only if**: kind = "constant_thickness"

Lines generated from the models, as in the reference. Open one for its card.

Sy is declared too, for step 4: a steady solve never reads it.

Next: Step 2: the mapped network and the gauge, which adds the mapped stream network.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/staircase/step2.html -->
# Step 2: the mapped network and the gauge

**Task**: Compare the cells where the simulated water table reaches the surface with the mapped river network and the gauge.
**Time**: 15 to 25 s for the run, 40 to 60 s for the command.
**Needs**: The example files (The staircase). Nothing is downloaded.
**Gives**: Four figures and five files, with the mapped network among them.

Step 2 adds two pieces of data, read from local files: the mapped stream network and the discharge gauge at the outlet. The run is still steady. The point is the comparison: the cells where the simulated water table reaches the surface should lie where the map draws a stream. The figures show where they agree and how far each simulated cell is from the map.

## The file

The file
`step2_local_data.toml` inherits `step1_minimal.toml` · + new · ~ changed · keys link to their card

```
1# Step 2: step 1 plus the mapped river network and the gauge, read from local
2# files. Still steady: the network is compared with the simulated seepage.

15+[[data.hydrography.sources]]
16+source = "custom"

20+[[data.hydrometry.sources]]

23+station_ids = ["NANCON"]
24

28[display]
29~figures = [
30    "watershed_id_card",

The network is the GeoPackage `nancon_stream_network.gpkg`, which `hmp example add` put in `data/hydrography/`. The gauge is the `NANCON` station of `data/hydrometry/`, a daily record from 1982 to 2022. Nothing is downloaded. The run prints the same first two warnings as step 1: they are explained there.

## What you get

`display.figures` is a list, so step 2 replaces step 1’s list. Four figures:

| Figure | What it shows |
| --- | --- |

| `hydrographic_network_reference` | The mapped network alone |
| `seepage_network_confusion_map` | Three classes: valid where the two networks share a cell, excess where only the model has a stream, missing where only the map has one |

## Key fields

[data]

`# types = []` : Ordered list of data-manager types explicitly requested in [data].
**Path**: `data.types`
**More**: The launcher may append inferred types deduced from other sections (for example domain.zone_ids, flow.active_bc). Allowed values: 'crossings', 'dem', 'etp', 'geology', 'humidity', 'hydrography', 'hydrometry', 'intermittency', 'lake_abacus', 'lake_bathymetry', 'lake_geometry', 'lake_inflow', 'lake_levels', 'lake_outflow', 'lake_withdrawal', 'oceanic', 'piezometry', 'precipitation', 'radiation', 'recharge', 'runoff', 'soil_capacity', 'soil_moisture', 'substratum', 'temperature', 'water_quality', 'wind'.
**Accepted**: list of string

[[data.hydrography.sources]]

`# path = ‹path›` : Path to a vector file (SHP/GPKG/GeoJSON), raster (TIF/TIFF), or directory containing one.
**Path**: `data.hydrography.sources.path`
**Accepted**: path

Lines generated from the models, as in the reference. Open one for its card.

<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/staircase/step3.html -->
# Step 3: the same data, from the APIs

**Task**: Fetch the river network and the gauge from the BD Topage and Hub’Eau APIs instead of local files.
**Time**: About 40 s for the run once the data are cached. The first launch adds the downloads.
**Needs**: Network access on the first run, no key. The example files (The staircase).
**Gives**: Five figures and six files, with the permanent reaches of the network as a GeoPackage of their own.

Step 3 is step 2 with other sources. The network comes from BD Topage and the gauge from Hub’Eau, two French national APIs, instead of files on disk. Nothing else changes in the model. The answers are cached after the first launch, so a second run needs no network.

The first launch downloads from BD Topage and Hub’Eau. The later ones read the cache.

`sources__delete = true` empties the inherited list of sources before the new one is written, so no local key leaks into it. An API also needs a period, which the file gives: the three years that step 4 simulates.

## What you get

| Figure | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| `watershed_id_card` | As in step 1 |
| `hydrographic_network_reference` | Every BD Topage reach |
| `hydrographic_network_permanence` | Two maps of the network: all the mapped reaches, and only those that flow all year |
| `seepage_network_confusion_map` | As in step 2, against every reach of BD Topage |
| `downslope_distance_map` | As in step 2 |

The exports are step 2’s four, plus the permanent reaches as a GeoPackage of their own: six files in `share/nancon_step3_api/`.

## Key fields

[[data.hydrography.sources]]

`source = "custom"` : Data provider. required example value
**Path**: `data.hydrography.sources.source`
**More**: Any source id this installation resolves and that serves river linework is accepted, so a third-party source registered on the 'hydromodpy.data.source' entry-point group is named here by its id.
**Accepted**: string
**Example**: `"custom"`

[[data.hydrometry.sources]]

`# source = "hubeau"` : Data provider: 'custom' for user files, 'hubeau' for Hub'Eau API.
**Path**: `data.hydrometry.sources.source`
**Values**:
- `"custom"`
- `"hubeau"`
**Accepted**: "custom" | "hubeau"

`# product = "QmnJ"` : Hub'Eau variable code (e.g. 'QmnJ', 'QmM', 'HmnJ').
**Path**: `data.hydrometry.sources.product`
**Accepted**: string

[data.hydrometry]

`# date_start = "2019-01-01"` : Start of the data window (ISO date, e.g. '2019-01-01'). example value
**Path**: `data.hydrometry.date_start`
**More**: Optional: when neither bound is declared, the loader inherits [simulation.time].start_datetime, or [overview].date_start in overview mode. Declare it only to fetch a window WIDER than the simulation, typically a cache shared by several runs. Must be declared together with date_end.
**Accepted**: string
**Example**: `"2019-01-01"`

Lines generated from the models, as in the reference. Open one for its card.

## What can go wrong

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `step 'load_data' failed: NetworkError: Failed to load data manager 'hydrography': HTTP GET https://services.sandre.eaufrance.fr/geo/sandre failed after 4 retries`, exit code 16 (after four `WARNING` lines with the same URL) | The first launch has to reach BD Topage and the machine has no route to it, or the service is down. The run stops: a source the file declares is never skipped. | Run again when the network is back. Behind a proxy, set `HTTPS_PROXY`. To run offline, run step 2, which reads local files, or run step 3 once online: the cache then holds its data, and hmp run –frozen refuses any new download. |

The exit codes are listed on Exit codes.

Next: Step 4: the transient run. It repeats the local data of Step 2: the mapped network and the gauge.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/staircase/step4.html -->
# Step 4: the transient run

**Task**: Run the model month by month over 2000-2002 and see which cells flow, and for how long.
**Time**: 1 to 2 min for the run, 1.5 to 3 min for the command.
**Needs**: The example files (The staircase), which hold the observed recharge and runoff. Nothing is downloaded.
**Gives**: Five figures and seven files, among them a NetCDF of the water table and a CSV of the discharge.

Step 4 turns step 2 into a monthly transient run over 2000-2002. The recharge and the runoff are no longer one mean: 36 monthly values replace the steady rate. The first period is solved steady and gives the initial heads. K, Sy and Ss are assumed here, not calibrated. The question changes from where the water table reaches the surface to which cells flow, and for how long. The baseflow warning of steps 1 and 2 is gone: the runoff is loaded and added to the discharge.

## The file

The file
`step4_transient.toml` inherits `step2_local_data.toml` · + new · ~ changed · keys link to their card

```
1# Step 4: step 2 in monthly transient over 2000-2002, forced by the local
2# monthly recharge and runoff. K, Sy and Ss are assumed, not calibrated.
3# It builds on the local data of step 2; step 3 is the same model on API data.
4#
5#   hmp run step4_transient.toml
6
7+base_config = "step2_local_data.toml"
8
9[simulation]
10~name = "nancon_step4_transient"
11
12# One month is the default step. The first period is solved steady and gives
13# the initial heads.
14+[simulation.time]
15+start_datetime = "2000-01-01"
16+end_datetime = "2002-12-31"
17
18[flow]
19# Restated: an inherited "steady" is not undone by the default.
20~flow_regime = "transient"
21~param_list = ["K", "Sy", "Ss"]
22
23# Only matters where the aquifer is confined; MODFLOW 6 asks for a value.
24+[flow.param.Ss.field]
25+kind = "homogeneous"
26+unit = "m-1"
27+value = 1e-5
28
29# A list replaces the parent's, so the four families are written out.
30[data]
31~types = ["hydrography", "hydrometry", "recharge", "runoff"]
32
33# 36 monthly rates replace the steady mean of step 1.
34+[[data.recharge.sources]]
35+source = "custom"
36+path = "recharge"
37+station_ids = ["NANCON"]
38
39# The share of the gauged discharge the groundwater model does not produce.
40+[[data.runoff.sources]]
41+source = "custom"
42+path = "runoff"
43+station_ids = ["NANCON"]
44
45# What enters and leaves, the gauge against the simulation, the seepage of
46# October 2002, the driest month, then which cells flow and for how long:
47# the share of the three years each cell flows, and its class in 2002.
48[display]
49+time = "2002-10-15"
50~figures = [
51    "flux_timeseries",
52    "hydrograph_sim_obs",
53    "seepage_map",
54    "flow_persistence_map",
55    "flow_intermittence_map",
56]
57
58# One hydrological year, the driest of the record.
59+[display.overrides.flow_intermittence_map]
60+cycle = "2002"
61
62# The exports of steps 1 and 2, now of a transient run: the GeoTIFFs hold
63# December 2002, the last month. Two blocks more for what a record adds.
64
65# The water table over the 36 months: one NetCDF chronicle.
66+[[export__append]]
67+variables = ["head", "watertable_depth"]
68
69# Simulated and gauged discharge over the run: CSV, the model monthly and
70# the gauge daily.
71+[[export__append]]
72+variables = ["discharge", "discharge_obs"]
```

Command line

Python

```

This is also what `py1_run_and_plot.py` of the example does, before it draws its own figure. After the staircase lists the scripts.

Two points of the file are worth a second look. `flow.flow_regime` is written again, because an inherited `"steady"` is not undone by the default. `data.types` is written in full, because a list replaces the parent’s.

## What you get

Five figures. The instant of the one-instant figures comes from `display.time`, here 15 October 2002, the driest month according to the file.

| Figure | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| `flux_timeseries` | The components of the water balance through time, inflows positive and outflows negative |
| `hydrograph_sim_obs` | The simulated discharge against the gauged one |
| `seepage_map` | The seepage cells of October 2002 |
| `flow_persistence_map` | The share of the three years each cell flows: dark where the channel ran all year, pale where it ran only at the wettest steps |
| `flow_intermittence_map` | One calendar year, 2002 (`cycle = "2002"`): each cell is perennial, intermittent or dry |

Six export blocks write seven files in `share/nancon_step4_transient/`: the five files of the inherited blocks, now of a transient run (the GeoTIFFs hold December 2002, the last month), and two more.

| Block | File |
| --- | --- |
| `["head", "watertable_depth"]` | the water table over the 36 months, one NetCDF file |
| `["discharge", "discharge_obs"]` | simulated and gauged discharge, a CSV: the model monthly, the gauge daily |

## Key fields

[simulation.time]

`# start_datetime = "2019-01-01"` : Simulation window lower datetime bound used by launcher-level time alignment and forcing checks. example value
**Path**: `simulation.time.start_datetime`
**Accepted**: date "YYYY-MM-DD"
**Example**: `"2019-01-01"`

`# end_datetime = "2025-12-31"` : Simulation window upper datetime bound, interpreted as inclusive. example value
**Path**: `simulation.time.end_datetime`
**More**: Must be greater than or equal to start_datetime.
**Accepted**: date "YYYY-MM-DD"
**Example**: `"2025-12-31"`

[flow.param.Ss.field]

`# value = "1e-5 m/s"` : Specific storage of the `Ss` table, in 1/m. 1/m [1e-12, 0.001] only if kind = "homogeneous" calibrable · log example value
**Path**: `flow.param.Ss.field.value`
**More**: A value outside 1e-12 .. 0.001 1/m is refused.
**Accepted**: number or "<n> 1/m"
**Valid range**: [1e-12, 0.001] (refused outside)
**Unit**: 1/m
**Example**: `"1e-5 m/s"`
**Calibration**: yes, search space log, prior log_uniform, bounds belong to the site: write them in `calibration.parameters.<name>.bounds`; the valid range [1e-12, 0.001] caps them
**Only if**: kind = "homogeneous"
**Same as**: `flow.param.<id>.field.value`, with the unit and range of `Ss`

[display]

`# time = ‹string or integer›` : The instant every figure that draws one instant shows: a date ("2002-10-15"), "first" or "last".
**Path**: `display.time`
**More**: Each such figure draws the stress period that holds the date, so the same date names the same month on a monthly, a daily or a one-period steady run. A `time` in `[display.overrides.<figure>]` wins over it. Unset, each figure picks its own instant: the last period, or for the stream-network maps the state their calibration criterion read. A date outside a run skips the figure with the reason.
**Accepted**: string or integer

Lines generated from the models, as in the reference. Open one for its card.

The time step is not written: `simulation.time.step_value` defaults to one month.

Next: Step 5: every export, which writes the results in every format.


<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/get-started/staircase/step5.html -->
# Step 5: every export

**Task**: Write the results of step 4 in every format HydroModPy can export, and ask for more files once the run exists.
**Time**: 1 to 2 min for the run, 1.5 to 3 min for the command.
**Needs**: The example files (The staircase). Nothing is downloaded.
**Gives**: Eight figures and fourteen files, from GeoPackage to a portable archive of the run.

Step 5 does not change the model. It is step 4 with its results written out in every format HydroModPy can export. The file drops the inherited exports with `export__delete = true` and states its own list, one `[[export]]` block per request. A block says what (`variables`), when (`time` or `period`), and where and how (`format`, `file`, `crs`).

The map is the field of one of the exports below, `watertable_depth_2002-10-15.tif`, drawn.
