# Downslope distance between two networks

A mapped stream network and a simulated one rarely coincide. This page defines how far apart they are, measured along the paths the water takes, and the criterion built on that distance, the method of Abhervé et al. [2023]. It answers one question. Given a model that makes a network of streams and a map that draws another, how long is the walk downslope from one to the other, in each direction, and at which value of the calibrated ratio do the two walks balance?

How a model makes streams in plain words is on How the model makes streams. The keys of a calibration on a network are in [calibration.outputs].

Note

Scope. The page covers the distances, the criterion, what it identifies, and how the mapped network is drawn on the mesh. The simulated network itself, from the release flux to the flowing cells, is on Where the water table reaches the surface. The search that moves a parameter until the criterion reaches zero is described only where it shapes the criterion.

## The graph the distances follow

A distance follows a flow path, and a flow path exists only where the depressions are resolved. The code floods the model top on the mesh with the priority flood of Routing on the mesh: the descent D, (32), seeded on the border of the active domain, and reads the receivers \(r(n)\) of (34) on the flooded copy. The edge length \(\ell(n)\) is the distance from the centre of \(n\) to the centre of \(r(n)\).

The flood is seeded on the whole border, where water leaves the model, not on the outlet alone: sealing one outlet would fill a valley of the buffer up to a col of the divide. The criterion does not read the descent \(D\) the build stores (The graph of the stream criterion). The map is never burned into the surface: an observation never enters the routing surface or the model top.

## 1. The downslope distance to a set

For a target set \(T\), the distance from a cell to \(T\) is the length of its descent down to the first cell of \(T\):

(45)\[\begin{split} d_T(n) = \begin{cases} 0 & n \in T, \\ \ell(n) + d_T\bigl(r(n)\bigr) & n \notin T,\ r(n) \text{ exists}, \\ +\infty & n \notin T,\ r(n) \text{ does not exist.} \end{cases} \end{split}\]

With one receiver per cell, exactly one descending path leaves a cell, so there is no shortest path to search for. The distance is not a Euclidean nearest distance: a source fifty metres from a stream but across a divide is far away downslope. And it is not symmetric: \(d_{\mathcal{O}}\) on the simulated cells and \(d_{\mathcal{S}}\) on the mapped cells differ, which is what lets one cost weigh an excess of simulated stream against a missing one. An empty target gives \(+\infty\) everywhere and does not raise: an empty simulated network is the legitimate end of a search interval.

Fig. 61 Two networks on an 8 by 8 grid of 10 m cells, with the receivers of the flooded top. Left: from each simulated cell down to the map, the two hillside cells walk 42 m. Right: from each mapped cell down to the simulated network, the three upper cells walk 10, 20 and 30 m. The two means differ, and so do the cells that carry them. Every number is a call of `downslope_distance_to_mask`.

In the code: `downslope_distance_to_mask`.

## 2. The outlet, the catchment and the saturation length

The outlet \(o\) closes the catchment, usually at the gauging station. With \(A_d(n) = a_n + \sum_{m : r(m) = n} A_d(m)\) the area drained through \(n\), the outlet is the most drained cell within two neighbour rings of the cell nearest to the pour point the catchment was delineated from (two cells is the `SnapPourPoints` distance of the paper, read on the mesh). Without a pour point, the most drained cell of the delineated polygon closes the catchment, and without the polygon the largest basin of the mesh does, with a warning.

The catchment scored, and the longest descent in it, are read on the same graph:

(46)\[ \Omega_o = \{\, n : d_{\{o\}}(n) < \infty \,\}, \qquad L_{cap} = \max_{n \in \Omega_o} d_{\{o\}}(n) . \]

The delineated polygon builds the domain and places the outlet; it is not the support. Their symmetric difference over the area of the polygon is published as `catchment_mismatch`, with a warning above five per cent. \(L_{cap}\) is static: it is the value an unreachable cell takes in the means (5. The two mean distances).

In the code: `resolve_outlet`.

## 3. The two networks on the cells

The simulated network \(\mathcal{S}\) is the downstream closure of the sources \(\Sigma\), the cells whose release flux exceeds a share of their own recharge, (41). The release flux is the union of (40), the same union for the criterion and for the stored field. A steady phase reads one state of the run.

The mapped network \(\mathcal{O}\) is a set of lines, drawn on the cells by one of two rules chosen by `observed_rasterization`.

Heads (the default) keeps only where the map says a stream starts, and lets the receiver graph draw the rest: the path a ditch gave a mapped line is something a model on a DEM cannot reproduce, and drawn cell by cell it would count as error.

1. The lines are merged between junctions and free ends.
1. A free end is a head when the largest drained area within the radius \(r_s\) of it does not exceed the same quantity at the other end of its reach. The drained area decides, never the direction the line was drawn in.
1. A head lands on the nearest active cell within \(r_s\) that drains at least \(A_{d,\min}\), or is lost.
1. From each landing cell, the trace follows the receivers until the descent ends or meets a traced cell.
1. The foot of each dam of a lake with a declared spillway is a forced head: the stream under a reservoir has no free end. Only the MODFLOW 6 build stores the dam feet.

The traced map is connected to the outlet by construction.

Fig. 63 The heads rule on a toy valley of 25 m cells, from one call of `trace_from_heads`. The two upstream free ends drain less than the confluence and are kept; the downstream end drains more and is not a head. The drawn map follows the descent of the model, not the line.

Crossing keeps a cell when a mapped line crosses the segment joining the centres of two cells that share an edge: on a structured grid, the cell medians, which is what the WhiteboxTools tool `VectorLinesToRaster` of the paper tests. The map is one cell wide, like the simulated network. A reach that crosses no segment marks the cell holding its midpoint instead, and the count is published per trial as `n_observed_features_fallback`. This is the rule for a map that is not a tree: canals, braids, polders, karst.

In the code: `trace_from_heads`.

## 4. The supports and the targets

The means are taken over the catchment, without the water bodies \(\mathcal{E}\):

(47)\[ \Omega_o^\ast = \Omega_o \setminus \mathcal{E}, \qquad \mathcal{S}^\ast = \mathcal{S} \cap \Omega_o^\ast, \qquad \mathcal{O}^\ast = \mathcal{O} \cap \Omega_o^\ast . \]
- \(\mathcal{S}\) is closed downslope, \(\mathcal{O}\) is taken as drawn: closing the map would build observation out of the DEM.
- The target of \(D_{so}\) is \(T_{so} = \mathcal{O} \cup \mathcal{E} \cup \{o\}\). The outlet is added because mapped lines may stop short of it.
- The target of \(D_{os}\) is \(T_{os} = \mathcal{S}\).
- Water bodies stay in the graph and leave both supports: a lake cell in a support would add one zero per cell and move the root with the size of the lake.

The supports split the cells into three classes, published per trial: `n_valid` (\(\mathcal{S}^\ast \cap \mathcal{O}\), simulated where the map has a stream), `n_excess` (\(\mathcal{S}^\ast \setminus \mathcal{O}\), simulated where it has none) and `n_missing` (\(\mathcal{O}^\ast \setminus \mathcal{S}\), mapped where the model makes none).

The graph is not cut to \(\Omega_o\), the supports are: on a buffered domain many cells drain out of the basin and never meet the map.

## 5. The two mean distances

Write \(\hat d_T(n)\) for the distance in which an unreachable cell takes the value \(L_{cap}\). An unreachable cell is never dropped and never counted as infinite: \(+\infty\) would make the mean infinite, and dropping it would move the support with the parameter. With \(\mu(n)\) the weight of a cell,

(48)\[ D_{so} = \frac{\sum_{n \in \mathcal{S}^\ast} \mu(n)\, \hat d_{T_{so}}(n)}{\sum_{n \in \mathcal{S}^\ast} \mu(n)}, \qquad D_{os} = \frac{\sum_{n \in \mathcal{O}^\ast} \mu(n)\, \hat d_{T_{os}}(n)}{\sum_{n \in \mathcal{O}^\ast} \mu(n)} . \]

With \(\mu = 1\), each cell has one vote, as in the paper; with \(\mu = a_n\) the mean is weighted by area, which matters on a mesh refined along the streams. Both pairs are reported at every trial, and `weighting` selects the one the criterion reads.

\(D_{so}\) large means a simulated network spilling far from the mapped one, an excess. \(D_{os}\) large means a simulated network that never grew to the mapped one, a deficit. At a balanced point most distances are zero, so the means are carried by a few cells: they are tail statistics.

The unreachable shares \(f_{so}\) and \(f_{os}\) are reported on both sides. The bound `max_unreachable_fraction` guards \(f_{so}\) only: its target does not move between trials, and a large share means the surface is not conditioned. The target of \(f_{os}\) is the simulated network the calibration moves: at a high conductivity it retracts into the talwegs, and mapped cells legitimately have nothing left to descend into.

In the code: `mean_downslope_distance`.

## 6. The criterion

The criterion is equations 1 to 4 of Abhervé et al. [2023]:

(49)\[\begin{split} \begin{aligned} J_{signed} &= D_{so} - D_{os}, & J &= \lvert J_{signed} \rvert, \\ D_{optim} &= \tfrac{1}{2}\,(D_{so} + D_{os}), & r_{optim} &= D_{optim} / h_{obs} . \end{aligned} \end{split}\]

When the simulated network is empty, \(D_{so}\) has no support, and the residual is set to \(J_{signed} = -L_{cap}\): the negative value a root search needs at the end of its interval where nothing seeps.

The cost is \(J\), and its zero is a crossing. The two curves \(D_{so}\) and \(D_{os}\), drawn against the calibrated parameter, cross, and the crossing is the answer. \(D_{optim}\) is large at both ends of a sweep, so it has an interior minimum, and minimising it is a tempting substitute. It is a different estimator: nothing places its minimum at the crossing.

Fig. 65 \(D_{so}\) and \(D_{os}\) against \(K/\bar N\) on a toy catchment of 60 by 60 cells of 20 m. No solver runs: a cell is a source when the recharge it drains exceeds what a 30 m saturated thickness carries down its slope, \(\bar N A_d > K B s\,w\), and the map holds the cells draining more than 0.03 km². Every distance is a call of the code. The curves are steps, because the masks are discrete. The minimum of \(D_{optim}\) (dotted) is not at the crossing.

The two estimators are needed and are not interchangeable. Inside one model structure, \(J\) finds the parameter, and \(D_{optim}\) cannot separate two points that both balance. Between structures already balanced at \(J = 0\), only \(D_{optim}\) separates them. The code names them apart in `metric`: `distance_gap` is the cost \(J\) and carries the signed residual; `distance_mean` is \(D_{optim}\), a diagnostic. With two maps, each bound is this same pair evaluated once, and the cost is the sum of the weighted gaps. A run with a permanent map beside the full one, in one state, scores the state against the permanent map; the full map is scored at the same state as a validation and never enters the cost.

In the code: `seepage_distance_cost`.

## 7. When a result is valid

The length scale. \(h_{obs}\) is the median distance between the centres of cells that share an edge, over the mapped cells of \(\Omega_o\): the cell size on a regular grid, the size of the fine cells on a mesh refined along the streams. It is static, since the map does not move with \(K\).

The bound. The paper reads \(r_{optim} \leq 2\): two cells, one of which budgets for the error of the map. The code writes it as a length:

(50)\[ D_{optim} \leq V, \qquad V = 2\,\max(h_{obs},\ \sigma_o) . \]

With no declared accuracy, \(V = 2 h_{obs}\), the bound of the paper. A declared accuracy \(\sigma_o\) above \(h_{obs}\) widens \(V\) and leaves \(r_{optim}\) comparable with the paper. A declared `validity_length` replaces the computation. The bound is read on the trial the search returns, and qualifies the value without replacing it: a violation logs a warning, or is refused after the session is saved when `on_roptim_violation` is `"error"`. Each trial publishes `roptim` and `roptim_valid`.

The map against the surface. Wherever the mapped lines do not sit in the talwegs of the model top, the distances measure a disagreement between two datasets rather than hydrogeology. The code publishes the share of the downstream closure of the map that the map itself holds, inside the catchment:

(51)\[ \alpha_o = \frac{\lvert \mathcal{O} \cap \Omega_o \rvert}{\lvert \mathrm{closure}(\mathcal{O}) \cap \Omega_o \rvert}, \]

as `alpha_obs_closure_catchment`. A value below `alpha_warning_threshold` logs a warning, once per process.

## What the criterion identifies

Take a steady water-table aquifer with drains at the surface whose conductance is derived from \(K\), (35). Per unit area, the balance of a cell is

(52)\[ \nabla \cdot \bigl( K\, B\, \nabla h \bigr) + N = \frac{K}{b_d}\,\bigl(h - z^d\bigr)_+ , \]

with \(B\) the saturated thickness ((16)) and \(z^d\) the drain elevation, the cell top by default. Dividing by \(K\) gives

\[ \nabla \cdot \bigl( B\, \nabla h \bigr) + \frac{N}{K} = \frac{1}{b_d}\,\bigl(h - z^d\bigr)_+ , \]

which depends on \(N/K\) and on the geometry alone. When \(K\) is scaled by one factor everywhere and \(N\) keeps its shape, the head field, and so the seepage mask, the release flux and the criterion, depend only on \(K/\bar N\). What the criterion calibrates is that ratio, not \(K\). A \(K\) read from it inherits the recharge series entirely: report \(K/\bar N\) and name the recharge beside it.

When the search moves the homogeneous conductivity alone, the report publishes the ratio with what it rests on: `k_over_r` (\(K/\bar N\)), `k_optim_m_s`, `R_mean_m_s` (\(\bar N\)), `d_sat_m` (the saturated thickness averaged over the catchment, \(\bar B\)), and `t_over_r_m` (\(T/\bar N = K \bar B / \bar N\), a length). For any other search they are not published.

This is why a search that moves \(K\) is refused when a conductance does not follow \(K\) (see the limits).

## How a search reaches the zero

The masks are discrete, so \(J_{signed}\) steps over zero instead of reaching it, and the zero is a plateau whose width sets how precisely the parameter is known. A bisection therefore stops on the width of its bracket, on a logarithmic transform, never on the size of the residual. A coarse sweep runs first and sees every crossing; a bracket with no sign change is reported, not closed. The options are on Calibration methods and metrics.

## Assumptions

- Water leaves a cell by one receiver (single flow direction).
- The model top, flooded on the mesh graph, is the surface water follows.
- Distances are lengths along links between cell centres, not straight lines.
- The mapped network is independent of the DEM. It is never burned into the surface.
- The release flux is the whole of what leaves the aquifer for the surface.
- For the reading of \(K/\bar N\): the state is steady, the drain conductance follows \(K\), and \(K\) is scaled by one factor while \(N\) keeps its shape.
- The threshold \(\tau_\mathrm{s}\) and the mean recharge \(\bar N\) are frozen over a search.

## Limits

What the code refuses:

- a trial where more than the bound of the simulated support never reaches the map: the surface still holds depressions;
- a mapped network that lands on no active cell, or on no cell of the catchment. The message names the CRS as the first suspect;
- a heads rule that draws no stream: no free end on an active cell, every free end draining more than the other end of its reach, or every head lost;
- a release record in the budget that no declared package reads, which would report its water as dry land;
- a search that moves a conductivity while a drain has a fixed conductance, or while SFR or LAK is active: those conductances do not follow \(K\), so (52) does not hold. A search driving another parameter gets a warning instead;
- a bisection on more than one parameter, or on a parameter without a logarithmic transform.

What the code does not represent:

- Monotonicity. The criterion does not prove that \(J_{signed}\) varies one way with the parameter. It checks it on a sweep.
- \(r_{optim}\) is not a quality indicator. It measures agreement with the map, and it moves with the grid: refining a mesh lowers \(h_{obs}\) and raises \(r_{optim}\) at constant agreement. Two verdicts are comparable when their validity lengths are.
- Tail statistics. Reading \(r_{optim} \leq 2\) as “the typical gap is under two cells” is wrong when the median distance is zero.
- The surface is not repaired. `dem_correc_type` conditions the DEM before the catchment is delineated (`fill`, the tool of the paper, or `breach`[Lindsay, 2016], or `capped_breach`). The criterion always floods the model top on the mesh; a breached raster reaches it only through the domain and the outlet.
- Domain of validity. The method was built for unconfined aquifers in a temperate humid climate, with gentle gradients and a strong groundwater-stream connection. Outside that, the criterion still computes, and it means less.

## Parameters of this page

[[calibration.objective_blocks]]

`# metric = "rmse"` : Metric that scores this block against its observations.
**Path**: `calibration.objective_blocks.metric`
**Values**:
- `"rmse"` : Root-mean-square error, in the observed unit; penalizes large misfits most.
- `"nse"` : Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency against the observed mean; the standard choice for a level or discharge series.
- `"kge"` : Kling-Gupta efficiency; separates correlation, variability and bias when NSE alone is ambiguous.
- `"mae"` : Mean absolute error, in the observed unit; less sensitive to outliers than RMSE.
- `"nse_log"` : NSE on log-transformed series; weights low flows as heavily as peaks, good for recessions.
- `"nse_delta"` : NSE on the increments of the series rather than its level; a level is an integral and can hide flux errors that compensate, which only its increments show.
- `"nse_seasonal"` : NSE against the seasonal cycle rather than the overall mean; asks whether the model beats climatology.
- `"reservoir"` : Half nse_seasonal plus half nse_delta, built for an impounded level: a plain NSE there is beaten by the seasonal cycle, and the increments are what carry the flux errors.
- `"distance_gap"` : Balances the simulated stream network against the mapped one; zero marks the crossing.
- `"distance_mean"` : Mean spatial offset between simulated and mapped streams; a diagnostic, not a substitute for distance_gap.
**Accepted**: "rmse" | "nse" | "kge" | "mae" | "nse_log" | "nse_delta" | "nse_seasonal" | "reservoir" | "distance_gap" | "distance_mean"

[calibration.outputs.<name>]

`variable = "head"` : Simulated variable to extract (e.g. 'head', 'outlet_discharge'). required example value
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.variable`
**Accepted**: string
**Example**: `"head"`

`# observed_network = ‹"data.hydrography" | "geographic.river_network"›` : Where the mapped network comes from when it is not an explicit file. only if support = "network"
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.observed_network`
**More**: Exactly one of this and 'stream_geometry_path' must be set.
**Values**:
- `"data.hydrography"` : Reuses the network the hydrography data family already loaded (a local file or an osm / bdtopage / euhydro download), clipped to the delineated catchment. Costs nothing new to configure but ties the criterion to whatever that section resolved.
- `"geographic.river_network"` : Derives the network from the DEM by a drainage-area threshold. K/R shapes both where the water table reaches the surface and the accumulation the threshold is cut on, so the criterion partly fits a seepage density onto a geomorphological one; warned once and recorded on every run that uses it.
**Accepted**: "data.hydrography" | "geographic.river_network"
**Only if**: support = "network"

`# stream_geometry_path = ‹path›` : Vector file holding the mapped stream network, read only from here: the criterion resolves no geometry of its own and does not reuse the one the hydrography data family loaded. only if support = "network"
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.stream_geometry_path`
**More**: The way out of 'observed_network' when neither of its two sources is the one you want scored.
**Accepted**: path
**Only if**: support = "network"

`# minimal_stream_geometry_path = ‹path›` : Vector file holding the minimal map: the permanent network, which the map named by 'observed_network' or 'stream_geometry_path' (the maximal map, every mapped reach) contains. only if support = "network"
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.minimal_stream_geometry_path`
**More**: Read as it is, never filtered by attribute. The maximal map scored is the union of the two, and the share of the minimal map outside the maximal one is published. In one state, the state is compared to this map and the maximal map is scored beside it as a validation outside the cost, as Abherve et al. (2025) do; with 'extent', it is the minimal bound. At most one of this and 'minimal_observed_network'.
**Accepted**: path
**Only if**: support = "network"

`# tau_specific_ratio = 0.0001` : A cell releasing less than this fraction of its own recharge is not a seepage face. - >= 0 only if support = "network"
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.tau_specific_ratio`
**More**: Zero reproduces the purely geometric criterion of the paper. Frozen over the whole search: a threshold moving with the trial would cost the criterion its monotonicity.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: >= 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: -
**Only if**: support = "network"

`# weighting = "cell"` : Average one cell one vote (the paper) or weighted by cell area. only if support = "network"
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.weighting`
**More**: Both values are always reported; use 'area' on a mesh refined along the streams, where cell density is highest exactly where distances are smallest.
**Values**:
- `"cell"` : Every cell counts once in the average, as in the paper.
- `"area"` : Every cell counts in proportion to its area.
**Accepted**: "cell" | "area"
**Only if**: support = "network"

`# diagonal_neighbors = true` : Descend over shared nodes, the eight D8 neighbours of a quad mesh. only if support = "network"
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.diagonal_neighbors`
**More**: True is the paper: its distances are traced by WhiteboxTools on a D8 pointer, and the delineation that produced the catchment uses one too. False descends over shared edges only, four neighbours (D4), and departs from the paper. It is not a second-decimal choice: on a synthetic valley whose talweg runs along the grid diagonal, the most accumulated cell collects 100 per cent of the domain over shared nodes and 6.6 per cent over shared edges. On a mesh whose faces are not all quadrilaterals no cell has a diagonal and the descent walks shared edges either way; on a Voronoi mesh the two graphs are the same one.
**Accepted**: true | false
**Only if**: support = "network"

`# observed_rasterization = "heads"` : How the mapped network is drawn on the mesh cells. only if support = "network"
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.observed_rasterization`
**More**: 'crossing' keeps the cell holding each point where a line crosses the segment joining two edge-sharing cell centres. On a structured grid it reproduces WhiteboxTools VectorLinesToRaster, the paper's tool, and draws the map one cell wide like the simulated network, so a model that matches the map scores J = 0. 'touch' keeps every cell the line touches, corners included, and replays a session made before 2026-09; it thickens every diagonal step of the map and departs from the paper. 'heads' keeps only the free ends of the map whose largest drained area within heads_snap_radius does not exceed that of the other end of their reach, lands each on a nearby cell and draws the rest down the criterion's own descent: the field ditches and rectified reaches below a head stop counting as model error, and the drawn map reaches the outlet. Keep 'crossing' for a map that is not a tree: canals, braids, polders, karst.
**Values**:
- `"heads"`
- `"crossing"`
- `"touch"`
**Accepted**: "heads" | "crossing" | "touch"
**Only if**: support = "network"

`# heads_snap_radius = 100.0` : Under observed_rasterization = 'heads', the largest distance, a length (a bare number is in metres), between a mapped stream head and the centre of the cell it lands on. m only if support = "network" only if observed_rasterization = "heads"
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.heads_snap_radius`
**More**: A head with no landing cell that close is lost, draws nothing and is counted in n_heads_lost. Read only under 'heads'.
**Accepted**: number or "<n> m" (a bare number is read in the canonical unit)
**Unit**: m
**Only if**: support = "network" and observed_rasterization = "heads"

`# heads_min_drained_area_km2 = 0.02` : Under observed_rasterization = 'heads', the drained area in km2 a cell needs before a head may land on it, so a head next to its valley lands in the valley and not on the ridge cell beside it. km2 >= 0 only if support = "network" only if observed_rasterization = "heads"
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.heads_min_drained_area_km2`
**More**: Read only under 'heads'.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: >= 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: km2
**Only if**: support = "network" and observed_rasterization = "heads"

`# observed_position_accuracy = ‹number or "<n> m"›` : Positional accuracy of the mapped network. m only if support = "network"
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.observed_position_accuracy`
**More**: It enters the automatic validity length only: the cell size h there is max(h_obs, this), because a map is not placed better when the mesh is refined. roptim stays Doptim / h_obs, the paper's Eq. 3. Unset is the literal reading of the paper.
**Accepted**: number or "<n> m" (a bare number is read in the canonical unit)
**Unit**: m
**Only if**: support = "network"

`# validity_length = "auto"` : Validity bound of Eq. 4, a length: the calibration is valid when Doptim <= this. m only if support = "network"
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.validity_length`
**More**: 'auto' is 2 h, the paper's two cells, where h is h_obs, the cell size on the mapped network, raised to 'observed_position_accuracy' when one is declared. A length such as '150 m' is used as it is. The bound qualifies the result and never penalises the cost.
**Values**:
- `"auto"`
**Accepted**: "auto" or number or "<n> m" (a bare number is read in the canonical unit)
**Unit**: m
**Only if**: support = "network"

`# on_roptim_violation = "warn"` : What a violation of Eq. 4 does: Doptim above 'validity_length'. only if support = "network"
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.on_roptim_violation`
**More**: The bound is read once, on the trial the search returns, as the paper reads it at the optimum, and on each bound in the cost of the two-bound mode; every trial still records 'roptim', 'roptim_valid' and 'validity_length_m'. 'warn' logs it and returns the value, because a calibration is asked for a number. 'error' raises after the session is saved, so a staged calibration freezes nothing and runs no phase that depends on this one.
**Values**:
- `"warn"`
- `"error"`
**Accepted**: "warn" | "error"
**Only if**: support = "network"

`# max_unreachable_fraction = 0.05` : Bound on 'frac_unreachable_so' alone: the share of the simulated network whose descent never meets the mapped one, whose target does not move between trials. - [0, 1] only if support = "network"
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.max_unreachable_fraction`
**More**: Beyond a few per cent the routing surface is not conditioned and D_so would be a fiction. The reciprocal share, 'frac_unreachable_os', is reported and deliberately left unbounded: its target is the simulated network, which the search itself retracts.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: [0, 1] (refused outside)
**Unit**: -
**Only if**: support = "network"

`# alpha_warning_threshold = 0.9` : Below this value of 'alpha_obs_closure_catchment' the run warns that its distances carry a top-versus-map disagreement on top of the hydrogeology. alpha is the share of the downstream closure of the mapped network the network itself covers, measured on the MODEL TOP and on the catchment. ]0, 1] only if support = "network" expert
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.alpha_warning_threshold`
**More**: It changes nothing that is computed: the criterion is scored the same way above and below it.
**Accepted**: number

[calibration]

`# method_options = {}` : Options of the method, named as that method names them: points_per_dim for 'grid', sampler for 'optuna', sweep_points for 'bisection'.
**Path**: `calibration.method_options`
**More**: They belong to one method, so a calibration that gives them writes method beside them. A key the method does not take is refused when the file loads.
**Accepted**: table { key = any value }
**Was**: `calibration.optimizer_kwargs`

[geographic]

`# dem_correc_type = "fill"` : How the DEM is conditioned before the catchment is delineated.
**Path**: `geographic.dem_correc_type`
**More**: 'fill' (default) only raises cells: each closed depression is raised to its spill level, then a small gradient on the flats lets every cell drain. 'breach' mostly lowers cells: it carves a path through the barrier that closes a depression, after raising single-cell pits to their lowest neighbour, with no limit on length or depth and no fill afterwards (least-cost breaching, Lindsay 2016); it changes far fewer cells than 'fill' and can dig deep. 'capped_breach' lowers and raises: it breaches only within the limits of [geographic.capped_breach] (a maximum cumulative lowering and a maximum length, in metres), then fills every depression the limits refused (the hybrid of Lindsay 2016). The depth limit is a sum over the cells of a path, so it does not give the same landscape at every grid resolution. 'fill' is the default because it is the tool of the paper behind the network criterion (FillDepressions, Abherve et al. 2023), and the criterion itself fills the model top on the mesh by a priority flood: one conditioning rule from the DEM to the score.
**Values**:
- `"breach"`
- `"fill"`
- `"capped_breach"`
**Accepted**: "breach" | "fill" | "capped_breach"

[solver]

`# drain_bed_thickness_m = 1.0` : Metres. m > 0 expert
**Path**: `solver.drain_bed_thickness_m`
**More**: Thickness of the drain BED in the fallback conductance C = K * cell_area / bed_thickness, used when no drainage conductance is declared. A drain bed is the clogging layer at the bottom of a watercourse, decimetres to a metre; it is NOT the aquifer, and the layer thickness this used to borrow (30 m on the Nancon) has no physical relation to it. The value matters because it sets how much head the drain itself imposes to pass the recharge: dh = R * bed_thickness / K, independent of the cell size. On the Nancon at R = 439 mm/yr, 30 m gives 4.17 m of head at K = 1e-7 m/s and makes the drain the limiting resistance over two decades of a [1e-7, 1e-3] search; 1 m gives 13.9 cm and 0.1 m gives 1.4 cm. In this method the drain is a seepage face, so it must never limit: K and the recharge decide where water surfaces, not the boundary condition. Proportionality to K is preserved either way, so the K/R invariance the network criterion rests on is untouched.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: m
**Example**: `1.0`, `0.5`, `0.1`

Lines generated from the models, as in the reference. Open one for its card.

# How water leaves the aquifer

Water enters the saturated zone as recharge and leaves it through a few exits. Each exit is a boundary package of the solver: a drain where the water table reaches the ground, a fixed head at the sea, a stream that routes what it receives, a lake that stores it. The laws are those of MODFLOW. These pages give the way HydroModPy builds each exit, and how the cells where the water table reaches the surface become a simulated network. The keys of a routed network and of a lake are in [flow.sinks_sources.sfr] and [flow.sinks_sources.lakes].

Note

Scope. MODFLOW 6 builds every exit below. MODFLOW-NWT builds the drains, the sea, the side heads and the evapotranspiration package, and no stream, lake or water mover: a file that lists `"sfr"`, `"lake"` or `"reservoir"` in `flow.active_bc` with another solver in `solver.backend` is refused when it is read. The Boussinesq solver has its own surface exchange, on Boussinesq theory.

## The exits in one table

| Exit | Law | MODFLOW 6 | MODFLOW-NWT | Switched on by | Page |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Drain at the ground surface | one-sided, head dependent | DRN | DRN | `"drainage"` in `flow.active_bc` | Drains and evapotranspiration at the top of the model |
| Evapotranspiration from the water table | linear in depth | EVTA | EVT | `"etp"` in `flow.active_sinks_sources`, or a negative recharge | Drains and evapotranspiration at the top of the model |
| Sea | fixed head | CHD | BAS and CHD | `"ocean"` in `flow.active_bc` | Fixed heads: the sea, the rivers and the sides |
| River head, lateral heads | fixed head | CHD | lateral heads only | `"stream"`, `"west_side"` and the other sides | Fixed heads: the sea, the rivers and the sides |
| Lake or reservoir | storage, head dependent bed and banks | LAK | none | `"lake"` or `"reservoir"` | Lakes and reservoirs |
| Stream network | routed flow, head dependent streambed | SFR | none | `"sfr"` | Streams and the water mover |
| Transfer between exits | a rule on a provider flow | MVR | none | a mover key of an exit | Streams and the water mover |

Wells are a prescribed flux and not an exit. Recharge is not an exit either, but the evapotranspiration is drawn by an exit package, so both are on Drains and evapotranspiration at the top of the model.

Fig. 49 One cross-section, five columns, each with the exit the build gives it. A fixed head holds every layer of its column. A drain sits at the top of its cell, or half a band lower. A reach replaces the drain of its cell and keeps its bed inside the cell. A lake makes its top layer inactive and exchanges with the cells below and beside it.

Where the water goes once a drain has released it, and why a mesh needs a routing surface of its own, is on Routing on the mesh: the descent D. Which cells count as flowing streams is on Where the water table reaches the surface.

## The order the build assembles them

The order matters, because each exit masks the others.

1. The lake cells are made inactive in their top layers, so that every other exit sees the aquifer without them.
1. The fixed heads are placed: sea, river, sides.
1. The descent \(D\) is built from the model top, the fixed-head cells and the lakes.
1. The recharge and the evapotranspiration are written, with no recharge on a lake cell.
1. The drains are written on every cell, minus the cells that host a reach or a lake bed.
1. The lake, then the stream network, then the water mover, which names the packages above.

In the code: `run_pre_processing`.

## The budget closes

The budget is the one of MODFLOW: each package reports its flow into the cells, \(\Phi_{n,p}\), positive into the aquifer, and the terms close against the change of storage. The solver prints the percent discrepancy of the sum, and the options that bound it are on The solvers of the aquifer. The budget terms are those of Langevin et al. [2017]. The input of each package is in the MODFLOW 6 input and output guide.

HydroModPy stores the terms as `recharge`, `evapotranspiration`, `drain`, `drain_to_mover`, `stream`, `lake`, `constant_head`, `well` and `storage`. The part of the drain handed to the mover leaves the aquifer through its own record and enters the stream or the lake as water from the mover, so the package budgets of SFR and LAK close the rest.

## Assumptions common to every exit

- A drain acts on the top layer. A fixed head acts on every layer of its column. A reach and a lake exchange with the cells that hold them.
- The recharge, the rain and the ETP are constant over a stress period.
- Water routed by the mover reaches its receiver in the same period.
- No overland flow is solved. A drain that is not routed discharges where it is, and the water leaves the model there. The water balance counts it, and no surface routing carries it on.
- Fixed heads: the sea, the rivers and the sides
- Routing on the mesh: the descent D
- Drains and evapotranspiration at the top of the model
- Lakes and reservoirs
- Streams and the water mover
- Where the water table reaches the surface

<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/theory/exits/drains-and-et.html -->
# Drains and evapotranspiration at the top of the model

Two exits act at the top of the model. A drain discharges where the water table reaches the ground. The evapotranspiration package draws water where the water table is shallow. Recharge is not an exit, but it is written by the same step of the build and it decides what the drains carry, so it opens this page.

## Recharge in

MODFLOW 6 reads the recharge as one array per stress period (RCHA), put on the top layer or on the first active layer below it (RCHA input guide). HydroModPy adds one rule: the recharge is set to zero on lake cells. The lake already takes its own rain through LAK, and otherwise RCHA would move the recharge of a lake cell to the first active cell under the lake, so the rain would be counted twice.

The recharge comes from a series or a grid that the run loads, or from the daily soil reservoir of The daily soil reservoir. How it becomes one value per stress period, and how a negative recharge is split, is on Rain and evaporation: the forcing.

In the code: `mask_recharge_on_lake_cells`.

## Evapotranspiration out

Both MODFLOW solvers use the same linear law [Harbaugh, 2005, Langevin et al., 2017]: the package draws water at the full rate \(E^\mathrm{et}_n\) when the head is at or above the surface \(z_\mathrm{et}\), and at a rate that falls linearly to zero at the depth \(d_\mathrm{ext}\) below it (input guides: EVTA, EVT). HydroModPy chooses the rate, the surface and the depth from three sources.

| Source | Rate \(E^\mathrm{et}_n\) | Surface \(z_\mathrm{et}\) | Depth \(d_\mathrm{ext}\) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MODFLOW 6, deficit of a negative recharge | the deficit \(N^-_k\) | \(z_{\mathrm{top},n}\) | `evt_extinction_depth` |
| MODFLOW 6, the ETP the soil reservoir left unmet | that residual ETP | \(z^d_n - o_\mathrm{et}\) | `extinction_depth` |
| MODFLOW-NWT, the loaded ETP and the deficit | the ETP as loaded, plus the deficit | \(z_{\mathrm{top},n} - o_\mathrm{et}\) | `extinction_depth` |

\(z^d_n\) is the drain elevation of the cell (below): the top, or the top lowered by half the band, and the top when the run has no drain. The surface of the soil residual sits there because the soil has already taken the ETP it could, and what is left may only draw from water that would otherwise reach the drain. The card of `surface_offset` says which value applies to which solver.

The sea cells, the river cells and the lake cells carry no aquifer evapotranspiration: a lake evaporates through LAK. The deficit of a negative recharge is also kept off the cells that have no active layer.

The word `"etp"` in `flow.active_sinks_sources` acts differently by solver. Under MODFLOW-NWT the loaded ETP drives the package. Under MODFLOW 6 it acts in soil mode only, where it sends the residual ETP of the reservoir to EVTA; outside soil mode MODFLOW 6 ignores it and logs a warning. The Boussinesq solver refuses it.

In the code: `build_evt_array_stress_period_data`.

## The drain law

The drain is the one-sided law of the DRN package of both MODFLOW solvers [Harbaugh, 2005, Langevin et al., 2017]: it removes water in proportion to the head above the drain elevation \(z^d_n\) and never feeds the aquifer (input guide: DRN). In HydroModPy the drain stands for seepage at the ground surface. There is one row per cell, in the top layer, at the elevation of the top. The cells outside the model domain, the sea cells and the river cells carry no row. The rows are dropped later in the cells that host a connected reach (Streams and the water mover) and in the cells of a lake bed that stays active (Lakes and reservoirs). A drain does not read \(D\): its elevation is \(z_{\mathrm{top},n}\), never the filled \(\tilde z_n\).

## The conductance

When the file declares a conductance, every cell takes it as a conductance per cell, with the floor: \(C_n = \max(C^\mathrm{decl}, C_\mathrm{min})\). When it declares none, which is the case of example 04, each drain derives its conductance from the conductivity of its cell:

(35)\[ C_n = \max\!\left(\frac{K_n\,a_n}{b_d},\ C_\mathrm{min}\right). \]

The thickness \(b_d\) is that of the clogging layer at the bottom of a watercourse, decimetres to a metre. It is not the thickness of an aquifer layer. A cell passes its own recharge when the head stands above the drain elevation by

(36)\[ h_n - z^d_n = \frac{N_n\, a_n}{C_n} = \frac{N_n\, b_d}{K_n} . \]

The excess does not depend on the size of the cell. It depends on \(K/N\), the ratio a network calibration searches (Downslope distance between two networks), and on \(b_d\). The drain is meant to be a seepage face: \(K\) and the recharge decide where the water surfaces, and the drain must not limit it. The floor \(C_\mathrm{min}\) exists only for a degenerate cell, a zero conductivity for instance, whose formula would give a conductance MODFLOW reads as no drain at all.

A zero or a negative declared value selects the derivation; it does not close the boundary. The conductance is static unless the value is a series. A period is written only when the declared value changes, and MODFLOW 6 reuses the last data for the periods left out.

The bed thickness \(b_d\) is `solver.drain_bed_thickness_m`. The Boussinesq solver derives its drain conductance with the same \(b_d\), without the floor (Boussinesq theory).

In the code: `hk_fallback_drain_conductance`.

## The discharge band

A single drain elevation says that the land inside a cell is flat. The USGS remedy is a sub-cell discharge band, not an edit of the elevation [Langevin et al., 2017], with a depth that can come from the standard deviation of the fine land surface elevations inside the cell [Feinstein et al., 2020]. With a band of depth \(\delta\) (`solver.drain_band_depth_m`), the drain sits lower and its conductance grows:

(37)\[ z^d_n = z_{\mathrm{top},n} - \frac{\delta}{2}, \qquad C^{\delta}_n = C_n\,\frac{b_d}{\delta}. \]

The factor is the bed thickness and not the cell area: the conductance it scales is already \(K_n a_n / b_d\), so the product is \(K_n a_n / \delta\), the conductance of a band of depth \(\delta\). With the derived conductance, \(b_d\) drops out. The cell begins to discharge before the head reaches its mean elevation, and discharges harder as the head climbs into the band. No elevation is raised and no DEM is rewritten. MODFLOW 6 solves its own band with a smooth curve; this rule is the piecewise equivalent, applied alike by both MODFLOW solvers.

The seepage mask of Where the water table reaches the surface reads the band: a banded cell discharges at \(z_{\mathrm{top},n} - \delta/2\) and never climbs back to its top, so the run keeps \(\delta\) in its store for every reader.

In the code: `drain_discharge_band`.

## The other answer: no drain in the pits

`solver.sink_fill` sets the conductance to zero in every cell that sits in a closed depression of the top. The depressions are found on the solver mesh by a priority flood seeded on every cell water can leave the domain through, counted on the shared faces that MODFLOW connects. Both MODFLOW solvers read the same mask. No manual or USGS document removes a discharge boundary where a pit is found, and the card of the key says so. The band and this key answer the same question in opposite directions, and a file that sets both is refused.

## One cell, by hand

A cell of 25 m by 25 m (\(a_n = 625\) m²), \(K = 10^{-7}\) m/s, and a recharge of 439 mm per year, \(1.39 \times 10^{-8}\) m/s. The conductance and the head the drain needs to pass the recharge, from (35), (36) and (37):

| Drain bed \(b_d\) | Band \(\delta\) | \(C_n\) (m²/s) | Drain elevation | Head above it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 30 m | none | \(2.08 \times 10^{-6}\) | \(z_\mathrm{top}\) | 4.17 m |
| 1 m | none | \(6.25 \times 10^{-5}\) | \(z_\mathrm{top}\) | 13.9 cm |
| 0.1 m | none | \(6.25 \times 10^{-4}\) | \(z_\mathrm{top}\) | 1.4 cm |
| 1 m | 0.5 m | \(1.25 \times 10^{-4}\) | \(z_\mathrm{top} - 0.25\) m | 7.0 cm |

The first row takes a layer thickness as the bed. The drain, not the aquifer, then limits the discharge. In the last row the head stands 7.0 cm above a drain 25 cm under the top: the cell passes its recharge 18 cm under the ground.

Fig. 53 The four rows of the table as curves, from `hk_fallback_drain_conductance` and `drain_discharge_band`. The dashed line is the discharge that passes the recharge of the cell. The 30 m bed reaches it 4.17 m above the top, off the figure.

## Assumptions

- A drain is a seepage face: the head the drain itself needs to pass the recharge is small beside the thickness of the aquifer.
- The land inside a cell is flat, unless a band is declared.
- Recharge is a flux set from outside. It does not read the water table.

## Limits

- A drain cell has one elevation. The band is the one remedy. It applies to every drain cell alike and classifies nothing.
- A declared conductance has a floor under MODFLOW 6 only. MODFLOW-NWT takes it as it is.
- The ETP is not read under MODFLOW 6 outside soil mode. A loaded ETP is ignored, with a warning.

## Parameters of this page

[flow.bc.<name>]

`# value = ‹number or list of number›` : Boundary-condition value, scalar or one value per stress period.
**Path**: `flow.bc.<name>.value`
**More**: On a drainage boundary it is a conductance in m2/s, and it may be left out: the run then derives it from the conductivity, C = K * cell_area / solver.drain_bed_thickness_m, which keeps the drain proportional to K and makes K/R the quantity a network calibration searches. A zero or negative number selects that same derivation, so it does NOT mean a closed boundary; write a positive conductance to impose one.
**Accepted**: number or list of number

[solver]

`# drain_band_depth_m = 0.0` : Metres. m
**Path**: `solver.drain_band_depth_m`
**More**: Depth D of the sub-cell discharge band every drain cell gets instead of a single elevation: the drain sits at top - D/2 and its conductance is multiplied by top_layer_thickness / D. The multiplier is the thickness and not the cell area because the conductance it scales is already Kv*A/b, so scaling by b/D gives Kv*A/D, which is CDRN exactly; scaling by A/D would give an m3/s where a conductance is m2/s, too high by A/b. The cell therefore starts discharging before the head reaches its mean elevation, and discharges harder the higher the head climbs into the band. This answers the one question the USGS documents about a model top, that the land inside a cell is not flat: UZF1 exposes the same depth as SURFDEP, 'the average undulation depth within a finite-difference cell', and MODFLOW 6 carries it into DRN as DDRN, with HDRN = land surface - DDRN/2 and CDRN = Kv*A/DDRN. MODFLOW 6 solves its DDRN band with a smooth (linear then cubic) curve; the option here is the piecewise equivalent of the same idea, applied identically by both MODFLOW backends, so a later switch to the native smooth form is a documented refinement and not a surprise. It does NOT move the topography: no elevation is raised, no DEM is rewritten, and every other package sees the surface it would have seen. The seepage criterion is the one reader that cannot: a banded cell discharges at top - D/2 and never climbs back to top, so the mask follows the band and the run persists D in its store for every figure drawn afterwards. It classifies no cell: every drain cell gets the same band, so nothing has to be sorted into artefact and real. Pick D the way Feinstein et al. 2020 (Groundwater 58:524-534, doi:10.1111/gwat.12931) do, from the standard deviation of the fine land-surface elevations inside a cell; they obtain 0.61 m. Mutually exclusive with solver.sink_fill, which answers the same question by removing drains instead. Default 0.0: one elevation per drain, unchanged from every earlier run.
**Accepted**: number
**Unit**: m
**Example**: `0.0`, `0.5`

`# sink_fill = false` : Dimensionless.
**Path**: `solver.sink_fill`
**More**: Remove the drain from every cell sitting in a closed depression of the model top, by setting its DRN conductance to zero. A closed depression has no outlet, so water reaching it ponds instead of seeping into a stream, and a drain there invents a discharge point. The depressions are measured on the solver mesh, by a priority flood seeded on every cell water can leave the domain through; both MODFLOW backends read the same mask. This does NOT move the topography: no elevation is raised, no DEM is rewritten, and every other package sees the surface it would have seen. Refused when the mask cannot be built. The depressions are counted on the four shared faces MODFLOW connects, not on the eight neighbours a raster fill uses: measured on the Nancon, 4.56 per cent of the mesh against 2.12 per cent, a factor of two that is the neighbourhood and nothing else. NOT SANCTIONED BY ANY SOURCE: no manual, no USGS document and no guideline removes a discharge boundary where a pit is detected, and measured here it degrades both scores. The remedy the USGS does document for the same question is solver.drain_band_depth_m, which gives every cell a discharge band instead of taking the drain away. Default false, which drains every cell as before.
**Accepted**: true | false
**Example**: `false`, `true`

`# drain_bed_thickness_m = 1.0` : Metres. m > 0 expert
**Path**: `solver.drain_bed_thickness_m`
**More**: Thickness of the drain BED in the fallback conductance C = K * cell_area / bed_thickness, used when no drainage conductance is declared. A drain bed is the clogging layer at the bottom of a watercourse, decimetres to a metre; it is NOT the aquifer, and the layer thickness this used to borrow (30 m on the Nancon) has no physical relation to it. The value matters because it sets how much head the drain itself imposes to pass the recharge: dh = R * bed_thickness / K, independent of the cell size. On the Nancon at R = 439 mm/yr, 30 m gives 4.17 m of head at K = 1e-7 m/s and makes the drain the limiting resistance over two decades of a [1e-7, 1e-3] search; 1 m gives 13.9 cm and 0.1 m gives 1.4 cm. In this method the drain is a seepage face, so it must never limit: K and the recharge decide where water surfaces, not the boundary condition. Proportionality to K is preserved either way, so the K/R invariance the network criterion rests on is untouched.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: m
**Example**: `1.0`, `0.5`, `0.1`

`# drain_conductance_floor_m2_s = 1e-12` : m2/s. s > 0 expert
**Path**: `solver.drain_conductance_floor_m2_s`
**More**: Floor applied to every DRN conductance, whether declared or derived from hk. It exists for degenerate cells only, a zero-thickness or zero-conductivity cell whose formula would divide by zero or emit a zero-conductance drain MODFLOW reads as absent. It is not a physical choice and moving it does not tune anything: a real conductance on a real cell is many orders of magnitude above it. Raise it only to make a degenerate mesh audible.
**Accepted**: number
**Valid range**: > 0 (refused outside)
**Unit**: s

[flow.sinks_sources.recharge]

`# negative_to_evt = true` : When true, negative recharge values are routed to the solver EVT package and RCH receives the non-negative clipped recharge. dev
**Path**: `flow.sinks_sources.recharge.negative_to_evt`
**Accepted**: true | false

# Fixed heads: the sea, the rivers and the sides

A fixed head takes the head of a cell out of the solution. The flux across the cell becomes a result. HydroModPy uses it for the sea, for a river given as a head, and for the sides of the model.

## The law

A fixed head takes the cell out of the solution in every layer and every period: \(h_n = h^\mathrm{bc}\), the value that the boundary, or its forcing, gives for the period. This is the CHD package of MODFLOW 6 (input guide, [Langevin et al., 2017]) and of MODFLOW-2005 [Harbaugh, 2005].

The flux across the cell is stored in the budget as `constant_head`, and the share of it that crosses a river cell as `constant_head_stream` (Where the water table reaches the surface reads that share). HydroModPy builds neither the GHB nor the RIV package, so a fixed head is never a conductance-limited exchange. A river that must exchange through a streambed is a stream network (Streams and the water mover).

## The sea

The sea cells are the cells of the model domain whose DEM is not above the highest sea level of the run:

(31)\[ \mathcal{C}_\mathrm{sea} = \{\, n \in \text{domain} : z^\mathrm{dem}_n \leq \max_t h_\mathrm{sea}(t) \,\} . \]

A cell below that level far inland is in the set: the code does not test the connection to the sea. The drains stay on the other cells. The level is set in [flow.bc].

MODFLOW-NWT selects its cells by the same DEM, with one difference: its constant-head rows take \(z^\mathrm{dem}_n < h_\mathrm{sea}\), and its `ibound` takes \(z^\mathrm{dem}_n \leq h_\mathrm{sea}\).

In the code: `ocean_chd_support_mask`.

## The rivers and the sides

The river cells are the river cells of the mesh support, or the cells with the `support_label` given to the boundary. A side boundary is the cells along one side of the model. A cell that falls in two sets keeps the last head written, in the order sea, river, side.

One CHD package carries the three. The build therefore writes which cells are sea and which are river in a file beside the solver files, and the extraction reads it to tell a river head from a sea head. That is how the river share of the constant-head flux reaches the stored budget.

In the code: `assemble_constant_head_stress_period_data`.

## Limits

- The sea is not a density model. There is no interface between fresh and salt water, and no tide inside a period. The sea is a fixed head with the level of its period.
- The sea cells are selected by their DEM, with the one difference between the two MODFLOW solvers given above.
- A river head is a fixed head. A river that exchanges through a bed is a stream network. Stream heads need MODFLOW 6 or Boussinesq: MODFLOW-NWT has the sea and the sides.

## Parameters of this page

**Path**: `flow.active_bc`
**More**: 'lake' and 'reservoir' build a MODFLOW 6 LAK package, so only the modflow6 solver takes them. An empty list builds no boundary.
**Accepted**: list of string
**Example**: `["ocean"]`, `["west_side", "east_side", "drainage"]`

`# value = ‹number or list of number›` : Boundary-condition value, scalar or one value per stress period.

**More**: On a drainage boundary it is a conductance in m2/s, and it may be left out: the run then derives it from the conductivity, C = K * cell_area / solver.drain_bed_thickness_m, which keeps the drain proportional to K and makes K/R the quantity a network calibration searches. A zero or negative number selects that same derivation, so it does NOT mean a closed boundary; write a positive conductance to impose one.
**Accepted**: number or list of number

<!-- https://docs.hydromodpy.fr/dev/theory/exits/lakes.html -->
# Lakes and reservoirs

A lake is a boundary package laid on the aquifer grid. Its cells are made inactive in their top layers, and the LAK package of MODFLOW 6 holds the storage and the exchange through connections it builds itself. The stage is a result. The keys of a lake are in [flow.sinks_sources.lakes].

## The balance

The LAK package of MODFLOW 6 solves a water balance of the lake: the stage \(s_L\) is the unknown, and the volume \(V_L\) and the surface area \(A_L\) are looked up in the stage-volume-area table of the lake. The lake gains rain, runoff and managed inflow, loses evaporation, withdrawal and outlet discharge, and exchanges with the aquifer through its connections (input guide, [Langevin et al., 2017], chapter 7). The outlets go to the outside, to another lake or to the mover (Streams and the water mover).

HydroModPy checks the table before MODFLOW 6 sees it. The table has at least two rows. The stage increases strictly, the volume increases strictly with it, the surface area does not decrease, and no volume or area is negative.

In the code: `build_lake_table`.

## The connections

MODFLOW 6 gives each connection the conductance of the bed and the aquifer in series, \(C^\mathrm{lak}_c\), from the leakance \(\lambda_b\) and the contact area. A leakance of zero seals the bed. HydroModPy builds two kinds of connection for each lake column:

- one vertical connection to the first active cell under the occupied layers: the leakage towards the aquifer, through the vertical conductivity;
- one horizontal connection per occupied layer across every edge shared with an active neighbour that is not a lake cell: the bank seepage, through the horizontal conductivity. Its width is the length of the shared edge, its length the distance from the neighbour centre to the edge, and its elevations those of the neighbour layer clipped to the vertical extent of the lake.

A cutoff wall seals the horizontal connections to the cells behind it.

In the code: `build_lake_connectiondata`.

## Two ways to hold the footprint

In the fixed-area mode, the footprint cells are inactive and the table alone gives the storage. In the active-shore mode, `dynamic_area`, the bed cells stay active with the carved bathymetry as their top. A cell exchanges with the lake while it is under water, and recharges as land when the shore falls below its bed. The drain rows of those cells are removed: a drain there would send the leakage of the lake straight back to the streams, through the aquifer, the drain and the mover, and the exchange would recirculate.

## What falls on the lake

The rain and the evaporation of a lake are the catchment means of the loaded precipitation and ETP, unless the lake declares its own. The runoff is the catchment runoff rate times the catchment area \(A\). It reaches the lake directly only when no stream network routes the runoff; otherwise it arrives through the reaches and the mover (Rain and evaporation: the forcing). A declared forcing wins over these defaults.

The managed inflow and the withdrawal are set to zero in the steady periods. A steady period has no storage term, and a managed flux that does not balance the natural budget has no equilibrium stage: the solve would diverge.

By default the stage is free from the first period. With `steady_stage_hold`, and a run that starts with a steady period, the build holds it at the starting stage (LAK status constant) through the steady warm-up, and frees it on the first transient period. A managed reservoir whose observed level is far from the natural equilibrium then keeps that level, and the aquifer settles around it.

The package takes one smoothing depth for the wet and dry transition of the lake edge, `surfdep`: the largest declared among the lakes.

## The mask on the other packages

The lake cells carry no recharge and no aquifer evapotranspiration: the lake takes its own rain and evaporates through LAK. Without the mask, MODFLOW 6 would hand the recharge of an inactive lake cell to the first active cell below it, and the rain would be counted twice (Drains and evapotranspiration at the top of the model).

## Limits

- A lake has one stage. The volume and the surface area follow the table, and the lake exchanges with the cells under and beside its footprint, and with no other.
- A lake needs MODFLOW 6. The check stops a file that declares one with another solver.
- A lake in soil mode needs a stream network. The check refuses a lake without `"sfr"` when the soil reservoir is declared, because the water that seeps out of the ground reaches the lake only through the streams.
- The active-shore mode is harder for the solver. Many cells change between wet and dry at once. A larger `surfdep` helps, and blurs the shoreline.

**Path**: `flow.sinks_sources.lakes.<name>.bed_reconstruction.dynamic_area`
**More**: When True the lake-bed cells stay ACTIVE with the carved bathymetric bed as their cell top and one VERTICAL LAK connection each; MODFLOW 6 then toggles recharge/ET per cell (IWETLAKE) so a cell exchanges with the lake when submerged and recharges as land when the shoreline recedes below its bed. When False the footprint is deactivated (fixed-area reservoir, the classic inactive-footprint carve).
**Accepted**: true | false

[flow.sinks_sources.lakes.<name>.outlets.mover]

`# mvrtype = "FACTOR"` : How much of the outlet flow the mover passes to the receiver, given value.
**Path**: `flow.sinks_sources.lakes.<name>.outlets.mover.mvrtype`
**Values**:
- `"FACTOR"` : Moves the share value (from 0 to 1) of the flow.
- `"UPTO"` : Moves the flow, capped at value.
- `"EXCESS"` : Moves only the part of the flow above value.
- `"THRESHOLD"` : Moves value once the flow exceeds it, and nothing below it.
**Accepted**: "FACTOR" | "UPTO" | "EXCESS" | "THRESHOLD"

# Routing on the mesh: the descent D

Where the water of a drain goes next is a question of routing. A mesh top has pits that a DEM routed on its own grid never had, and a pit holds the water it receives. Routing needs a surface on which every cell has a way down. The model top is not that surface, and raising it would change the ground the solver sees. The descent \(D\) solves this on a copy: the copy is filled, the receivers of every cell are read on it, and it never goes back to the solver. The drain elevations, the streambeds and the reach tops keep reading \(z_\mathrm{top}\).

## The flood

\(D\) is the result of a priority flood [Barnes et al., 2014]. Its seeds are the cells of the rim of the routable domain and the fixed-head cells (Fixed heads: the sea, the rivers and the sides). The flood visits the cells in order of their filled level, from the lowest seed up. A cell \(m\) reached from a cell \(n\) of filled level \(\tilde z_n\) takes

(32)\[\begin{split} \tilde z_m = \begin{cases} \tilde z_n + \epsilon_m & \text{if } z_{\mathrm{top},m} \leq \tilde z_n + \eta,\\ z_{\mathrm{top},m} & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \end{split}\]

The step \(\epsilon_m\) is 1 mm. When the run has a channel network (below), the step is 1 mm on the channel cells and 2 mm elsewhere, so that a filled flat climbs faster away from the channel than along it and its steepest descent heads into the channel.

The tolerance \(\eta\) is twice the drop under which the receiver graph sees no descent. With \(\Delta z\) the range of the top over the routable cells, in metres,

(33)\[ \eta = 2 \max\bigl(10^{-9},\ 10^{-9} \max(\Delta z,\ 1)\bigr)\ \mathrm{m}, \]

that is \(2 \times 10^{-9}\) m when the relief is under a metre, and \(2 \times 10^{-9}\) times the relief above. A cell within \(\eta\) of the flood level is raised too, so that no link of the receiver graph drops by less than the tolerance of that graph.

A lake is crossed, never used as a seed. Its cells keep their top and are flooded to their spill level like any depression, so the lake drains through its outlet and the cells below a dam keep draining downstream. The role of a sink belongs to the walks that read \(D\): they stop at the first lake cell.

In the code: `build_descent`.

## The receivers

On the filled copy, the receiver \(r(n)\) of a cell is its steepest-descent neighbour [O'Callaghan and Mark, 1984]. Only the neighbours lower by more than the tolerance \(\eta_r = 10^{-9} \max(\Delta\tilde z,\ 1)\) m count, where \(\Delta\tilde z\) is the range of the filled copy:

(34)\[ r(n) = \underset{m \in \mathcal{N}_D(n),\ \tilde z_n - \tilde z_m > \eta_r}{\arg\max}\ \frac{\tilde z_n - \tilde z_m}{\lVert x_n - x_m \rVert}, \qquad r(n) = -1 \text{ if there is none.} \]

The filled range is a little wider than the range of the top, and the factor 2 of (33) covers that difference. The distance is between cell centres, so a diagonal step on a square grid is \(\sqrt 2\) cells long and wins only when it is steeper.

The neighbours \(\mathcal{N}_D(n)\) are the cells that share a node with \(n\) on a quad mesh (diagonals included, as in the D8 descent) and the cells that share a face on any other mesh. A seed keeps its steepest descent too, so that an accumulation passes through a fixed-head cell. The walks that must end where water leaves the model read the receiver with \(-1\) on the fixed-head cells.

Every link of \(D\) descends, so the receiver chains never cycle and every routable cell reaches a seed. The build refuses a \(D\) where a cell has no way down.

## A pit, by hand

A 3 by 3 grid of squares of 10 m, with a pit in the middle and a lower cell on the south side. The seeds are the eight rim cells, and a seed keeps its top. The flood starts at the lowest, the south cell at 4 m, and reaches the centre. The centre is below the flood level, so it takes \(4 + 0.001\) m.

Fig. 51 The model top, and the filled copy with the receiver of each cell, from one call of `build_descent`. The five northern cells drain to the centre, now the lowest neighbour. The two southern corners drain to the south cell: it drops 1 m over 10 m, the centre 0.999 m over 14.1 m. The centre drains south. The south cell has no lower neighbour, and water leaves the model there. The pit is raised on \(D\) only: its top in the solver stays 3 m.

## The channel tree

When the run generates a stream network (see Streams and the water mover), \(D\) follows it. That network was traced on the D8 pointer of the DEM routing. On the mesh, a cell that holds a pixel of it is a channel cell, and it is pinned to the next channel cell along the network. A pinned cell drains to its pin, adjacent or not, even where the top climbs along the channel. Without the pins, \(D\) would descend its own flats by flood order and run beside the channel. A cell outside the channel keeps its steepest descent. A run with `geographic.river_network.enabled` off has no pinned cell.

## What D is used for

- Stream reaches and drainage routing (Streams and the water mover).
- Accumulation of the outflow of each cell (Where the water table reaches the surface).
- The flow direction figure, and the foot of each dam read by the heads rule of the stream criterion.

Both MODFLOW solvers build it at every run and store it with the mesh. A run stored without it gets one rebuilt on read from the stored top, without pins, fixed-head seeds or lakes, and the log says so. MODFLOW-NWT seeds \(D\) on the cells it writes as a fixed head, and builds no stream head and no lake.

## The graph of the stream criterion

The stream-network criterion (Downslope distance between two networks) does not read \(D\). It floods its own copy of the model top with the same flood, and reads its receivers with (34). The two answer two questions: \(D\) routes water in the model, the criterion graph measures distances on the top. They differ in these ways.

| | The descent \(D\) | The criterion graph |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Seeds | the rim of the routable domain and the fixed-head cells | the border of the active domain |
| Lakes | crossed, flooded to their spill level | part of the graph, removed from the supports of the means |
| Channel | pinned to the generated network | free |
| Raised cells | below the flood level, or within \(\eta\) above it | below the flood level |
| Neighbours | D8 on a quad mesh | D8 on a quad mesh unless `diagonal_neighbors` is false |

Both use the step \(\epsilon\) of 1 mm off a channel. The flood and the receivers always read the same neighbour graph: a flood that walked eight neighbours while the receivers read four would leave filled cells that spill over a diagonal the receivers cannot take.

## Assumptions

- Water leaves a cell by one receiver (single flow direction).
- The filled copy is a computation. It changes no head and no elevation the solver reads.

## Limits

- Meshes without diagonals. On a mesh whose faces are not all quadrilaterals, the neighbours are the cells sharing a face, whatever the key asks.
- A run stored before \(D\) was kept routes on a \(D\) rebuilt without pins, fixed-head seeds or lakes.

[calibration.outputs.<name>]

`# diagonal_neighbors = true` : Descend over shared nodes, the eight D8 neighbours of a quad mesh. only if support = "network"
**Path**: `calibration.outputs.<name>.diagonal_neighbors`
**More**: True is the paper: its distances are traced by WhiteboxTools on a D8 pointer, and the delineation that produced the catchment uses one too. False descends over shared edges only, four neighbours (D4), and departs from the paper. It is not a second-decimal choice: on a synthetic valley whose talweg runs along the grid diagonal, the most accumulated cell collects 100 per cent of the domain over shared nodes and 6.6 per cent over shared edges. On a mesh whose faces are not all quadrilaterals no cell has a diagonal and the descent walks shared edges either way; on a Voronoi mesh the two graphs are the same one.
**Accepted**: true | false
**Only if**: support = "network"
