# Where the water table reaches the surface

The model produces sources, not a stream network. A cell where the aquifer releases water to the surface is a point where water appears, not a reach. The simulated network is built from those points, in four levels that should not be confused:

1. the cells where the water table reaches the drain: the seepage mask;
1. how much water the aquifer releases in each cell: the release flux;
1. where the water goes on the descent \(D\): the accumulated flux;
1. the cells a stream criterion counts as flowing: the simulated network.

The last section lists the diagnostics that compare a network with a mapped one. The criterion a calibration minimises is on Downslope distance between two networks.

Fig. 57 The four levels on a toy valley. The water table is a subdued copy of the top, not a solve; every step after it is a call of the code: `seepage_mask`, the outflow of a drain, `accumulate_on_downhill_graph` on \(D\), and `build_simulated_network` with \(\tau_\mathrm{s} = 0.5\). In the last map, the light cells join the sources downstream: they carry water and release none.

## 1. The seepage mask

The water table of a cell is the head of its uppermost layer with a finite head. A cell seeps in period \(t\) when the water table reaches the drain:

(39)\[\begin{split} m_n(t) = \begin{cases} 1 & h^{\mathrm{wt}}_n(t) \geq z_{\mathrm{top},n} - \delta/2,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases} \end{split}\]

With no band, \(\delta = 0\) and the test is against the top (Drains and evapotranspiration at the top of the model). A solver that reports a surface release flux of its own, the Boussinesq solver, uses that flux instead: the cell seeps where the flux is positive. The mask says that the water table reached the ground, not how much water left.

In the code: `seepage_mask`.

## 2. The release flux

The budget gives the flow \(\Phi_{n,p}\) of each package into each cell, negative when the aquifer loses water. The drain outflow \(q^\mathrm{drn}_n\) is the drain flow added to the part handed to the mover, then clipped to its positive part in each layer and summed over the layers. A run whose streams are an SFR network sends most of its water through that package, so the drain alone misses it. The release flux is the union of every path from the aquifer to the surface:

(40)\[ q^\mathrm{rel}_n(t) = q^\mathrm{drn}_n(t) + \max(-\Phi_{n,\mathrm{sfr}}, 0) + \max(-\Phi_{n,\mathrm{lak}}, 0) + \max(-\Phi^{\mathrm{stream}}_{n,\mathrm{chd}}, 0) + \max(q^{\mathrm{ex}}_n, 0). \]

\(\Phi^{\mathrm{stream}}_{n,\mathrm{chd}}\) is the fixed-head flux of the cells that carry the river role (Fixed heads: the sea, the rivers and the sides), stored as `constant_head_stream`. The last term is the surface excess of the Boussinesq solver, the only path out of that solver, already an outflow. The plain fixed-head term stays out: a sea or a side boundary is water leaving sideways, not a release to the surface.

The stream-network criterion reads the same union off the budget, so the network a calibration scores and the network the maps draw come from one quantity. A run stored before the river share of the fixed head was stored lacks that one term.

The release flux is rebuilt on read from the per-cell budget, which a run keeps by default (`simulation.results.keep_per_cell_budget`).

In the code: `release_flux_stack`.

## 3. The accumulated flux, on D

The drain outflow is routed downstream on the stored descent \(D\) (Routing on the mesh: the descent D): the accumulated flux \(F_n\) of a cell is its own outflow plus that of every cell upstream, the usual flow accumulation on a single-flow-direction graph [O'Callaghan and Mark, 1984]. High values mark the confluences and the persistent branches. \(F_n\) is a routed diagnostic: the same water is counted again in every cell downstream, so the sum of \(F\) over the cells is not a water budget. Use the budget for a mass balance. \(F\) is the field `accumulation_flux`, and the same routing applied to the release flux gives `release_accumulation_flux`. The Boussinesq solver, whose store holds a top and no mesh connectivity, stores a \(D\) built from the D8 pointer of WhiteboxTools on its filled top, for a raster run, and routes on it.

A cell is active in period \(t\) when a field, \(F\) for instance, exceeds a threshold. A time rule reduces the periods to one mask:

| Mode | Active when |
| --- | --- |
| `last` | the cell is active at the chosen period, the last by default |
| `any` | the cell is active at least once |
| `persistent` | the cell is active in at least a given share of the periods |
| `always_active` | the cell is active in every period (`perennial` is a synonym) |
| `persistence` | not a mask: the share of the periods where the cell is active |

A steady run uses `last` by default, since it has one state. A transient run uses `persistent`, with a share of one half unless another is given. An always-active mask is active at every period of the window analysed, which is not a steady network.

The derived fields are not stored: they are rebuilt on read from the per-cell budget, which a run keeps by default with `simulation.results.keep_per_cell_budget` (see [simulation]).

In the code: `accumulate_on_downhill_graph`.

## 4. The simulated network

The network that a calibration scores, and that the stream maps draw, is not a threshold of \(F\). It is built from the release flux on the graph of the stream criterion (The graph of the stream criterion), in two steps.

The sources. A cell is a source in period \(t\) when its release exceeds a share of its own recharge, strictly:

(41)\[ \Sigma(t) = \{\, n : q^\mathrm{rel}_n(t) > \tau_\mathrm{s}\,\bar N\,a_n \,\} . \]

\(\bar N\) is the unweighted mean of the finite recharge rates over the periods and the cells. The threshold is a flux per unit of area, not a discharge, so that the network follows the physics and not the refinement of the mesh: a fixed discharge would be nine times harsher on a cell three times smaller. A value of zero is the purely geometric criterion. The test is made on the flux, not on the head, which moves a lot when the drain conductance moves. \(\bar N\) is read back from the built model at every trial of a calibration, and a change between two builds is logged as a warning: the threshold is meant to be frozen over a search.

The closure. The simulated network \(\mathcal{S}\) is the downstream closure of the sources: every cell the water of \(\Sigma\) flows through, \(\Sigma\) included. When a visible flow \(\Phi_\mathrm{vis}\) is set, a cell of the closure must also carry it, as the release of the sources routed down the same graph:

(42)\[ \Phi_n(t) = \sum_{m\,:\,m \rightsquigarrow n} q^\mathrm{rel}_m(t)\,\mathbb{1}[\,m \in \Sigma(t)\,] \;\geq\; \Phi_\mathrm{vis} , \qquad \Phi_n(t) > 0 . \]

The sum runs over the sources whose chain passes through \(n\). The visible flow is a discharge with its unit, or a share of the discharge at the outlet in the same period; zero is the geometric definition. The routed discharge never falls downstream, so the network stays closed downstream whatever the threshold. It is a routed seepage discharge, not a river discharge: no runoff and no bed loss enter it.

The flowing cells are the field `simulated_active_network`, 1 where a stream flows and 0 elsewhere. It is rebuilt on read from the release flux (itself rebuilt from the per-cell budget) and from a stored network on which the graph is rebuilt. It is never stored, and it needs the release terms of the per-cell budget, which a run keeps by default.

Over a transient run, the criterion counts, for each complete calendar year, the periods each cell flows, and builds a maximal and a minimal extent from those counts. Durations are counted in periods, never in days. How a network is scored against a mapped one is on Downslope distance between two networks.

In the code: `build_simulated_network`.

## Comparing a network with a map

A run stores up to three line networks, each under a role:

| Role | The network |
| --- | --- |
| `reference` | the mapped network read from `data.hydrography` |
| `reference_permanent` | the reaches of the mapped network that flow all year, when the source says which |
| `generated` | the network traced on the routing of the DEM, `geographic.river_network` |

The roles `simulated_active` and `mesh_constraint` are reserved names that no run writes today: the simulated network is the cell field above. A mapped network is never a model input: it enters a criterion, a figure or a diagnostic, never the model top or the routing.

Three families of diagnostics compare a mask of active cells \(A\) with a network. None of them is the criterion of a calibration.

Overlap of cells. \(M\) is the set of catchment cells a network crosses, within an optional buffer, and \(A\) the active cells of a field (by default the accumulated flux above zero, with the time rule above). The scores are the usual set scores of \(A\) against \(M\), published as `network_coverage_ratio` (the share of \(M\) in \(A\)), `active_precision_ratio` (the share of \(A\) in \(M\)), `cell_f1_ratio` (their harmonic mean) and `cell_jaccard_ratio` (the intersection over the union), by `cell_field_network_overlap_metrics`.

Planar distance. The straight-line distance from each active cell centre to the nearest line of the network is \(\delta_{A\to M}\), and from each network cell centre to the nearest active cell \(\delta_{M\to A}\). Each direction gives its mean, median, 95th percentile and maximum, then

(43)\[ \bar\delta = \tfrac12\bigl(\overline{\delta_{A\to M}} + \overline{\delta_{M\to A}}\bigr), \qquad \rho_\delta = \frac{\overline{\delta_{A\to M}}}{\overline{\delta_{M\to A}}} , \]

published as `bidirectional_distance_mean_m`, `planar_distance_ratio` and its logarithm `planar_distance_log10_ratio` (`cell_field_network_distance_metrics`). A planar distance ignores the divides. The downslope distance of Downslope distance between two networks does not.

Overlap of lines. Between two line networks, a reference \(R\) and a candidate \(G\) (by default the mapped and the generated networks), each buffered by a tolerance of 50 m by default. The metrics are the share of the reference length inside the buffer of the candidate (`reference_coverage_ratio`), the share of the candidate length inside the buffer of the reference (`candidate_match_ratio`), the length ratio `length_balance_ratio`, the missing and extra shares, their harmonic mean `length_f1_ratio` and the Hausdorff distance of the two networks (`Run.hydrographic_network_comparison_metrics`).

## Assumptions

- The release flux is the whole of what leaves the aquifer for the surface.
- The threshold \(\tau_\mathrm{s}\) and the mean recharge \(\bar N\) are frozen over a search.

## Limits

- The accumulated flux is not a budget. It counts the same water in every cell downstream.
- The simulated network is a mask computed on read. It is not a stored line network.
- The size of the threshold. \(\tau_\mathrm{s}\) is a share of a cell’s own recharge. A cell that collects drainage from upslope releases more than the recharge that falls on it, so a small share excludes few cells. No value is given here as the one to use.

# Streams and the water mover

A stream network (SFR) routes the water it receives from reach to reach and exchanges water with the aquifer through its bed. The water mover (MVR) hands the outflow of one package to another: a drain to a reach, a reach to a lake, a lake to a reach. Both need MODFLOW 6. The keys of a network are in [flow.sinks_sources.sfr].

## What a reach is

An SFR network is a set of reaches. Each reach \(j\) has a length \(L_j\), a width \(w_j\), a gradient \(S_j\), a bed top \(z^{\mathrm{rtp}}_j\), a bed thickness \(b_s\), a bed conductivity \(K_b\) and a Manning roughness \(n_M\). It exchanges water with the aquifer cell under it, and passes its flow to the reach below.

The reaches are the cells that the generated stream network crosses, cut by the mesh, or the rows of an explicit table of reaches. An observed network never becomes a reach. With `rectify_on_mesh`, the cells of the generated network are the seeds of a single-flow-direction channel re-derived on the descent \(D\) (Routing on the mesh: the descent D): from every seed, the receivers of \(D\) are followed one cell at a time until the trace reaches a lake, a fixed-head cell or a channel cell already traced. The result is one cell wide, continuous on \(D\), follows the thalweg of \(D\), and ends at a real sink. Short parallel stubs beside a longer channel are demoted to hillslope drainage. Each cell keeps the width, the stream order and the bed properties of the seed whose trace reached it. The gradient is \(S_j = \max(S_j^{\mathrm{delineated}}, S_\mathrm{min})\).

In the code: `rectify_reach_graph`.

## The bed

The beds of a network are placed by one solve, in two passes. The cell is the hard constraint and the downhill order the soft one. Each reach has a box from its own cell:

(38)\[ z^{\mathrm{bot}}_j + b_s + 0.1\ \mathrm{m} \;\leq\; z^{\mathrm{rtp}}_j \;\leq\; z^{\mathrm{top}}_j - \beta_\mathrm{inc}, \]

where \(z^{\mathrm{top}}_j\) and \(z^{\mathrm{bot}}_j\) are the top and the bottom of the reach cell, and \(\beta_\mathrm{inc}\) is zero when the incision is not set. A bed never sits above the ground of its own cell. When the incision is set, the bed may also not sink more than `max_bed_sag` below the upper bound. An empty box stops the build and names the reach. Inside the boxes the bed descends downstream by at least \(S_\mathrm{min}\) times the mean length of two neighbouring reaches. Where a traced channel climbs and the box and the order cannot both hold, the box wins and the build logs the worst step, so a defect of the trace cannot drag a bed far below the ground of its cell.

In the code: `solve_reach_bed_profile`.

## Flow and exchange

The flow balance of a reach, the exchange through the streambed and the stage from Manning’s equation for a rectangular section are the MODFLOW 6 SFR package [Langevin et al., 2017] (chapter 7; input guide: SFR). HydroModPy fills it as follows.

- The exchange goes through the streambed with a conductance of \(K_b / b_s\) times the wetted area of the bed, built from `streambed_k` and `streambed_thickness`. The stage uses `manning` and the gradient floored by `min_slope`.
- With `connected_to_aquifer` off, the network is pure routing and has no exchange with the aquifer.
- The inflow of the headwater reaches is split by drainage area. The catchment runoff of the period (Rain and evaporation: the forcing) is distributed over all the reaches by length. Rain and evaporation are rates, the same on every reach, applied by MODFLOW 6 to the reach area.
- A cell that hosts a connected reach loses its drain row: its baseflow goes into the stream through the bed, not out of the model through a drain. The drain rows of the cells around stay, and `route_drainage` sends their outflow to the stream (below).

## The numerical choice

MODFLOW 6 can skip the extra Picard iterations of SFR when the reaches are numbered from upstream to downstream. HydroModPy numbers them that way and sets the maximum to 1, except when `route_drainage` is on. The mover then feeds the reaches, and that exchange belongs to the nonlinear coupling, not to the routing order: one pass per outer iteration would let the inflow creep while the head has settled.

In the code: `build_sfr_package_args`.

## The water mover

The MVR package takes water from a provider, a feature of one package, and gives it to a receiver, a feature of another, by a rule (FACTOR, UPTO, EXCESS or THRESHOLD) [Morway et al., 2021]; input guide: MVR. HydroModPy writes records for three connections, and writes MVR last, after every package it names.

| Provider | Receiver | Rule | Set by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| a drain cell of the basin | the first reach or lake met on \(D\) | FACTOR, value 1 | `route_drainage` |
| a terminal reach | a lake | the rule of the network | `outflow_to_lake` |
| a lake outlet | another lake, a reach, or the reach at the foot of the dam | the rule of the outlet | `flow.sinks_sources.lakes.<name>.outlets.mover.mvrtype` |

Fig. 55 The three connections of the mover. The orange arrows are MVR records, with their rule and the key that sets them. The dashed arrow is the routing of SFR itself.

## Routing the hillslope drainage

With `route_drainage`, every drain cell in the basin of \(D\) hands its whole outflow to the water body it would physically reach. The walk starts at the drain cell and follows the receivers of \(D\), the version that stops on a fixed-head cell. It ends at the first connected reach cell or lake cell. A cell whose chain leaves the model first keeps a plain drain, and so does a cell outside the basin.

The basin is the set of cells whose chain passes through the catchment outlet. The outlet follows the rule of the stream criterion: the most drained cell near the outlet the catchment was closed on, else inside the catchment polygon, else the largest basin of the domain.

On a quad mesh \(D\) steps along diagonals, and a chain can cross a reach between two cells that only touch at a corner. When both cells beside a diagonal step are reach cells, the walk ends on the lower of the two.

The provider of a record is the position of the drain in the list of its period. The drain must therefore be static, with a single period of data: a series of conductances would renumber the providers and send the water to the wrong place, and the build refuses it. The budget stores the part the mover took as its own record, `drain_to_mover`.

In the code: `build_drainage_mover_records`.

## Assumptions

- A reach is one cell wide, has one downstream reach (or the declared bifurcation), and has a rectangular section.
- The bed of a reach and its cell are one: the reach exchanges with the cell under it.
- Water routed by the mover reaches its receiver in the same period.

## Limits

- SFR and MVR need MODFLOW 6. The check stops a file that lists `"sfr"` and names another solver.
- One SFR network per model. A second one stops the build.
- A bed near the water table toggles. MODFLOW 6 switches a reach between connected and disconnected at \(z^{\mathrm{rtp}}_j - b_s\). A bed placed near the depth the water table reaches in a season can change state at every outer iteration and stall the solve. The box of (38) keeps every bed inside its cell for this reason.
- No overland flow beyond SFR and the mover. The runoff reaches the streams as a forcing, not through the ground.

**Path**: `flow.sinks_sources.sfr.<name>.rectify_on_mesh`
**More**: From every delineated cell the descent D, a filled copy of the model top, is traced one neighbour at a time until it reaches a lake, the outlet of D, or an already-traced cell. The union of those paths is the channel: one cell wide (a single downstream per cell, so no braiding), continuous on the descent graph (shared faces, or shared nodes on a quad mesh), following the thalweg of D (so the surface flow follows the reach), and always reaching a real sink (no inland dead-end that leaks its flow out). The streambed top is read on the model top, never on D. D is a copy and never returns to the solver.
**Accepted**: true | false

# Rain and evaporation: the forcing

The aquifer model does not see days: it sees stress periods, and one rate per cell for each period. This page gives the rules that turn daily series and daily grids into those rates. How the outputs are put back on the same periods is on Time alignment of outputs and observations. The keys are in [flow.sinks_sources.recharge] and [simulation].

The period, unit, coverage and runoff rules are the same under the three solvers; sections 5 and 7 note where they differ. The daily soil reservoir (The daily soil reservoir) is here one more source of daily grids.

## 1. The window is cut into periods

The edges start at \(b_0 = t_0\) and advance by one step \(\Delta t\) until the first edge that reaches the end of the last day:

(1)\[ b_{k+1} = b_k + \Delta t, \qquad b_{n_\mathrm{per}} = t_\mathrm{end} + 1\ \text{day}\quad(+ 1\ \text{hour for an hourly step}). \]

Period \(k\) is the half-open interval \([b_k, b_{k+1})\). The end date is part of the run, so the last edge is the day after it. A step that does not land on that edge is refused: the window is not aligned with the step.

Edges can also be given explicitly, as `window.period_bounds`. The code sets them, and no TOML key does. `flow.ic` of type `steady_state` uses this for its auxiliary steady model: one period that spans the whole window (5. Steady periods and first_clim).

In the code: `build_simulation_time_boundaries`.

## 2. One series per variable

The data layer hands a variable over as station records or as grids. Two rules reduce them to the shape the flow needs.

Stations. Several stations are averaged at each stamp, with equal weights. A single station is used as it is.

Spatial mode. `spatial_mode` decides what stays a series and what stays a grid:

| Mode | Stations | Grids |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `auto` | one series | kept as a grid |
| `homogeneous` | one series | reduced to one spatial mean per stamp |
| `heterogeneous` | placed on the cells if they have coordinates, else one series | kept as a grid |

Under `auto`, station records with coordinates become a grid only when no series can be built from them. A grid is not resampled when it is loaded: it is placed on the cells of the solver mesh once the mesh exists, by the method of `interpolation_method` (`nearest`, `linear` or `idw`). The ETP has the same two keys.

In the code: `resolve_forcing`.

## 3. Units

Every data manager hands rain, ETP, recharge and runoff over in mm/day. The binders convert them with the fixed factor \(1/(1000 \times 86400)\) m/s per mm/day, whatever `units` says. That key is read for a rate written in the file: `values` and a numeric `first_clim` are converted from it to m/s when the flow is built.

A sample is a rate. The code averages samples and never sums them: a monthly total in mm must be turned into mm/day before it is given to the model.

## 4. A record gets one value per period

One rule holds for every forcing record: a series, a station, or a grid with a time axis, which is averaged cell by cell of its own grid before it is placed on the mesh.

Samples inside the period. Period \(k\) takes the equal-weight mean of the \(n_k\) samples stamped inside it:

(2)\[ \bar x_k = \frac{1}{n_k} \sum_{t_j \in [b_k,\, b_{k+1})} x_j \qquad \text{if } n_k > 0 . \]

The mean has equal weights, so it is the time mean only for a record with one sample per equal step. Several gridded records that cover one period are averaged the same way, with equal weights.

No sample inside. A sample is the rate of the interval from its stamp to the next stamp. The last sample stands for one step \(\Delta t_r\) of the record, the median spacing of its stamps, and a record of one sample stands for all later time. A period with no sample inside is covered when the interval of the latest earlier sample reaches into it, and takes that sample. So daily data on hourly periods, and a gap inside a record, are covered.

Not covered. A period that no interval reaches, before the first stamp or after the end of the last step, is not covered. `coverage_policy` decides: `"error"`, the default, stops the run and names the periods; `"warn"` warns once per record; `"ignore"` says nothing. Under the last two, the period takes the nearest sample in time: the last one after the record, the first one before it.

Fig. 15 A weekly record on six monthly periods, matched by `samples_by_period`. Each sample stands for the interval up to the next one, and the last for one step. March holds no sample and takes the one in force; May is still inside the last step; June is past it and stops the run by default.

Four records on monthly periods from 1 January 2000, from calls of `align_forcing_series_to_simulation_window`:

| The record | Window | Under `"error"` | The periods take |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| daily, 1 mm/day in January, 3 in February, 5 in March | January to March | runs | 1, 3, 5 |
| 2 on 1 January and 6 on 1 March | January to March | runs | 2, 2 (in force), 6 |
| one sample, 4 on 1 February | January to March | stops: January is before the first stamp | 4, 4, 4 under `"warn"` |
| 60 daily samples from 1 January, valued 0 to 59 | January to June | stops: March to June are after the last step | 15, 45, then 59 four times under `"warn"` |

The `last` rule. A forcing declared by a CSV file under a well, a lake, a stream network or a boundary has an `aggregate` key, for example `flow.sinks_sources.lakes.<name>.rainfall.aggregate`. `"mean"` is the rule above. `"last"` reads the record as a state that holds until it changes: period \(k\) takes the latest sample at or before \(b_k\), and no coverage check applies. The rain, ETP, recharge and runoff of the data layer have no such key.

In the code: `samples_by_period`, `enforce_coverage`.

## 5. Steady periods and `first_clim`

A steady period stands for the long-term state a run starts from. It does not take the rate of its own dates. `first_clim` sets the rate \(\hat N\) of every steady stress period, and of no other period:

(3)\[\begin{split} \hat N = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{n_\mathrm{per}} \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n_\mathrm{per}-1} N_k & \texttt{"mean"},\\[1.5ex] N_0 & \texttt{"first"},\\[0.5ex] F & \text{a number } F,\ \text{in the units of the values.} \end{cases} \end{split}\]

The mean has one weight per period, whatever the length of the period. The steady periods are every period of a steady run, and period 0 of a transient run when `flow.first_period_steady` is true, in the three solvers. A transient period keeps its own rate, whatever its index. Under MODFLOW-NWT the ETP follows the same rule with `first_clim`.

Four periods with rates 2, 4, 9 and 1, from calls of `apply_first_clim`:

| Period 0 | `"mean"` | `"first"` | the number 7 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| first period steady | 4 | 2 | 7 |
| first period transient | 2 | 2 | 2 |

Periods 1 to 3 keep 4, 9 and 1 in both rows.

A run that starts from a steady state of its own (`flow.ic`, type `steady_state`) builds an auxiliary steady model for that state, with `first_clim` set to `"mean"`, or to the prescribed rate. The starting states are the types of [flow.ic].

In the code: `apply_first_clim`.

## 6. Negative recharge goes to the ETP package

A net recharge can be negative: a series of rain minus ETP, for example. With `negative_to_evt`, it is split into a recharge part and a deficit part:

(4)\[ N^+_k = \max(N_k,\, 0), \qquad N^-_k = \max(-N_k,\, 0). \]

The recharge package receives \(N^+_k\) and the evapotranspiration package \(N^-_k\). A transient period keeps its own split. A steady period takes `first_clim` on each part: `"mean"` gives the mean of \(N^+_k\) and the mean of \(N^-_k\), `"first"` gives \(N^+_0\) and \(N^-_0\), and a number \(F\) gives \(\max(F, 0)\) and \(\max(-F, 0)\). So the net rate of a steady period, \(\hat N^+ - \hat N^-\), is always the one `first_clim` states: the mean of the net rates, \(N_0\), or \(F\).

A negative number for `first_clim` needs `negative_to_evt`, or the file is refused. With `negative_to_evt` off, a negative rate in the file is refused when it is read. The deficit is drawn from the water table near the top of each cell, down to the extinction depth \(d_\mathrm{ext}\), and not under the sea, a river head or a lake (Drains and evapotranspiration at the top of the model).

In the code: `split_net_recharge`.

## 7. What the solver does with N and E

The recharge package adds \(N_k\) times the cell area to each cell, and the evapotranspiration package removes at most \(E_k\), less as the head falls to the extinction depth. Both are constant during a stress period. The packages are documented by MODFLOW: RCHA and EVTA in MODFLOW 6 ([Langevin et al., 2017]), RCH and EVT in MODFLOW-2005 and MODFLOW-NWT ([Harbaugh, 2005, Niswonger et al., 2011]). What HydroModPy decides is which rate reaches the ETP package:

- MODFLOW-NWT. The loaded ETP drives the package, with the deficit of 6. Negative recharge goes to the ETP package.
- MODFLOW 6 without a soil reservoir. The loaded ETP is ignored, with a warning if `"etp"` is in `flow.active_sinks_sources`. Only the deficit reaches the package.
- MODFLOW 6 with a soil reservoir. The ETP the soil could not meet reaches the package.
- Boussinesq. `"etp"` in `flow.active_sinks_sources` is refused.

Under MODFLOW 6 the recharge is set to zero on lake cells: the lake gets its own rain through the lake package. The law, the surface and the depth of the ETP package are on Drains and evapotranspiration at the top of the model.

## 8. Runoff is not recharge

The runoff of the data layer, `data.runoff`, never enters the aquifer as a diffuse term. It enters the model, when it enters at all, as a volume per time:

(5)\[ Q^\mathrm{ro}_k = \bar q^\mathrm{ro}_k\,A , \]

where \(\bar q^\mathrm{ro}_k\) is the catchment mean of the runoff, in m/s, put on the periods by the rule of 4. A record gets one value per period, and \(A\) the catchment area.

- With an active stream network, \(Q^\mathrm{ro}_k\) is shared among the reaches by their length and routed downstream. A forcing written in the file wins over the loaded series, and a lake then gets no direct share, so the same water is not counted twice (Streams and the water mover).
- Without a network, a declared lake receives \(Q^\mathrm{ro}_k\) directly (Lakes and reservoirs).
- Without either, the runoff stays outside the flow.

A lake also gets the catchment mean of the loaded rain and ETP as open-water rates, unless it declares its own.

When a calibration compares a simulated drain budget with a gauge, the runoff is added to the simulated discharge, averaged on each period and multiplied by the catchment area, or by the area the gauge drains (Time alignment of outputs and observations). If a stream network already carries the runoff, nothing is added.

## 9. The soil reservoir as a source of grids

With a soil reservoir (`flow.sinks_sources.recharge.soil`), the data layer loads rain and ETP, and the reservoir computes three daily grids in mm/day: recharge, the ETP it could not meet, and runoff. The binders take them where they would take a loaded recharge, ETP and runoff, so they go through the rules of 4. A record gets one value per period and 8. Runoff is not recharge. A daily step gives one slice per period; a monthly step gives the mean of the daily slices of the month.

A soil run refuses a steady first period, since that period would hold the recharge of one day only. A soil run therefore has no steady period, and `first_clim` acts on none of its periods. The daily rules are on The daily soil reservoir.

## Assumptions and limits

- Constant within the period. Rain, ETP and runoff are one value per period and per cell. Recharge is a flux set from outside and does not read the water table.
- `"mean"` weights each period equally. On periods of unequal length, the steady rate is not the time mean of the record.
- The ETP is not read under MODFLOW 6 outside soil mode. A loaded ETP is ignored, with a warning.
- Aggregation by `last` exists for declared forcings only. The data layer always takes the mean.

**Path**: `simulation.time.coverage_policy`
**More**: A sample is the rate of the interval up to the next sample, and the last sample stands for one step of the record (the median spacing of its dates). A period that no sample reaches, before the first date or after the end of the last step, is not covered. 'error' stops the run, 'warn' warns once per record, 'ignore' says nothing; under 'warn' and 'ignore' the period takes the nearest sample in time. The rule is the same for a series, a station and a grid: rain, ETP, recharge, runoff and the declared CSV forcings read as rates (aggregate = 'mean').
**Values**:
- `"error"`
- `"warn"`
- `"ignore"`
**Accepted**: "error" | "warn" | "ignore"
**Example**: `"error"`, `"warn"`

[flow]

`# first_period_steady = true` : For transient flow, mark the first solver stress period as steady-state.
**Path**: `flow.first_period_steady`
**More**: Ignored for steady flow, where all solver periods are steady.
**Accepted**: true | false
**Example**: `true`, `false`

[flow.sinks_sources.recharge]

`# units = "mm/day"` : Unit of 'values' and of the recharge data source.
**Path**: `flow.sinks_sources.recharge.units`
**More**: Data-manager outputs use mm/day by convention; set it when you write 'values' in another unit. The run converts the rate to m/s.
**Accepted**: string
**Example**: `"mm/day"`, `"m/day"`, `"m/s"`

`# first_clim = "mean"` : Recharge rate of every steady stress period: every period of a steady run, and the first period of a transient run when flow.first_period_steady is true. dev
**Path**: `flow.sinks_sources.recharge.first_clim`
**More**: 'mean' is the mean of the per-period rates, one weight per period; 'first' is the rate of period 0; a number is that rate, in the units of values. A transient period keeps its own rate. The same rule holds for one value per period and for one grid per period, under every solver. With negative_to_evt, the steady period takes the rule on the recharge part and on the deficit part, so its net rate is the one stated here.
**See**: flow.first_period_steady
**Accepted**: string or number
**Example**: `"mean"`, `"first"`, `2.0`

`# negative_to_evt = true` : When true, negative recharge values are routed to the solver EVT package and RCH receives the non-negative clipped recharge. dev

**Accepted**: true | false

**Path**: `flow.sinks_sources.recharge.spatial_mode`

- `"homogeneous"`
- `"heterogeneous"`

`# interpolation_method = "nearest"` : Spatial interpolation method for gridded/point data onto the MODFLOW grid. dev
**Path**: `flow.sinks_sources.recharge.interpolation_method`
**More**: Options: 'nearest', 'linear', 'idw'.
**Values**:
- `"nearest"`
- `"linear"`
- `"idw"`
**Accepted**: "nearest" | "linear" | "idw"

**Path**: `flow.sinks_sources.etp.first_clim`
**More**: 'mean' is the mean of the per-period rates, one weight per period; 'first' is the rate of period 0; a number is that rate. A transient period keeps its own rate.

# The groundwater flow problem

What head does the aquifer hold, in every cell and at every time? This page gives the geometry HydroModPy builds for that head, the properties that enter it and the state it starts from. The flow equation itself is MODFLOW’s and is read at its source. For the same subject in plain words, see What the model computes. What each solver supports is listed in Solvers.

Note

Scope. Three solvers read the same `[flow]` section: MODFLOW 6 (the default), MODFLOW-NWT and the in-house Boussinesq solver. They solve the same physical problem and not the same discrete equations. The balance of the two MODFLOW solvers is in What the solvers solve. The Boussinesq form is on Boussinesq theory. What enters and leaves the aquifer (recharge, drains, streams, lakes, wells) has its own pages: Rain and evaporation: the forcing, The daily soil reservoir and How water leaves the aquifer. Where the one-layer reading stops being true is at the end of Limits.

## The domain

Two surfaces bound the aquifer.

The top \(z_\mathrm{top}\) is the digital elevation model of the catchment, read from `data.dem`. By default the grid takes the value of the DEM at the centre of each cell, and nothing else moves the top. `modflow6.sgrid.top_sampling.mode` can ask for a statistic over the pixels of the cell instead, with a lower value for the cells that hold a channel (5. The top of a cell).

The bottom \(z_\mathrm{bot}\) comes from a depth model, chosen by `domain.depth_model.kind`. Four kinds exist:

| Kind | Bottom | Reads |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `constant_thickness` | \(z_\mathrm{bot} = z_\mathrm{top} - H_c\) | `domain.depth_model.thickness` |
| `flat_substratum` | \(z_\mathrm{bot} = z_s\) | `domain.depth_model.substratum_elevation` |
| `raster_substratum` | \(z_\mathrm{bot} = \min\bigl(Z_r + \zeta,\ z_\mathrm{top} - H_\mathrm{min}\bigr)\) | the raster of `data.substratum`, in metres, on the datum of the DEM |
| `raster_thickness` | \(z_\mathrm{bot} = \min\bigl(z_\mathrm{top} - \lambda Z_r + \zeta,\ z_\mathrm{top} - H_\mathrm{min}\bigr)\) | the raster of `data.substratum`, in metres below the top |

A flat substratum is an elevation, not a depth: where the land surface drops under it, no aquifer is left. A raster kind:

1. reprojects the raster onto the grid of the top;
1. refuses the run if one cell of the domain has no raster value, so the raster must cover the whole extent of the domain, buffer included when `geographic.domain_extent` is `"box"`;
1. applies \(\lambda\) and \(\zeta\);
1. lowers the bottom to \(z_\mathrm{top} - H_\mathrm{min}\) wherever it would come closer to the top than that, and logs a warning that counts the cells;
1. refuses the run if every cell needs that correction, since no aquifer would remain.

Fig. 19 The four depth models on one valley, as `build_domain` returns them. Look at the valley floor of the two raster kinds: where the raster bottom (dotted) comes within \(H_\mathrm{min}\) of the top (8 m here), the cells (dots) are lowered to \(z_\mathrm{top} - H_\mathrm{min}\).

Take a top of 120 m everywhere and a raster that holds 40 m, or 85 m for the elevation kind, in every cell but one. The table gives the bottom of that cell, as `build_domain` returns it (the check ran the function).

| Depth model | Raster value | \(\zeta\), \(\lambda\) | Bottom |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `raster_thickness` | 40 m | 5 m, 1 | 85 m |
| `raster_thickness` | 40 m | 0 m, 2 | 40 m |
| `raster_thickness` | 0.5 m, with \(H_\mathrm{min} = 1\) m | 0 m, 1 | 119 m, with a warning |
| `raster_substratum` | 85 m | -5 m | 80 m |

A raster kind needs the raster. `data.substratum` takes exactly one source. A file that inherits a constant thickness removes it with `thickness__delete` when it switches to a raster ([domain], The grammar of a HydroModPy file).

The thickness of an aquifer is an assumption in this model, not a result. No equation below estimates it. The field of the constant thickness declares itself calibrable, in log space. In the code: `Domain._build_surfaces`.

## The solver grid and its layers

The grid samples \(z_\mathrm{top}\) and \(z_\mathrm{bot}\) at the centre of each cell (the cell layout is on The mesh). A cell with no finite value in either surface becomes inactive in every layer. The grid is refused when \(z_\mathrm{bot} \ge z_\mathrm{top}\) on a valid cell. On a runtime mesh, a warning names the columns thicker than 500 m and than 10 times the median: a raster nodata value read as an elevation produces them (8. The checks the code applies).

The thickness is then cut into \(n_\mathrm{lay}\) layers. The bottom of layer \(j\) is

(14)\[ z_{\mathrm{bot},j} = z_\mathrm{top} - H\,p_j , \qquad p_{n_\mathrm{lay}} = 1 . \]

The shares \(p_j\) are the same for every cell. Three rules build them, chosen by `modflow6.sgrid.vertical.genmtd_lay`:

| `genmtd_lay` | \(p_j\) |
| --- | --- |
| `constant` | \(j / n_\mathrm{lay}\) |
| `decay`, with \(\rho\) read from `modflow6.sgrid.vertical.lay_decay` | \((1 - \rho^{j}) / (1 - \rho^{n_\mathrm{lay}})\) |
| `list` | the running sum of `modflow6.sgrid.vertical.lay_proportions` |

The `decay` rule needs \(\rho > 1\), and the file is refused otherwise: the layers then thicken with depth. With \(\rho = 2\) and four layers they hold 1, 2, 4 and 8 fifteenths of the column, from the top down. A `list` must sum to 1. With one layer, \(p_1 = 1\) and the column is one cell. MODFLOW-NWT reads the same keys under `modflownwt.sgrid.vertical`.

Fig. 21 Four layers in a column of 100 m, from `_compute_layer_proportions`. Look at the decay columns: the larger \(\rho\), the thinner the top layer and the thicker the bottom one.

What the layers can represent. Every layer reuses the planar cells and their connections, and only the top and the bottom of the column vary from cell to cell. Geology therefore varies through the properties of each layer and cell (The properties), not through surfaces of its own. A stratigraphy whose interfaces cross the proportions, a layer that disappears, or a connection that changes from one layer to the next is not represented. MODFLOW 6 builds every grid, structured or not, as a vertex grid (`DISV`), never as `DISU`. The Boussinesq solver has no layers: it works on one triangle per column. In the code: `_compute_layer_proportions`.

## The properties

Each property is a field: one value for the whole domain, or one value per zone ([flow.param]). How a zone map becomes one value per cell is on From a zone map to the cells.

| Property | Needed by a steady run | Needed by a transient run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MODFLOW 6 and MODFLOW-NWT | \(K\) | \(K\), \(S_y\), \(S_s\) |
| Boussinesq | \(K\) | \(K\), \(S_y\) |

The Boussinesq solver reads no \(S_s\). In a steady MODFLOW run, a missing \(S_y\) or \(S_s\) is filled with zero. In a transient run, a missing one stops the run. Example 04 gives the three values, one for the whole catchment:

`flow.param.K.field.value in step4_transient.toml`

```
flow.param.K.field.value
  Hydraulic conductivity   m/s   valid 1e-14 .. 100
  Hydraulic conductivity of the K table, in m/s.
  form       number or "<n> m/s"
  default    not set
  calibrate  log, prior log_uniform
  only if    kind = "homogeneous"
  current    5e-05   set by step1_minimal.toml:52
```

`flow.param.Sy.field.value in step4_transient.toml`

```
flow.param.Sy.field.value
  Specific yield   -   valid 0.0001 .. 0.5
  Specific yield of the Sy table, dimensionless.
  form       number
  default    not set
  calibrate  log, prior log_uniform
  only if    kind = "homogeneous"
  current    0.05   set by step1_minimal.toml:58
```

`flow.param.Ss.field.value in step4_transient.toml`

```
flow.param.Ss.field.value
  Specific storage   1/m   valid 1e-12 .. 0.001
  Specific storage of the Ss table, in 1/m.
  form       number or "<n> 1/m"
  default    not set
  calibrate  log, prior log_uniform
  only if    kind = "homogeneous"
  current    1e-05   set by step4_transient.toml:27
```

A depth factor. A property can carry a `field_vertical_profile`. The value of layer \(j\) in a column is the value of the field times \(f(d_j)\), where \(d_j\) is the depth of the middle of the layer below \(z_\mathrm{top}\). For `mode = "exponential"`:

(15)\[ f(d) = e^{-d/d_c}, \qquad \text{or } \max\bigl(e^{-d/d_c},\ f_\mathrm{min}\bigr) \text{ when } f_\mathrm{min} \text{ is set.} \]

Without `min_factor`, the factor has no floor and tends to zero with depth. For `mode = "tabulated"`, the factor is a linear or stepwise interpolation of the table you give, equal to the first and last factor outside the table. With one layer, \(d_j\) is half the thickness: the profile then gives one factor per cell and no variation with depth.

Fig. 23 The depth factor for \(d_c = 20\) m, from `FieldParam.vertical_factor`. Each layer of a four-layer decay column takes the factor at its centre (dots), not an average over its thickness. Look at the deepest layer: without a floor its factor would be 0.03, with \(f_\mathrm{min} = 0.05\) it stays at 0.05.

Vertical conductivity. MODFLOW 6 reads \(K_z = K / \beta\), with \(\beta\) the `modflow6.process_specific.vka`, layer by layer, so a depth factor on \(K\) reaches \(K_z\). A parameter with the id `Kv` replaces it with a conductivity per cell, and a file that gives `Kv` and a `vka` other than 1 is refused.

The code refuses a \(K\) that is zero, negative or not finite on an active cell. A heterogeneous \(K\) whose zones do not cover the whole domain produces exactly that. In the code: `FieldParam.vertical_factor`.

## What the solvers solve

MODFLOW 6 and MODFLOW-NWT write Darcy’s law and mass conservation for the head in each cell, by control volumes, with one head per cell at its centre [Harbaugh, 2005, Langevin et al., 2017]; chapter 2 of Langevin et al. [2017] gives the control-volume form. The derivation is not repeated here. Three pieces of it are used by other pages of this site, so they are written once.

In a catchment the aquifer is mostly unconfined. The head can sit below the top of a cell, and then the thickness that carries flow is the saturated thickness

(16)\[ B(h) = \min\bigl(\max(h - z_\mathrm{bot},\ 0),\ H\bigr) . \]

For a cell \(n\), the balance of one time step is

(17)\[ \sum_{m \in \mathcal{N}(n)} G_{nm}\,(h_m - h_n) + \sum_{p} \Phi_{n,p} = \frac{1}{\delta t}\Bigl[\,S_s\,a_n\,B_n\,(h_n - h_n^\mathrm{old}) + S_y\,a_n\,(B_n - B_n^\mathrm{old})\Bigr] . \]

The left side is the water that enters the cell during the step: the exchange with the neighbours and the stress packages. The right side is the change of the volume stored. \(h^\mathrm{old}\) is the head at the start of the step. This is the one statement of the balance on the site; the solver pages refer to it. Between two cells of a layer, the conductance joins the two half cells in series:

(18)\[ \frac{1}{G_{nm}} = \frac{c_{nm}}{K_n\,B_n\,w_{nm}} + \frac{c_{mn}}{K_m\,B_m\,w_{nm}} , \]

with \(w_{nm}\) the width of the shared face and \(c_{nm}\) the distance from the centre of \(n\) to that face. Under the Newton formulation, the series is built with the full cell thicknesses and multiplied by the saturated fraction of the upstream cell ([Langevin et al., 2017]).

What HydroModPy sets:

- Every cell is convertible. `icelltype = 1` in the MODFLOW 6 `NPF` package, `iconvert = 1` in `STO`, `laytyp = 1` in the MODFLOW-NWT `UPW` package. The specific yield \(S_y\) acts while the water table is inside the cell, and \(S_s\) above the top of a full cell. In example 04, \(S_y = 0.05\) and \(S_s B \le 3 \times 10^{-4}\), a ratio of about 170.
- No `CELL_AVERAGING` option. The series average of the equation above is the MODFLOW 6 default.
- Newton, with under-relaxation, by default. MODFLOW-NWT is the Newton formulation of MODFLOW-2005 [Niswonger et al., 2011], on the same convertible layers and a structured grid. The options and the stopping tests are on The solution: Newton and IMS.
- Voronoi faces bisect the centres. That is the case the two-point form of (18) needs. Elsewhere, the XT3D correction is on XT3D on irregular meshes.
- The Boussinesq solver writes the same balance on triangles. Its edge flux takes the harmonic mean of \(K\) and the arithmetic mean of \(B\) of the two cells, and its storage has no \(S_s\). See Boussinesq theory.

The smoothing of \(B\) near the bottom of a cell is on The solvers of the aquifer.

## Time

The run is cut into stress periods of length \(\Delta t\), one per forcing value (Rain and evaporation: the forcing). Within a period the forcing is constant. Each period is cut into \(n_\mathrm{sub}\) equal time steps \(\delta t = \Delta t / n_\mathrm{sub}\), and the time integration is the backward Euler scheme of [Langevin et al., 2017]: (17) is written with the stress and the conductances at the end of the step. The time step multiplier is 1, so the steps of a period are equal. The one exception is `modflow6.runtime.mf6_ats`: with it, MODFLOW 6 may cut a transient step further where the solver does not converge, never above the step asked for. The Boussinesq solver takes one step per period.

[simulation.time]

`# step_value = "1 month"` : Forcing/stress-period time-step scalar or inline token '<value> <unit>' (for example '30 day').
**Path**: `simulation.time.step_value`
**More**: This controls the temporal aggregation step for forcing series (for example recharge/runoff) and the resulting stress periods. Not read by a steady run (flow.flow_regime = 'steady'), which is one stress period over the whole window, its forcings averaged over it.
**Accepted**: integer or number or string
**Example**: `"1 month"`, `"10 day"`

`# substeps_per_period = 1` : Number of solver time steps within each stress period, the one knob that buys transient accuracy. >= 1 dev
**Path**: `simulation.time.substeps_per_period`
**More**: The default of 1 integrates a whole period in a single backward-Euler step, which is not a neutral choice: on a seasonally recharged hillslope drained by DRN cells it moves the monthly discharge by 4 to 28 % against a refined run, across the whole plausible bedrock range, and a calibration scored on discharge absorbs that into the fitted parameters. The right count compares the aquifer response time `tau = L^2 S / (K b)` with the period length, and the solver cost is linear in it; 30 gives daily steps inside monthly periods. Consumed by the MODFLOW backends as DIS NSTP / TDIS nstp, and by the Boussinesq backend, which solves each period in as many backward-Euler steps of equal length. Every solver stores one result per period: the head at the end of the period and each flux as the mean of its steps, weighted by their length.
**Accepted**: integer
**Valid range**: >= 1 (refused outside)

Lines generated from the models, as in the reference. Open one for its card.

The solver time step is a numerical choice: a period solved in one step differs from the same period in several. Time steps gives the size of that difference on a test case.

`flow.flow_regime` picks the regime. A `steady` run is one steady period over the whole `[simulation.time]` window, whatever step the file writes. In a `transient` run, `flow.first_period_steady` marks the first period as steady, in the three solvers. In a steady period the right side of the balance is zero, the storage plays no part, and the heads settle where the forcing of that period puts them. Example 04 states the regime:

`flow.flow_regime in step4_transient.toml`

```
flow.flow_regime
  Whether the flow is solved as one equilibrium state or through time over the stress
  periods of [simulation.time].
  form       "steady" | "transient"
  default    "transient"
  value      "steady"  Solves one equilibrium state, with no storage term: one stress period over the whole [simulation.time] window, whatever its step_value says, with the forcings averaged over the window.
  value      "transient"  Solves the heads through time; it starts from the state [flow.ic] gives.
  current    "transient"   set by step4_transient.toml:20
```

In the code: `sto_period_settings`.

## The starting heads

The head at the start of the run, \(h_0\), is declared in the flat table `[flow.ic]`. Its value is the same in every layer of a column. `bottom` is the bottom of the deepest layer.

| `type` | \(h_0\) |
| --- | --- |
| `top` | \(z_\mathrm{top}\) |
| `top_offset` | \(z_\mathrm{top} - v\), with \(v\) the `value` |
| `bottom` | \(z_{\mathrm{bot},n_\mathrm{lay}}\) |
| `custom` | \(v\) |
| `steady_state` | the solution \(h^\star\) of the steady problem under a constant recharge, see below |
| `spinup_cyclic` | the state a cyclic run settles at, see below |

In every case, a cell on an imposed head (an ocean, a stream or a side boundary) starts at that head. `top` is a full aquifer; the card of `flow.ic.h.type` gives the default.

The equilibrium. For `steady_state`, the code first solves an auxiliary steady problem with the same solver, the same grid and the same properties. Its recharge is a constant, set by `flow.ic.h.source`: the mean of the whole record, or the rate that you state. The result is \(h_0\):

\[ \nabla\!\cdot\!\bigl(K\,B(h^\star)\,\nabla h^\star\bigr) + \bar N + q_\mathrm{bc}(h^\star) = 0 , \qquad h_0 = h^\star , \]

where \(\bar N\) is the constant recharge and \(q_\mathrm{bc}\) the exchanges with the boundaries per unit area, held at the value of the first period (`flow.ic.h.boundary_condition_policy`).

The settled cycle. For `spinup_cyclic`, the run repeats its own period. Cycle \(c + 1\) starts from the heads where cycle \(c\) ended, \(h_\mathrm{end}^{(c)}\), and the first cycle starts from `flow.ic.h.first_cycle_from`. The loop stops when

(19)\[ \max_n \bigl|\,h^{(c+1)}_{\mathrm{end},n} - h^{(c)}_{\mathrm{end},n}\,\bigr| \le \varepsilon_h , \]

with \(\varepsilon_h\) the `flow.ic.h.tol_head`, or after `flow.ic.h.max_cycles` cycles. The maximum counts every cell, not the mean.

Fig. 25 The stopping test of (19), applied by `cycles_have_settled` to 200 cells of which 10 drift slowly. Look at the two curves: the mean change falls under \(\varepsilon_h\) at cycle 6, the largest change only at cycle 10, and the largest change decides. With the default of 4 cycles, this loop would stop before it settles.

When the first period is steady. With `flow.first_period_steady` at its default, period 0 is solved as a steady state, and the heads above are only the first guess of that solve. They change the convergence and not the state reached. To make the run start from a state you choose, set it to `false` (see [flow.ic]).

A run can also restart from the last time step of an earlier run (`flow.restart_from`). That state replaces \(h_0\). In the code: `build_head_initial_condition_array`.

## What enters and leaves

The stress terms \(\Phi_{n,p}\) of the balance come from packages. Each one has its page.

| Term | MODFLOW 6 package | Page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recharge \(N\) | `RCHA` | Rain and evaporation: the forcing, The daily soil reservoir |
| Evapotranspiration that the soil did not meet, or a negative recharge routed to evaporation | `EVTA` | The daily soil reservoir, Rain and evaporation: the forcing |
| Drainage at the land surface | `DRN` | How water leaves the aquifer |
| Imposed heads: ocean, stream, sides | `CHD` | How water leaves the aquifer |
| Wells | `WEL` | How water leaves the aquifer |
| Stream reaches, lakes, flow barriers, water transfers | `SFR`, `LAK`, `HFB`, `MVR` | How water leaves the aquifer |

Recharge and injection are positive when water enters the aquifer, and a well with a negative rate pumps. Where no boundary is activated, the edge of the domain carries no flow. The two keys that activate them are `flow.active_bc` and `flow.active_sinks_sources`.

## Limits

- Shallow and unconfined. Every cell is convertible. The code is built for the saturated zone of a catchment, from the surface down to a substratum that you place. The thickness is chosen, not computed.
- No unsaturated flow. The code builds no `UZF` package. The water that reaches the water table is a recharge, given or computed by the daily soil store of The daily soil reservoir.
- No density-dependent flow, no compaction, no delayed yield. The code builds neither a `BUY` nor a `CSUB` package, and the specific yield releases its water at once.
- Constant forcing, impervious edges. The forcing is constant over a stress period. The bottom and the sides of the domain are impervious, except where a boundary is activated.
- A bottom above the top is refused. So is a bottom that equals it, and a raster that leaves one cell without a value.
- Layers cannot pinch out. They share one rule of proportions, and the thickness cannot fall below \(H_\mathrm{min}\) with a raster kind.
- Boussinesq has one layer and no \(S_s\). It reads \(K\) and \(S_y\) only.
- Newton and rewetting exclude each other in MODFLOW 6.
- A steady first period is refused with the soil reservoir. The reservoir sends a daily recharge that is zero after a dry day, and a one-period steady state would start the run from a drained aquifer.
- Each solver has its own boundaries. What each solver supports is listed in Solvers, and the file is refused when the solver cannot carry a boundary it asks for.

### Where the one-layer reading stops

A model with one layer, and the Boussinesq solver always, are Dupuit by construction: the flow is horizontal and the head does not vary with depth [Brutsaert, 2005, Dupuit, 1863]. Over a flow path of length \(L_h\) through a saturated thickness \(B\), the vertical head difference against the horizontal one scales as \(\beta\,(B / L_h)^2\), an order of magnitude without prefactor. With \(B = 30\) m and \(\beta = 10\), that is 0.036 under hillslopes of 500 m and 0.9 under hillslopes of 100 m, where Dupuit no longer holds. Within about \(B\sqrt{\beta}\) of a stream (100 m here, one or two cells of a 75 m grid), the flow converges and bends upwards. A one-layer model leaves that resistance to the conductance of the drain or of the stream cell (How water leaves the aquifer).

The water table follows the topography, and the drains carry much of the outflow, when the criterion of Haitjema and Mitchell-Bruker [2005] exceeds 1. It compares the recharge, times the squared distance between streams, with the conductivity, the thickness and the largest rise of the land above the streams, and it assumes a uniform recharge and thickness. Below 1, the drains act along the streams only.

HydroModPy has no seepage face below the top of a cell. The drains of the top layer and the surface closures of the Boussinesq solver take the water at the cell top, and a stream imposed as a head fixes the head of the whole cell. With `modflow6.sgrid.vertical.nlay` above 1 and a ratio `modflow6.process_specific.vka`, MODFLOW 6 and MODFLOW-NWT carry one head per layer, so the vertical resistance enters the solution. The code computes none of these ratios and refuses no model for its aspect ratio. A depth factor ((15)) shortens the effective thickness.
